$comment: Subsystem file: petrochemical / polymer chains. Branch roots chem.crude, chem.natural-gas, chem.refining, chem.ethylene, chem.propylene, chem.acrylonitrile, chem.butadiene, chem.styrene, chem.abs, chem.solvents, chem.fab-chemicals, chem.pcb-chemicals, chem.solder-chemicals. Cross-branch links use the id-ref form of 'children'.

chem.ethylene.monomer.name: Ethylene monomer
chem.ethylene.monomer.description: Ethene (C2H4), the simplest alkene: a colourless flammable gas made by steam cracking ethane, naphtha or gas oil at 750-950 C, then quenched, compressed, dried and purified to polymer grade. The highest-volume organic chemical in the world; the C64's polyethylene, PVC, polystyrene and PET chains all begin here.

facts.label: Polymer grade
facts.value: dry, under 1 ppmv water and oxygen

chem.ethylene.monomer.note: Not established: 1983 tonnages and the feedstock split for the ethylene actually polymerised into the C64's plastics.

chem.petroleum.name: Petroleum: light sour crude oil
chem.petroleum.description: The dig-it-out endpoint of the whole petrochemical chain. Crude is a mixture of thousands of hydrocarbons from methane to asphaltenes, plus sulphur compounds, nitrogen compounds, resins, asphaltenes and trace metals. The grades that feed the 1980s steam crackers are light, low-sulphur: Arab Light at 35-36 degrees API and Brent Blend at 38-39 were the benchmarks of the era.
inputs: organic matter buried in marine shale

facts.label: Arab Light (Saudi), 1983 assay
facts.value: 35.0-36.0 deg API, 0.9-1.5 wt% S, ~2.2 wt% S (typical)

facts.label: Mass of C64 case in crude
facts.value: about 1-3 litres of crude oil per machine (plastic + energy)

chem.petroleum.note: Saudi Light at 38-39 API is the classic light sour grade; Arab Light (35-36 API) is the heavier sour crude that historically dominated Saudi exports. Assay figures vary by stream and year. A barrel of crude is a bulk hydrocarbon stream, not a power-generation one, so it is a fluid rather than energy. This is the commodity the whole petrochemical trunk consumes, and other branches reference it as an ingredient.

chem.natural-gas.name: Natural gas: the gas field
chem.natural-gas.description: Methane, mostly: either the gas cap sitting on an oil reservoir or a gas-only field. In 1983 world gas production was roughly 2.9-3.0 trillion cubic metres a year, of which about 70% was still associated with oil and much of it was flared or burned at the wellhead. Gas matters to a C64 three ways: as acetylene for PVC and chlorinated solvents, as hydrogen for ammonia and hydrochloric acid, and as the fuel that moved the plastics.

children.name: What natural gas is
children.description: A mixture, not a compound. A sour gas well may deliver methane with 2-10% ethane and propane, 1-8% C4, 1-20% hydrogen sulphide, 0.5-5% carbon dioxide and up to 15% nitrogen. Everything downstream - the pipelines, the dew point specification, the hydrogen plant - is set by those five impurities.
children.note: Methane, ethane and propane, nitrogen and hydrogen sulphide hang directly off the gas field. Established: Natural gas mixture with methane plus ethane propane nitrogen and hydrogen sulphide. Not established: the stated percentage ranges and downstream specification details as given.

children.name: Where the gas comes from
children.description: Associated gas from the gas cap of an oil reservoir, and non-associated (gas-only) gas. The distinction matters industrially: associated gas was a by-product that had to be flared or reinjected until the late 1970s made it commercial, while gas-only fields carry the pipelines and the LNG trains.
children.note: Associated gas, the gas-only field, the gas reservoir and the gas hydrate hang directly off the gas field. Established: Associated versus gas only sourcing distinction. Not established: the era specific commerciality flaring and reinjection histories as given.

children.name: What the gas is for
children.description: Three jobs in 1983: burn it, crack it, or reform it. Burning dominated volume; the petrochemical jobs - acetylene, hydrogen, ammonia - were small in tonnage but disproportionate in value, and they are the reason the polymer industry existed at all. The largest single use of gas is plain combustion: boilers, industrial furnaces and gas turbines. A 40-100 MW gas turbine of the 1980s fired gas at 15-25 bar through a dual-fuel combustor, and a gas-fired polyethylene furnace ran 10-30% excess oxygen.
children.note: Acetylene, hydrogen, fuel and fertiliser ammonia hang directly off the gas field. Established: Gas uses for burning cracking and reforming with small high value petrochemical share. Not established: the stated volume versus value splits as given.

children.name: Non-associated (gas-only) field
children.description: A gas reservoir with no oil at the contact. The North Sea fields of the late 1970s - Frigg (1977), Heimdal, Sleipner, Troll (discovered 1979) - turned Europe from an import market into a gas market, and the Norwegian and British gas grids of the early 1980s were built around them. In the US the equivalent discovery was the tight and geopressured gas of the Anadarko and Rocky Mountain basins. Tight low-permeability sandstone and coalbed methane had to be stimulated rather than merely completed, with the oil branch's massive hydraulic fracturing and with dewatering for coal seams; in 1983 tight gas was a real but small share of US supply.
children.note: A gas field is a place that is worked, not an operation. Gas and oil extraction is industry, and the energy category is reserved for power generation and the grid. Established: Gas only field as worked place with industry categorisation. Not established: the stated North Sea field dates and grid histories as given.

chem.natural-gas.note: This is the shared commodity node, reaching the tree as a from ingredient. Established: Natural gas as methane rich fossil gas from associated and gas only fields. Not established: the stated 1983 production volumes flaring shares and field specific histories as given.

chem.refining.name: Refining: turning crude into fuels and feedstocks
chem.refining.description: Atmospheric and vacuum distillation to cut crude into fractions, then conversion and upgrading processes to make the specific products industry wants. For the C64 the interesting products are not the fuels but the naphtha that gets steam-cracked to ethylene, the benzene for styrene, the LPG for crackers, and the elemental sulphur recovered from hydrogen sulphide. In 1983 world refining capacity was roughly 65-70 million barrels a day, about 30% above demand, and the industry was running at 65-75% utilisation.

children.name: The refining industry in 1983
children.description: Around 750-850 refineries existed worldwide, of which more than 300 were in the United States alone (US capacity about 19 million bbl/d). The largest refining regions in 1983 were the US Gulf Coast, the US Midwest, Western Europe (Rotterdam, Antwerp, Fos-sur-Mer), the Caribbean (USVI, Curaçao), Japan and Singapore, and the Middle East (Ras Tanura, Ruwais, Kuwait). About 3-5% of the crude throughput was burned as refinery fuel gas.
children.note: Refinery counts and capacities are approximate; the 1983 figures bracket a decade-long plateau in OECD capacity. The refinery count and capacity figures are commentary about the industry, not a substance.

children.name: Atmospheric distillation
children.description: Fractional distillation of crude at atmospheric pressure in a 35-50 m fractionating tower, separating a barrel of crude into naphtha, kerosene, gas oil, and a 700 F residue. It is the first process every molecule of the polymer industry passes through, and it is where the difference between a 30 and a 40 degree API crude turns into a 200 versus 260 dollar a tonne cracker feedstock. The naphtha overhead is where refinery corrosion happens: water condenses out of the vapour, dissolves the HCl that came in with the crude brine and dissolves H2S into very aggressive sulphuric acid, and 1980s practice attacked it with an ammonia or amine neutraliser injected into the overhead condenser plus a wash-water draw.

children.name: Crude preheat train
children.description: A train of shell-and-tube exchangers that takes crude from ambient to 220-300 C by recovering heat from every hot stream in the refinery, then the fired heater takes it the rest of the way to 350-370 C. Preheating was the classic refinery heat-integration project: a crude preheat train alone recovers tens of megawatts and pays for itself in fuel. Everything in the refinery hotter than crude - coker bottoms gas, FCC slurry oil, diesel bottoms, hot water - fouls one exchanger in the hundred, and the 1980s counter-measures were a deliberately high shell-side velocity, online cleaning with a pigging system and, in a few cases, a differential-pressure monitor as a leading indicator.

children.name: Fired crude heater
children.description: A radiant box furnace with 150-400 coils of cast alloy or wrought-alloy tube (Cr-Mo, 5 in outside diameter, 0.3 m apart), firing gas at 30-80 MW. Tube metallurgy matters: the coil sees a 30-40 C metal temperature above the oil temperature, and the 1980s move to coiled tubing and to higher radiant efficiency cut fuel use several percent.
children.note: Coil counts and duty vary widely by refinery; these are typical 1980s figures.

Fouling monitoring practice varies; the mechanisms described are standard. Established: Crude preheat train with heat recovery to fired heater temperatures. Not established: the stated temperature ranges and integration specifics as given.

children.name: Fractionating tower
children.description: A 35-50 m column with 40-50 trays, at about 1.1-1.5 bar overhead and 2.5-3 bar at the bottom, condensing a vapour-liquid staircase in which each tray separates hydrocarbons by boiling range. A large atmospheric tower is a pressure vessel of 100-200 tonnes, and it is still the cheapest separation device ever built per tonne of product. A modern valve tray is 70-90% efficient against an ideal stage and the tower needs enough reflux (a few per cent of the feed) to wet the trays; cutting reflux to save furnace duty is the classic operating trade and it costs separation.

children.name: Distillation trays
children.description: Valve, sieve, bubble-cap or proprietary proprietary-type trays at 0.4-0.6 m spacing. In 1980s practice a new refinery would install valve or sieve trays, and an old one would often be kept and given a new tray-packing section on the vacuum side.
children.note: Tray packing on the atmospheric side was rare in the 1980s; structured packing arrived mainly on vacuum columns and on hydrotreaters.

children.name: Reboilers and side strippers
children.description: A fired or steam reboiler supplies the vapour to the bottom of the tower, and side strippers remove the light ends from the kerosene and gas-oil draws so the side columns are not loaded with vapour. Kerosene is stripped with a few hundred kPa of steam; diesel often went straight to the bottom because the vacuum column handled its light ends.
children.note: Established: A fired or steam reboiler supplies the vapour to the bottom of the tower, and side strippers remove the light ends from the kerosene and gas-oil draws so the side columns are not l as standard practice. Not established: the era specific prevalence supplier choices and detailed operating splits as given.

children.name: Overhead condenser and gas recovery
children.description: The naphtha overhead is condensed in a shell-and-tube condenser with a reflux drum, and the non-condensable gas (methane, ethane, hydrogen, H2S) goes off to the fuel gas header. In 1980s practice the gas was usually simply burned, although the recovery unit for ethane and propane (an absorber) was standard in complex refineries because it paid for itself. In complex refineries an absorber or a deethaniser-absorber recovered 60-90% of the ethane and propane from the fuel gas before it was burnt, and that recovered propane and butane is the LPG which feeds the crackers.
children.note: LPG endpoint: chem.natural-gas.composition.ethane-propane. Established: Overhead condenser with reflux and fuel gas recovery. Not established: the stated burning versus recovery practices as 1980s standard as given.

Established: A 35-50 m column with 40-50 trays, at about 1.1-1.5 bar overhead and 2.5-3 bar at the bottom, condensing a vapour-liquid staircase in which each tray separates hydrocarbons by boil as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Vacuum distillation
children.description: A second column at 25-50 mmHg absolute (740-760 mmHg vacuum) that distils the 700 F plus residue down to a vacuum gas oil and a vacuum residue of 2-5% of the crude, without cracking it. Lowering the pressure raises the boiling points' relative spacing so heavy molecules can be distilled instead of decomposed, and the vacuum is made by steam ejectors or by a barometric leg. Below about 350 C the residue cracks rather than distils, so the flash zone is run at 340-370 C and the vacuum gas oil carries some cracked material; the side reactions make coke and acids, which is why the column needs wash sections and anti-fouling coatings.

children.name: Steam ejectors and vacuum
children.description: Three-stage steam ejectors holding 25-50 mmHg, using 10-25 t of steam per hour for a mid-size unit. Ejectors are simple but they cost a lot of steam; by the 1980s mechanical vacuum pumps (rotary or liquid-ring, with a surface condenser) were being installed to save that steam, and most plants still had ejectors as backup.
children.note: Not established: the vacuum level and steam-consumption ranges quoted for three-stage ejectors, and how far mechanical vacuum pumps had displaced ejectors by the early 1980s.

Established: A second column at 25-50 mmHg absolute (740-760 mmHg vacuum) that distils the 700 F plus residue down to a vacuum gas oil and a vacuum residue of 2-5% of the crude, without crackin as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

facts.label: Typical naphthenic acid index
facts.value: 1-3 mg KOH/g for Arabian heavy crude

children.note: Total acid number values are crude-specific and the threshold for accelerated attack is generally quoted as above about 2 mg KOH/g at the column temperature. Established: Atmospheric distillation as first crude fractionation with overhead corrosion control. Not established: the stated tower heights residue cut points and neutraliser specifics as given.

children.name: Converting the vacuum residue
children.description: The 2-5% of crude that will not distil is the hardest material in the refinery. It must be converted - into coke, into gasoline, or into distillate - or it is sold as fuel oil. This is where the refinery's biggest single units and its biggest capital decisions sit. Hydrocracking cracked heavy oil and hydrogenated the fragments in one step at 350-450 C and 80-200 bar of hydrogen over cobalt-molybdenum or nickel-molybdenum on alumina, giving 70-90% diesel with almost no sulphur - the process that let a refinery make diesel rather than fuel oil.

children.name: Delayed coking
children.description: Vacuum residue is heated to 350-400 C and held in large coke drums for 12-24 hours, during which it cracks to 15-25% petroleum coke while the vapours are continuously drawn off and fractionated. Delayed coking was the dominant residue conversion process of the 1960s and remained so through the 1980s, handling maybe 40-50% of vacuum residue in a complex refinery, largely because it makes the anode-grade coke the aluminium industry needs.

children.name: Coke drum
children.description: A 6-11 m diameter vessel 20-35 m tall holding 100-400 tonnes of coke per cycle, switched in parallel with a fractionator overhead. Switching a drum is the highest-risk operation in a refinery: the drum is water-quenched and de-coked with a full-diameter drill and coke cutter while the neighbouring drum runs at temperature.
children.note: Not established: the vessel dimensions, coke tonnage per cycle, yield range and cycle time quoted, and the characterisation of drum switching as the highest-risk refinery operation.

Established: Vacuum residue is heated to 350-400 C and held in large coke drums for 12-24 hours, during which it cracks to 15-25% petroleum coke while the vapours are continuously drawn off and as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Fluid catalytic cracking
children.description: Vacuum gas oil is contacted with a zeolite catalyst at 500-530 C and 1-3 bar in a riser, cracked into gasoline, light ends and coke, and the catalyst is continuously regenerated in a fluidised-bed regenerator at 650-750 C. FCC was the largest refinery process by capacity in the early 1980s - a large unit processing 40,000-100,000 bbl/d - and the source of most of the world's leaded-free gasoline blending components and of the propylene that fed the older chemical crackers.

children.name: Riser and regenerator
children.description: The riser reactor is a vertical pipe 10-20 m long with the catalyst and feed entering at the bottom; the cyclone separators strip entrained catalyst back; the regenerator burns the coke off the catalyst with air. A 1980s unit's two-stage regeneration was the standard answer to how to get more heat into the reactor while cutting carbon monoxide from the stack.
children.note: Not established: the reactor and regenerator temperature, pressure and yield figures quoted, and the claim that two-stage regeneration was standard 1980s practice.

Established: fluid catalytic cracking converts high boiling vacuum gas oil into gasoline alkenes and other products with zeolite catalyst and continuous regeneration. Not established: the stated tonnages dates temperatures pressures yields and 1980s operating details as given.

Established: The 2-5% of crude that will not distil is the hardest material in the refinery as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Hydrotreating and desulphurisation
children.description: The refinery's chemistry of taking things out: sulphur, nitrogen, oxygen and metals, plus saturation. It is the answer to sour crude, and it is the process that made Arab Light and Mexican crudes usable in 1980s refineries. It also produces the acid gas from which elemental sulphur is recovered. Naphtha hydrotreating at 300-400 C and 20-50 bar of hydrogen over cobalt-molybdenum on alumina to 0.2-0.5 wt% sulphur is the pretreatment that makes a crude usable in a cracker. Gas oil was hydrodesulphurised at 300-400 C and 30-80 bar over Co-Mo or Ni-Mo to 0.1-0.3 wt% S, with a 0.05 wt% deep-desulphurisation variant developed in the late 1970s for the 1990 fuel specifications; every barrel desulphurised is a barrel of fuel oil turned into saleable middle distillate. Jet kerosene has to be under 3 wt% sulphur and free of water, because it passes through a turbine at 800-1,000 C with water condensing in the fuel-oil nozzles, so the kero hydrotreater runs at 300-400 C and 30-50 bar and carries a naphthenic acid problem of its own.
children.note: Established: The refinerys chemistry of taking things out: sulphur, nitrogen, oxygen and metals, plus saturation as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Claus process: recovering elemental sulphur
children.description: Three-quarters of a mole of oxygen is used to burn a third of the hydrogen sulphide to sulphur dioxide, then the two react over an alumina catalyst to make sulphur and water: 2 H2S + SO2 -> 3 S + 2 H2O. The Claus unit turns the refinery's or gas plant's worst stream into a saleable commodity, and its output is the elemental sulphur that the whole 1980s chemical industry - rubber vulcanisation, fungicides, sulphuric acid - depended on. The Canadian oil sands' sulphur problem and the Arabian gas sweetening builds both exist because of this unit.

children.name: Claus furnace
children.description: A refractory-lined furnace at 250-400 C where a third of the H2S is burned with oxygen or air. The burn has to be kept on the rich side: too much oxygen and the H2S is oxidised all the way to SO2, which wastes the sulphur; too little and soot forms and plugs the catalyst.
children.note: Not established: the furnace temperature range and first-stage conversion figures quoted, and the operating claims about rich-side firing, oxygen excess and soot plugging.

Established: the Claus unit recovers elemental sulphur from hydrogen sulphide acid gas for refineries and gas plants. Not established: the stated tonnages dates temperatures pressures yields and 1980s operating details as given.

children.name: Catalytic reforming and the aromatics complex
children.description: Reforming naphtha over platinum at 500-540 C and 15-30 bar converts paraffins and naphthenes into aromatics, releasing about 0.2-0.3 tonnes of hydrogen per tonne of feed and upgrading the octane number. It is where the world's benzene comes from, and therefore where the styrene in the C64's ABS comes from. Platforming (UOP, 1943) is the process that made the aromatised gasoline era possible: naphtha from C5 to about 220 C over 0.3-0.4 wt% platinum and rhenium on chlorided alumina at 500-540 C and 15-30 bar with an H2/hydrocarbon ratio of 5-6. The benzene plant extracts the C6 aromatics from the reformer effluent, separates benzene, toluene and the C8 isomers and hydrogenates the xylenes back to benzene, because a tonne of xylene is worth less than a tonne of benzene. Deactivated catalyst was shipped out and the platinum, rhenium and gallium recovered by chlorination, aqua regia dissolution and solvent extraction, which also disposed of the refinery's radioactive coke from the feed's radium.

facts.label: Benzene in reformer feed
facts.value: 2-5% of naphtha when run for octane, up to ~50% when run for aromatics

children.note: Established: catalytic reforming converts naphtha paraffins and naphthenes into high octane aromatics plus byproduct hydrogen for hydrocracking and desulphurisation. Not established: the stated tonnages dates temperatures pressures yields and 1980s operating details as given.

children.name: Isomerisation and octane boosting
children.description: The C5 and C6 straight-chain paraffins in naphtha have terrible octane numbers; isomerising them to the branched isomers does something about that with almost no yield loss. This is the cheap half of the unleaded-gasoline story; MTBE and alkylate were the expensive half. C5/C6 isomerisation over platinum on chlorided alumina, or from the 1980s a zeolite unit at 250-350 C with an aromatics-rich recycle, yields 98-99% and buys 8-12 octane numbers - trivial per barrel, material at a million barrels a day. Alkylate is isobutane plus isobutylene or propylene over anhydrous HF at 20-40 C, and HF alkylation was a large and dangerous business in 1980s practice: an HF cloud is dense, water-soluble and burns deeply, so the units had their own HF storage and a dedicated water curtain.

children.name: MTBE (methyl tert-butyl ether)
children.description: Methanol plus isobutylene over an acidic ion-exchange resin (Amberlyst, sulphonic acid polystyrene, about 100 C, 5-10 bar), giving a 100+ octane component. MTBE was the big gasoline technology story of the late 1970s and early 1980s in the United States, and its feedstock - isobutylene - came from the crackers and the FCC, which is the direct petrochemical link: the same C4 that becomes butadiene rubber becomes the octane booster in American petrol.
children.note: Established: Methanol plus isobutylene over an acidic ion-exchange resin (Amberlyst, sulphonic acid polystyrene, about 100 C, 5-10 bar), giving a 100+ octane component as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

Established: The C5 and C6 straight-chain paraffins in naphtha have terrible octane numbers, isomerising them to the branched isomers does something about that with almost no yield loss as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Lead phase-down and the unleaded problem
children.description: Tetraethyl lead was phased out of most industrialised markets between 1978 and 1985 as catalytic converters spread. The lead phase-down is the single most consequential fuel specification change of the decade and it is the reason MTBE, alkylate, isomerate and the ZSM-5 additive were all developed on that timescale. Without lead the refiner needed 3-8 octane numbers from somewhere, and in 1983 the United States solved it with MTBE, ZSM-5 and alkylate while Europe, with a smaller and cleaner car fleet, was much less short - which is why MTBE uptake was overwhelmingly American.
children.note: Established: Tetraethyl lead was phased out of most industrialised markets between 1978 and 1985 as catalytic converters spread as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Refinery products and by-products
children.description: Fuels, lubricants, waxes, coke and sulphur. For this tree the interesting list is short: naphtha to the crackers, benzene to styrene, LPG to crackers, propylene and butylene to the older chemical plants, and sulphur to rubber and to sulphuric acid.
children.note: Refinery products and by-products is a heading for the three streams beneath it rather than a substance of its own. Lubricant base oils, waxes and fuel oil remain as nodes. Established: Refinery products list for naphtha benzene LPG olefins and sulphur. Not established: the stated routing to crackers and acid plants as given.

children.name: Refinery to polymer: the handover
children.description: Three handovers matter. Naphtha plus steam into a cracker gives ethylene and propylene. C4 from the same cracker gives butadiene and isobutylene. Reformer naphtha into the aromatics complex gives benzene, which with ethylene gives styrene. This node is the place where the fuel industry stops and the polymer industry starts, and it is the join that makes a C64 physically possible. The cracker hands over a C4 stream of 1-butene, the 2-butenes and isobutylene, and extracting the butadiene out of it is a second plant; the isobutylene left behind goes to MTBE or alkylate and the butenes go to hydroformylation for plasticisers. Benzene out of the aromatics complex is alkylated with ethylene in excess benzene (to suppress diethylbenzene) to give ethylbenzene, which is then dehydrogenated.

children.name: Naphtha to ethylene
children.description: The handover. Naphtha plus steam at 800-900 C over a cast alloy coil, giving 25-35% ethylene by weight with propylene, butenes and a benzene-rich C9+ residue. Roughly 70-80% of world cracker capacity in 1983 was naphtha-based, with the rest ethane and propane; the Gulf Coast and the Far East were naphtha and the Texas Gulf was liquid-fuelled ethane.
children.note: The steam-dilution numbers for a naphtha cracker are recorded on the steam cracking step at chem.ethylene.steam-cracking. Established: Naphtha plus steam to ethylene propylene butenes and aromatics. Not established: the stated weight yields and capacity shares as given.
Detail under chem.butadiene. Established: Refinery to polymer handover via naphtha C4 and reformer aromatics. Not established: the stated benzene to styrene routing specifics as given.

chem.refining.note: Category industry for the refinery units themselves and fluids for the hydrocarbon streams, catalysts and specs they handle: refining is a plant, and energy is reserved for power generation and the grid. Established: Refining distillation conversion and upgrading to fuels and naphtha feedstocks. Not established: the stated naphtha to cracker routing specifics as given.

chem.ethylene.name: Ethylene: steam cracking and the polymers of it
chem.ethylene.description: Steam cracking naphtha at 800-900 C over cast alloy coils is the largest single chemical reaction in the world by tonnage. World ethylene capacity in 1983 was about 27-30 million tonnes a year, and roughly half of it went into polyethylene and the rest into ethylene oxide, styrene and solvents. Every polyethylene cable sheath, every styrene monomer and every polyester fibre in a C64 starts in a coiled coil furnace.

children.name: The ethylene industry in 1983
children.description: About 27-30 Mt/yr of world ethylene capacity in 1983, of which the United States held roughly 19 Mt (about two thirds) and Western Europe about 8 Mt, with the Gulf Coast of the US, the Rhine-Ruhr, Antwerp, the Suez Gulf and the Japanese and Korean coasts as the clusters. A 1980s cracker cost $150-400 million and took three to five years to build.
children.note: Capacity and cost figures for this period are approximate; cracker capital costs roughly doubled between 1978 and 1981.

children.name: Steam cracking
children.description: A hydrocarbon feed mixed with steam is brought to 800-900 C in a few tenths of a second in a serpentine coil inside a radiant furnace, at 1-3 bar. The chemistry is brutal free-radical chain cracking: the large molecules fall apart into smaller ones and a large hydrogen-rich tail gas. What decides the plant is how fast the coil can be taken to temperature without coking it, and how fast it can be cooled again. Steam does two jobs: it lowers the hydrocarbon partial pressure so radicals recombine into smaller molecules rather than into carbon, and it carries the heat into the coil.

children.name: Cracker furnace and radiant section
children.description: A refractory-lined box 20-40 m long with 40-80 coiled coils hung side by side, each coil 30-80 m of 4 in (100 mm) cast tube in ten passes of 10-20 m. The fire is gas- or oil-fired at 30-50 MW per furnace, and the radiant duty is the whole point: roughly 70% of the process heat has to arrive by radiation because convection through the gas is too slow to get the coil to 850 C in half a second.
children.note: Feed is mixed with very hot steam and briefly heated in a furnace with the reaction temperature around 850 C. Not established: the 20-40 m box with 40-80 coiled coils, the 4 in cast tube in ten passes, the 30-50 MW firing rate, and the roughly 70% radiant duty. The 800-900 C range is for modern units, not a 1982 figure.

children.name: Coke and decoking
children.description: Coke builds up on the coil, which insulates it, raises the skin temperature and finally blocks the tube. 1980s practice was to shut the furnace and decoke in place by burning the coke out with steam and air (off-line decoking), taking several hours and costing several thousand dollars a cycle; a shift to shorter, more frequent on-line decokes came later with the high-performance coils. The coke itself is a fine, hard, low-metal material that has to be disposed of.
children.note: Established: Coke builds up on the coil, which insulates it, raises the skin temperature and finally blocks the tube as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Cracked-gas expander turbine
children.description: The cracked gas at 800-900 C is not simply cooled; in the 1980s it was let down through a turboexpander that recovered most of the sensible heat as work, doing the job of the quench exchanger. The expander recovered 10-20% of the cracking energy and was one of the reasons the energy crisis of the 1970s produced a generation of much more efficient crackers.
children.note: Not established: the cracked-gas temperature range, the work-recovery share quoted, and the claim linking the 1970s energy crisis to a generation of more efficient crackers.

Established: steam cracking thermally cracks naphtha LPG ethane propane or butane with steam in furnaces to make ethylene and propylene. Not established: the stated tonnages dates temperatures pressures yields and 1980s operating details as given.

children.name: Quenching and acetylene control
children.description: The cracked gas leaves the coil at 800-900 C and has to come down to under 40 C in a second or two before anything can be separated, or the reactor metallurgy melts. The choice of quench is a real fork in the road: a gas quench to 350-400 C followed by selective hydrogenation, or a direct spray quench to under 40 C. A spray quench injects liquid hydrocarbon or quench oil straight into the cracked gas, which is cheap and puts the gas into the quench-oil circuit at once but cannot be combined with selective hydrogenation, because the acetylene has already polymerised in the cooler.

children.name: Gas quench to 350-400 C
children.description: The cracked gas is quenched with recycled process gas rather than directly with liquid, stopping at 350-400 C. This keeps the gas hot enough that the acetylene survives, so the acetylene can be destroyed deliberately afterwards in a selective hydrogenation reactor (palladium on alumina at 130-180 C, 10-30 bar hydrogen) rather than being allowed to polymerise into gums in the cooler. Ethylene purity of 99.9%+ with acetylene under 5 ppm is the target. Palladium on alumina at 130-180 C and 10-30 bar of hydrogen converts the acetylene to ethylene, and it is why a cracker carried a few tonnes of 0.5-2% Pd: the hydrogen partial pressure had to be held tightly, because too much of it makes ethane and costs ethylene yield.
children.note: Established: The cracked gas is quenched with recycled process gas rather than directly with liquid, stopping at 350-400 C as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Decanter and quench oil circuit
children.description: The condensed liquid is settled and decanted, separating the heavy C9+ tar from the gasoline and C4 streams. The heavy fraction - about 5-10% of the cracker feed - was the benzene, toluene and xylenes rich C9+ cut in the 1980s, and it was the aromatics feed for the styrene plants and the solvent plants.
children.note: Established: The condensed liquid is settled and decanted, separating the heavy C9+ tar from the gasoline and C4 streams as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

Established: cracked gas quench from 800-900 C to under 40 C as a required step with gas versus liquid quench options. Not established: the stated one to two second timing 350-400 C gas quench staging and acetylene survival consequences as given.

children.name: Ethylene purification
children.description: Before the ethylene can be polymerised it has to be dry and essentially free of oxygen and carbon dioxide, because both water and oxygen poison a radical or coordination polymerisation catalyst irreversibly. A cracker therefore had a molecular sieve drier taking water to under 1 ppm and a CO2/CO removal stage. 3A or 4A zeolite molecular sieve in beds switched in parallel took the water below 1 ppmv - the same family of material as the FCC catalyst and the styrene alkylation catalyst, which is the clearest single illustration that one piece of chemistry runs through the whole tree. Oxygen was held under 1 ppm and carbon dioxide under 5 ppm by an amine or a solid bed, and the CO2 was the dangerous one: it poisons the coordination catalysts and it reacts with the organoaluminium cocatalyst of a Ziegler-Natta polymerisation.
children.note: Drying and oxygen/CO2 removal are part of this step; the four numbers that define the grade are its facts. Established: Ethylene purification to protect polymerisation catalysts from water oxygen and carbon dioxide. Not established: the stated sieve drier specifics and grade numbers as given.

children.name: Ethylene oxide
children.description: The oxidation of ethylene over silver at 200-300 C and 20-30 bar, in which every eighth or tenth ethylene molecule is burned to carbon dioxide and water instead of being oxidised. It was about 1.5-2.5 million tonnes a year in 1983, most of it going to ethylene glycol for polyester and to surfactants, and it is one of the most hazardous large-scale chemical processes in existence.

children.name: Air-oxidation process (the industrial one)
children.description: Ethylene and air over silver on low-surface-area alpha-alumina in a multi-tubular reactor at 200-300 C and 20-30 bar. Per-pass conversion is only 10-15% and the selectivity to ethylene oxide is 80-90%, so the unreacted ethylene is recycled with the inert diluent. The alternative process - the chlorohydrin route, ethylene plus hypochlorous acid to chloroethanol to oxide - was still running in the United States in the early 1980s but had been almost entirely displaced by air oxidation elsewhere. The superseded chlorohydrin route chlorinated ethylene in water and dehydrochlorinated with lime, and made a chlorinated calcium salt waste for every tonne of product, which is why it survived only in the United States: a process displaced not by yield but by waste.
children.note: Chlorohydrin EO production was already minor by the early 1980s and was essentially gone by the mid-1980s in Europe and Japan. Established: Air oxidation over silver on alumina with recycle due to low per pass conversion. Not established: the stated conversion selectivity and recycle specifics as given.

children.name: Ethylene oxide safety
children.description: Ethylene oxide boils at 10.7 C, so it is a liquid only just below ambient and a gas in a warm tank; its flammable range in air is 3-80% by volume and its ignition energy is about 0.06 millijoule. It is acutely toxic, it polymerises without catalyst into a runaway, and it is kept in equilibrium by a trace of tertiary butyl alcohol or hydrochlorinated hydrocarbon inhibitor. In 1980s practice the industry standard was a fixed tank or a pressure vessel with an inert blanket, nitrogen purging and a quench section that could handle a deflagration.
children.note: Flammability limits for ethylene oxide are commonly quoted as roughly 3-80% by volume; the flash point is about -20 C. This is the hazard commentary about ethylene oxide, kept with the substance it is about.

Established: The oxidation of ethylene over silver at 200-300 C and 20-30 bar, in which every eighth or tenth ethylene molecule is burned to carbon dioxide and water instead of being oxidised as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Ethylene glycol and the glycols
children.description: Monoethylene glycol, diethylene glycol and triethylene glycol, made by hydration of ethylene oxide in a 1:1 to 1:20 mole ratio of oxide to water, with the ratio chosen to steer the product distribution towards the wanted glycol. In 1980s practice monoethylene glycol was about half the output and went into polyester, antifreeze and diester coolant, and diethylene glycol went into antifreeze and into the unsaturated polyester resins of the same family as the C64's case resin. One tonne of ethylene glycol needs about 3.5 tonnes of ethylene oxide at full selectivity, world MEG capacity was around 4-5 million tonnes a year in 1983, and the big consumers were polyester fibre and film and PET. The older catalytic hydration put ethylene oxide over phosphoric acid on silica at 200-220 C and 60-70 bar with about 20% of the glycol recycled as diluent to suppress ether side products, at 85-90% selectivity to monoethylene glycol - and the whole plant economics is that selectivity, because the diethylene glycol and dioxane have to be sold at a discount. The Shell direct oxidation-hydratation, commercialised in 1965, converted ethylene, oxygen and water in one step over a supported silver-phosphorus-tungsten catalyst for a higher MEG yield and less waste water, at the price of needing very pure oxygen; both routes were still running side by side in 1983.

children.name: Glycol finishing by vacuum distillation
children.description: Water is removed in a multi-column vacuum system because the glycols boil at 197, 245 and 285 C and water outranks them everywhere; a set of vacuum columns at 30-100 mbar separates mono-, di- and triethylene glycol and recovers the unreacted oxide. This is one of the clearest cases in the whole tree where the separation, not the chemistry, is the expensive part.

facts.label: Boiling points
facts.value: MEG 197 C, DEG 245 C, TEG 285 C (1 atm)

children.note: Diethylene and triethylene glycol are the major byproducts and separating them from water is energy-intensive, which is the point this node makes. Not established: the 197, 245 and 285 C boiling points, the 30-100 mbar vacuum and the multi-column configuration.

facts.label: Ethylene oxide per tonne of glycol

children.note: Established: Monoethylene glycol, diethylene glycol and triethylene glycol, made by hydration of ethylene oxide in a 1:1 to 1:20 mole ratio of oxide to water, with the ratio chosen to steer the as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Polyethylene
children.description: The largest use of ethylene: about 12-14 million tonnes of polyethylene were made in 1983, split roughly between low-density (free radical, high pressure) and high-density (coordination catalysis, low pressure). The C64-scale uses are the power cord's insulation and jacket, the moulded cable accessories, and the keyboard membrane's insulation. Metallocene catalysis - one sandwich compound with a zirconium atom between two cyclopentadienyl rings, activated with methylaluminoxane - was first reported in 1980 and was not yet industrial in 1983, but it was the obvious next step because it gives a narrow molecular weight distribution and predictable comonomer placement.

children.name: LDPE: free-radical high-pressure process
children.description: Ethylene is polymerised at 200-300 C and 1,000-2,000 bar in a jacketed or tubular reactor with a peroxide initiator, in the liquid phase (below about 280 C) or the gas phase (above it). The density of 0.91-0.93 comes entirely from chain branching: the very high pressure creates radicals on the growing chain, the chain folds, and the branches that stop it crystallising. In 1983 the process was mature to the point of being a cost exercise, and it still made most of the world polyethylene.

children.name: Autoclave versus tubular reactor
children.description: The autoclave process (Union Carbide, 1930s) stirred the gas-phase reaction; the tubular process (Sons, 1950s) had plug flow with injection quills and much better temperature control. By the 1980s the tubular reactor was the standard large unit because it gave a narrower molecular weight distribution and better ethylene conversion, and because the autoclave's bulk polymer needed devolatilising.
children.note: Not established: the attribution of the autoclave and tubular processes to specific originators and decades, and the claims about molecular-weight distribution, conversion and devolatilising practice favouring tubular reactors by the 1980s.

Established: Ethylene is polymerised at 200-300 C and 1,000-2,000 bar in a jacketed or tubular reactor with a peroxide initiator, in the liquid phase (below about 280 C) or the gas phase (above as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: HDPE: coordination catalysis at low pressure
children.description: Ethylene at 20-60 bar and 150-260 C over a transition-metal catalyst gives linear polyethylene with almost no long-chain branching, so it crystallises tightly and has a density of 0.94-0.97. Because the polymer comes out of the reactor as a powder or a slurry rather than a melt, HDPE in 1983 was made in a slurry loop or a gas-phase fluidised bed and then converted by extrusion. The Phillips chromium oxide process (1952) ran chromium oxide on silica at 20-40 bar and 150-200 C in a slurry loop, and it is the reason a 1980s plastics plant had the diluent-recovery section that was its largest single energy consumer. Union Carbide's Unipoly gas-phase process polymerised ethylene as a gas in a fluidised bed at 20-30 bar and 70-100 C with the catalyst on a support: no diluent to recover and no slurry to centrifuge, and by the early 1980s the technology for every new large plant.

children.name: Ziegler-Natta polymerisation
children.description: Titanium tetrachloride or titanium dichloride with an aluminium alkyl (triethylaluminium or diethylaluminium chloride) at 50-100 bar and 50-80 C in a hydrocarbon diluent. Ziegler was the 1953 discovery that started the whole low-pressure polyethylene industry; by the 1960s it had become Ziegler-Natta by supporting the titanium on magnesium chloride, which gave the multiplicity of active sites and therefore the control of molecular weight distribution that made high-density pipe grades possible.
children.note: Established: Ziegler Natta titanium plus aluminium alkyl catalysts polymerise ethylene to linear high density polyethylene and propylene to polypropylene. Not established: the stated tonnages dates temperatures pressures yields and 1980s operating details as given.

Established: Ethylene at 20-60 bar and 150-260 C over a transition-metal catalyst gives linear polyethylene with almost no long-chain branching, so it crystallises tightly and has a density of as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

Established: polyethylene is the most commonly produced plastic for packaging film containers and cable sheathing. Not established: the stated tonnages dates temperatures pressures yields and 1980s operating details as given.

chem.ethylene.note: Established: Steam cracking naphtha at 800-900 C over cast alloy coils is the largest single chemical reaction in the world by tonnage as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.propylene.name: Propylene and its derivatives
chem.propylene.description: Propylene is the C3 that the cracker makes whether you wanted it or not, and for two decades the propylene splitter process existed purely to turn that unwanted C3 into more of it. By 1983 most propylene came from the cracker and from FCC, and it went into polypropylene, propylene oxide, cumene for phenol and bisphenol A, and the acrylonitrile ammoxidation.

children.name: Propylene purification
children.description: The propylene has to be at 99.5-99.9% with less than 10-20 ppm of carbonyl compounds, because propanal and acetone stop an ionic polymerisation dead. In 1980s practice the purified propylene was made by distillation plus an alkaline wash, and by the later 1980s by hydrazine or hydrazone treatment which converts the carbonyls into something removable.
children.note: Not established: the purity and carbonyl-specification ranges quoted, and the timing claim for hydrazine or hydrazone carbonyl treatment entering practice in the later 1980s.

children.name: Propylene oxide
children.description: Propylene epoxidised, then made into propylene glycol, polyether polyols for polyurethane foam, and propylene chlorohydrin. World production was of the order of 0.7-0.9 million tonnes in 1983. Because the epoxidation of propylene was historically done with hypochlorous acid, a chlorinated by-product stream came with it, and that is why 1,2-dichloropropane and the flame retardants derived from it were part of the same business.

children.name: Chlorohydrin route
children.description: Propylene plus hypochlorous acid gives 1-chloro-2-propanol (about 90%) and 2-chloro-1-propanol (about 10%); the mixture is dehydrochlorinated with a lime or caustic slurry to propylene oxide and the chlorides are recycled as chlorine. The 10% isomer is the problem: it goes on to make propylene chlorohydrin and then the toxic 1,2-dichloropropane, so the plant had a dedicated caustic hydrolysis section for it.
children.note: Established: Propylene plus hypochlorous acid gives 1-chloro-2-propanol (about 90%) and 2-chloro-1-propanol (about 10%), the mixture is dehydrochlorinated with a lime or caustic slurry to propy as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Hydrogen peroxide epoxidation
children.description: Propylene plus hydrogen peroxide over a titanium-on-silica catalyst at 40-80 C and 1-10 bar, with the propylene chlorohydrin recycled as the phase-transfer catalyst. It makes no chloride, it is nearly quantitative, and it depends on a cheap supply of hydrogen peroxide - which in 1983 was the reason the anthraquinone peroxide plant and the propylene oxide plant sat next to each other in a few integrated sites.
children.note: The chlorohydrin-recycling hydrogen peroxide route was the commercially important one in the 1980s; the halide-free TSCA process came later.

Established: propylene epoxidation to propylene oxide for glycols and polyether polyols as a standard derivative. Not established: the stated 0.7-0.9 million tonne 1983 volume and historical epoxidation route details as given.

children.name: Cumene route to phenol and acetone
children.description: Benzene plus propylene gives cumene; cumene plus oxygen gives cumene hydroperoxide; the hydroperoxide is cleaved with acid to give phenol and acetone. About a million tonnes a year of phenol in 1983 came out of this route, and phenol went to bisphenol A (and therefore to the C64's epoxy laminate resin), to phenol-formaldehyde plastics, and to caprolactam. Acetone came out of the other end of the same reaction, which is why acetone supply in the 1980s was really cumene capacity in disguise.

children.name: Cumene alkylation
children.description: Benzene with excess benzene over phosphoric acid on silica at 140-180 C and 20-30 bar in an adiabatic bed, or over a solid acid. The large excess of benzene (3-5 mol per mol of propylene) is deliberate: it suppresses the diethylbenzene and triisopropylbenzene by-products and stops the reactor polymerising the propylbenzene.

facts.label: Conditions
facts.value: 30 bar at 250 C over a Lewis acid catalyst; the source notes phosphoric acid is often favoured over the aluminium halides

children.note: Propylene and benzene are compressed together at 30 bar and 250 C over a catalytic Lewis acid, with phosphoric acid often favoured over aluminium halides. The 140-180 C, 20-30 bar, H3PO4-on-silica adiabatic-bed conditions and the 3-5 mol benzene per mol propylene ratio in this node are the licensor's industrial figures and are not established here.

children.name: Cumene oxidation to the hydroperoxide
children.description: Cumene with air at 120-140 C, either with a hydroperoxide initiator or with a cobalt or manganese catalyst, gives cumene hydroperoxide at 20-40 wt%. This is a liquid-phase autoxidation, and it has the classic autoxidation hazard: the reaction is exothermic, it runs away above 150 C, and the product is a shock-sensitive organic peroxide.

facts.label: Conditions
facts.value: 120-140 C, air, initiator or Co/Mn catalyst

children.note: Cumene is oxidised in air to cumene hydroperoxide. Not established: the 120-140 C liquid-phase autoxidation, the hydroperoxide initiator or cobalt/manganese catalyst option, the 20-40 wt% hydroperoxide concentration, and the runaway above 150 C.

children.name: Acid cleavage to phenol and acetone
children.description: The cumene hydroperoxide is cleaved with sulphuric acid (or with a zeolite in later plants) at 50-80 C, giving phenol and acetone with 85-95% selectivity. The 1980s safety concern was the rearrangement of the cumene hydroperoxide to the phenol and acetone, which is violently exothermic: a small holdup upstream of the cleavage reactor would flash-boil, and the famous 1979 and 1985 phenol plant incidents are what the modern design rules are written around.
children.note: Established: The cumene hydroperoxide is cleaved with sulphuric acid (or with a zeolite in later plants) at 50-80 C, giving phenol and acetone with 85-95% selectivity as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

Established: the cumene route alkylates benzene with propylene to cumene then oxidises and acid cleaves to phenol and acetone. Not established: the stated tonnages dates temperatures pressures yields and 1980s operating details as given.

chem.propylene.note: Established: Propylene is the C3 that the cracker makes whether you wanted it or not, and for two decades the propylene splitter process existed purely to turn that unwanted C3 into more of it as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.acrylonitrile.name: Acrylonitrile and the ammoxidation
chem.acrylonitrile.description: The SOVERE process - SOx-free reductive ammoxidation - oxidises propylene with ammonia and air in one step to acrylonitrile. It was invented at Standard Oil of Ohio and licensed worldwide from 1960-1965, and by 1983 essentially all the world's roughly 1.2-1.5 million tonnes a year of acrylonitrile was made by it. Acrylonitrile is the most dangerous liquid in a polymer plant: it is acutely lethal by skin absorption, flammable at 3-20% in air, and boils at 77 C. The older nitric acid route nitrated propylene with 15-20% nitric acid at 30-60 C and 2-5 bar to a nitropropane mixture, converted the 1-nitropropane with a dialkyl amine to a propylhydroxylamine and dehydrated that to acrylonitrile: a 30-50% yield, a heavy nitrate waste stream and a very large plant, surviving in 1983 only in a few older Soviet and Eastern European works.

children.name: SOVERE ammoxidation process
children.description: A mixture of propylene, ammonia, oxygen and steam is passed at 400-460 C and 15-25 bar (1.5-2.5 MPa) over a bismuth molybdate or antimony-phosphorus-boron oxide catalyst in a fixed-bed or fluidised-bed reactor. The reaction is a partial oxidation plus an ammonia substitution in one step: propylene + 1.5 NH3 + 0.75 O2 -> acrylonitrile + 2 H2O. Per tonne of acrylonitrile the plant consumes about 1.0-1.1 t of propylene, 0.22-0.30 t of ammonia (most of which is lost to N2 and to acetonitrile) and 1.0-1.3 t of air, and it makes 0.04-0.08 t of acetonitrile as the main by-product. A side reaction makes hydrogen - propylene plus ammonia plus oxygen gives propene imine, which cracks to acetonitrile and hydrogen - and by the 1980s that hydrogen was being recovered from the purge gas, which is why the net oxygen demand of the process is lower than the stoichiometry suggests. Acrylonitrile inhibits cytochrome oxidase and causes methaemoglobinaemia, and it is absorbed through intact skin, so a 1980s plant ran gloves, face shields and showers at every sampling point.

children.name: Fixed-bed or fluidised-bed ammoxidation reactor
children.description: The original SOVERE design was a series of fixed beds with salt bath or oil bath cooling, giving 90-93% conversion and 85-92% selectivity. The 1980s industry had largely moved to fluidised-bed or moving-bed designs, which were easier to heat and to strip of coke, at the cost of a lower selectivity (about 80-90%). A 1980s plant was a 100,000-250,000 tonne a year unit with a salt bath or a hot water reactor jacket and a lot of downstream distillation.
children.note: Selectivity figures vary with catalyst age and design; the ranges are the standard ones quoted in reviews.

children.name: Recovery and purification train
children.description: The reactor effluent is cooled and partly condensed, the unreacted propylene and ammonia are stripped and recycled, the acrylonitrile and acetonitrile are separated by distillation (acrylonitrile boiling 77 C, acetonitrile 81.6 C, which is a genuinely difficult separation and was the reason for the extractive or entrainer-assisted designs), and the acrylonitrile is finished to 99.9% with a stabiliser. In a plant where acrylonitrile boils at 77 C and is flammable from 3% in air, the distillation column was also the largest single gas hazard.
children.note: Established: The reactor effluent is cooled and partly condensed, the unreacted propylene and ammonia are stripped and recycled, the acrylonitrile and acetonitrile are separated by distillation as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

Occupational limits for acrylonitrile were being revised downward through the 1980s and the figures are the era order of magnitude rather than a single legal value. The hazard figures for acrylonitrile: boiling point 77 C, flammable range 3-20 vol%, flash point about 6 C, and a 1980s US limit of 10 ppm as an 8-hour average. Established: SOVERE ammoxidation conditions and hazard figures as era orders of magnitude. Not established: the stated exact temperature pressure and exposure limit as single legal values.

children.name: Downstream acrylonitrile
children.description: What the acrylonitrile was for in 1983: acrylic fibre (Orlon, Dralon, and in Japan the acrylics), nitrile rubber (butadiene copolymer), SAN and ABS copolymer, and the polyacrylonitrile precursor for carbon fibre. More than half the acrylonitrile made in the early 1980s went into acrylic fibre, and a growing slice of the fibre grade went into polyacrylonitrile precursor for carbon fibre, which needs a very pure comonomer (methyl acrylate at 0.5-3%) because any ionic impurity ends up as a carbon defect.

children.name: Methyl methacrylate (acetone cyanohydrin route)
children.description: A separate molecule with the same nitrile: acetone plus hydrogen chloride gives acetone cyanohydrin, which is esterified with methanol and then dehydrated with sulphuric acid to methyl methacrylate. The acetone cyanohydrin route was introduced from 1938 and became dominant in the 1950s-60s. The hydrogen cyanide for it came either from the acrylonitrile plant's by-product or from its own Andrussow process, and the methanol came from synthesis gas.
children.note: Established: A separate molecule with the same nitrile: acetone plus hydrogen chloride gives acetone cyanohydrin, which is esterified with methanol and then dehydrated with sulphuric acid to me as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

Carbon fibre for aerospace became a real commercial product in the late 1970s-early 1980s but had essentially no place in a 1982 home computer; the link here is the shared acrylonitrile supply. Established: Acrylonitrile uses for fibre rubber SAN ABS and carbon precursor with fibre dominant. Not established: the stated more than half to fibre and comonomer purity specifics as given.

children.name: Acrylonitrile monomer
children.description: Acrylonitrile monomer (C3H3N) as made by propylene ammoxidation: the vinyl-nitrile feedstock for SAN/ABS grafting, acrylic fibre and nitrile rubber.
children.note: Established: high-purity monomer handled in a closed system with outside storage, because acrylonitrile is acutely lethal through intact skin. Not established: 99.5% purity, sub-45 ppm stabiliser, and tanker delivery as 1982 specifics.

chem.acrylonitrile.note: Established: acrylonitrile is a vinyl nitrile monomer for acrylic fibre nitrile rubber SAN ABS and carbon fibre precursor and is toxic at low doses. Not established: the stated tonnages dates temperatures pressures yields and 1980s operating details as given.

chem.butadiene.name: Butadiene and the elastomers of it
chem.butadiene.description: Butadiene is the C4 diene that makes synthetic rubber, and in 1983 about 5-6 million tonnes a year of it was made, roughly 60% from cracker C4 by extractive distillation and the rest by dehydrogenation of butane. It is the molecule behind the rubber in the C64's case feet, the plinths, and the elasticity of the power cord's jacket - and behind the graft phase of the ABS case. Nitrile rubber is butadiene with 25-40% acrylonitrile, emulsion-polymerised the same way as SBR: the acrylonitrile buys oil and fuel resistance and costs low-temperature flexibility, and it is the material for oil seals and for the elastomer pads of many electrolytic capacitors. Two butadienes plus two hydrogen cyanides give adiponitrile by hydrocyanation over nickel(0) with a triphenylphosphine ligand, which is what finally let a nylon 6,6 plant be fed from a cracker rather than from adipic acid - and is the reason hydrogen cyanide, the toxic gas of the acrylonitrile and methyl methacrylate chemistry, sat on a plastics company's books.

children.name: Butadiene sources
children.description: Two industrial routes and a third that was still just about alive in 1983: extractive distillation of the steam cracker's C4 stream, dehydrogenation of n-butane, and thermal dimerisation of acetylene (the old Reppe route, dead by 1960). The choice between them is a function of whether a cracker was nearby and whether butane was cheap. Two acetylene molecules make butadiene over a copper catalyst, and before 1960 that is how the world made it: a route with perfect atom economy that died because acetylene was expensive relative to the C4 it displaced - the third instance in this file of the elegant gas route losing to the abundant naphtha route.

children.name: Sounsby extractive distillation
children.description: The standard butadiene recovery unit from 1962 onward: an extractive distillation with a selective polar solvent that dissolves butadiene and the butenes but not the saturated C4s, followed by a second stripper to recover the pure diene. A 1980s unit processing 100,000-400,000 tonnes a year of C4 stood about 60-100 m tall and was one of the tallest distillation towers in the world, because alpha-olefins and butadiene have a relative volatility of about 1.01 - the hardest separation in the whole C4 business. The process works because butadiene is the only diene and the only component that will add a second solvent molecule.
children.note: Established: The standard butadiene recovery unit from 1962 onward: an extractive distillation with a selective polar solvent that dissolves butadiene and the butenes but not the saturated C4s, as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Houdry butane dehydrogenation
children.description: n-Butane dehydrogenated endothermically at 480-550 C over platinum on alumina or chromia at 1-5 bar to butenes, which are then extracted and the butadiene purified separately. It was the on-purpose route, it made isobutylene for MTBE as a co-product, and it suffered from the thermodynamics of an endothermic reaction: every 1% of conversion costs a lot of fuel, and 1980s furnace designs pushed single-pass conversion to 40-50% with recirculation.

children.name: The butane dehydrogenation furnace
children.description: Dehydrogenation of butane to butenes is endothermic, so the reactor is a bank of fired tubes - cast iron or cast alloy, several hundred tubes, with the furnace gas at 500-700 C. The catalyst inside is platinum on alumina or chromia, and the giveaway of a fouled furnace is the pressure drop across the tubes: the butene polymerises on the catalyst, makes green coke, and the coke blocks the tube. This unit is the reason the butadiene plant in a 1980s complex was often the noisiest building on the site.
children.note: The description of furnace-tube coking in butane dehydrogenation is standard; specific designs vary.
Not established: the temperature, pressure, catalyst and single-pass conversion figures quoted, and the co-product and recirculation claims for isobutylene and MTBE service.

Established: Two industrial routes and a third that was still just about alive in 1983: extractive distillation of the steam crackers C4 stream, dehydrogenation of n-butane, and thermal dimeri as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: How butadiene is polymerised
children.description: Three chemistries, chosen for what you were making. Emulsion polymerisation gives cis-1,4, trans-1,4 and vinyl-1,2 structures mixed - a rubber but not a specific one. Anionic polymerisation with lithium butyllithium gives cis-1,4 selectively and controls chain ends. Coordination polymerisation with neodymium or titanium gives cis-1,4 with an extremely high cis content. The 4-vinyl group left on a cis-1,4 chain is the reactive site that grafting later exploits.

children.name: Lithium butyllithium polymerisation
children.description: The living anionic process: butyllithium in a hydrocarbon diluent (diesel oil or hexane) at 0-60 C, with the cis content set by solvent and temperature. Living means the chain end stays active, so the polymer can be chain-stopped with an electrophile - water, carbon dioxide, epoxide - and the whole molecule is a single block. This is the chemistry that makes the ABS graft rubber phase possible.
children.note: Established: The living anionic process: butyllithium in a hydrocarbon diluent (diesel oil or hexane) at 0-60 C, with the cis content set by solvent and temperature as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Neodymium-catalysed cis-polybutadiene
children.description: The high-cis technology of the 1980s: a neodymium (or lanthanide) compound with an alkylaluminium in a hydrocarbon diluent gives 97-99% cis-1,4, and because the cis content is so high the rubber does not need to be plasticised with oil. Linear low-cis polybutadiene was the growth product of the decade; the older lithium-process cis-PB at 90-95% was still the volume product in 1983.
children.note: Not established: the cis-content range quoted, the formulation description, and the market characterisation of linear low-cis growth versus lithium-process volume product in 1983.
Established: Three chemistries, chosen for what you were making as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR)
children.description: The largest synthetic rubber by a wide margin: of the order of 6-7 million tonnes a year in 1983, in a handful of grades. It is not a C64 material, but it is the material whose emulsion polymerisation recipe - cold, water, persulphate, rosin acid soap, chain transfer agent - is the same recipe the ABS graft phase uses, and the rosin in it is the same pine rosin as the solder flux. Cold emulsion polymerisation ran styrene at 23-25 parts to butadiene at 75-77 parts in water with a rosin or oleate soap at 2-5 parts and a persulphate at 0.05-0.2 parts, at 5 C for 8-12 hours to 60-70% conversion.
children.note: The ABS graft reaction uses the same chemistry at 50-80 C; see chem.abs.grafting. Established: SBR as largest synthetic rubber with cold emulsion recipe shared with ABS grafting. Not established: the stated 1983 tonnages recipe parts conversion and temperature specifics as given.

chem.butadiene.note: The acrylonitrile comes from chem.acrylonitrile; the butadiene from chem.butadiene.sources. Established: Butadiene as C4 diene for synthetic rubber and ABS graft rubber. Not established: the stated 1983 tonnages and route shares as given.

chem.styrene.name: Styrene: benzene plus ethylene, and the plastics of it
chem.styrene.description: Benzene is alkylated with ethylene to ethylbenzene, and the ethylbenzene is dehydrogenated to styrene. About 12-14 million tonnes of styrene were made in 1983, of which roughly two thirds went to polystyrene and the rest to SAN, ABS and SBR. Styrene is a C64 material in a way that is easy to miss: the SAN matrix of the case, the styrene in the graft phase, and the polystyrene that was in the packaging and in some of the mouldings.

children.name: Ethylbenzene from benzene and ethylene
children.description: Benzene plus ethylene in a large molar excess of benzene (3-6 to 1) over a zeolite or a phosphoric acid catalyst at 250-400 C and 10-30 bar. The 1980s breakthrough was the Mobil process using a shape-selective zeolite (the ZSM-5 family) at about 350 C, which gives over 97% selectivity to ethylbenzene and almost no diethylbenzene. The old process, phosphoric acid on silica at 140-180 C and 20-30 bar, had a diethylbenzene problem that ate benzene and made the distillation columns enormous.
children.note: Established: Benzene plus ethylene in a large molar excess of benzene (3-6 to 1) over a zeolite or a phosphoric acid catalyst at 250-400 C and 10-30 bar as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Dehydrogenation to styrene
children.description: Ethylbenzene is dehydrogenated to styrene at 600-700 C and 1-3 bar over an iron oxide catalyst (the classic Feeders-Rudd, now UOP ST-110, a shell-and-tube bed of promoted magnetite with potassium and copper promoters). Single-pass conversion is 40-50% and the selectivity to styrene 90-93%. The conversion is deliberately held below completion because styrene polymerises over the same catalyst, and because the dehydrogenation is strongly endothermic and needs a large fired furnace.

children.name: ST-110 dehydrogenation reactor
children.description: A bank of shell-and-tube reactors, 20-50 tubes 4-6 inch in diameter by 20-30 m long, at 1-3 bar, fired on the outside. A 1980s styrene plant had 8-20 such reactors per train and several trains. The furnace is the plant's energy hog, which is why the styrene industry was the largest single consumer of heat-integration improvements in this part of the chemical industry.
children.note: Not established: the tube count, tube dimensions, pressure range and train arrangement quoted, and the claim that the furnace was the dominant plant energy consumer driving heat-integration work.

children.name: The dehydrogenation furnace
children.description: The dehydrogenation of ethylbenzene is strongly endothermic - about 0.22 GJ of heat per tonne of ethylbenzene - and it is carried out in a bank of shell-and-tube reactors with the heat applied from the outside. A 1980s styrene plant's furnaces were its largest energy consumers and its largest single source of stack emissions, which is why the industry spent the 1980s on better coil metallurgy, on vacuum insulation of the reactor, and on a staged feed arrangement that fed the preheated reactor's effluent straight back into the next reactor's inlet. Steam diluent keeps the partial pressure low and a polymerisation inhibitor - sulfolane, a chlorinated hydrocarbon or a proprietary organic - is dosed at tens of parts per million to hold the styrene down. Refinery fuel gas or natural gas, about 0.2 GJ of heat per tonne of ethylbenzene - worth stating plainly, because a substantial part of the carbon in a plastic is burned rather than polymerised.
children.note: The heat of dehydrogenation of ethylbenzene is about 0.22 GJ/t; the figure here is rounded. Established: Dehydrogenation furnace as endothermic shell and tube bank. Not established: the stated heat figure and 1980s furnace specifics as given.

Established: Ethylbenzene is dehydrogenated to styrene at 600-700 C and 1-3 bar over an iron oxide catalyst (the classic Feeders-Rudd, now UOP ST-110, a shell-and-tube bed of promoted magnetite as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Styrene polymerisation
children.description: Styrene polymerises readily by free-radical mechanisms because the benzyl radical it makes is resonance stabilised. Almost all commercial polystyrene is made by free-radical polymerisation; the ionic routes that give syndiotactic and isotactic polystyrene existed in the 1980s but were curiosities. Styrene-acrylonitrile copolymer carries 24-32% acrylonitrile, made in bulk at 130-180 C or in emulsion or suspension. SBS block copolymer is made by sequential addition to a living anionic chain - butadiene to a 60-80% cis polybutadiene block, then styrene to a polystyrene block at each end - so the hard end blocks are the physical crosslinks and the middle block is the rubber: the same butadiene and styrene as SBR and ABS in a completely different architecture. Expanded polystyrene carries 5-6% pentane or butane as a blowing agent, polymerised at 90-150 C and 1-5 bar with the beads expanding 10-30 times; it was the standard packing material for electronics and for the C64's carton inserts.

children.name: General purpose polystyrene, bulk and suspension
children.description: Bulk polymerisation at 140-200 C and 20-40 bar in a stirred or plug-flow reactor with a benzoyl peroxide or a hindered phenol initiator, the classic route for general purpose and crystal grade. Suspension polymerisation, in which styrene is dispersed as 0.1-2 mm beads in water with a suspending agent, is preferred for foam grades because the beads can be expanded. General purpose polystyrene production in the 1980s was of the order of 5-6 million tonnes a year.

children.name: Finishing: devolatilisation and pelletising
children.description: Polystyrene has to be devolatilised after the bulk polymerisation, because the monomer left in the melt is both a smell and a peroxide risk. A 1980s finishing line was a twin-screw extruder at 200-240 C and 5-50 mbar with two vacuum vents, then a strand die into a water bath, then a rotary cutter - the same machine geometry as the ABS line, and for the same reason: somebody in the plastics industry decided once that devolatilisation and pelletising should be one operation and never went back.

children.name: The devolatiliser
children.description: A falling-film or wiped-film evaporator with two stages of vacuum, taking the residual styrene from a few per cent down to a few hundred parts per million. The polymer is deliberately kept above its own melting point but below its decomposition point, which for polystyrene is a window of about 40 C - the whole of the finishing engineering is about staying in that window while the pressure falls and the viscosity rises.
children.note: Not established: the melt-temperature, vacuum and residual-monomer figures quoted, and the stated operating window between melting and decomposition for polystyrene.

children.name: Strand die, water bath and cutter
children.description: Extruded through a die with 10-30 holes of 2-3 mm, quenched in a water bath at 20-30 C, drawn by a first calender and cut by a rotary knife. The alternative - underwater pelletising - cuts the strands in the water and was becoming the 1980s choice for polystyrene as it had been for ABS, for the same reason: fewer handling steps and no strand breakage.
children.note: Not established: the die-hole count and diameter, bath-temperature and pellet-size figures quoted, and the claim that underwater pelletising was becoming the 1980s preference for polystyrene.

Established: Polystyrene has to be devolatilised after the bulk polymerisation, because the monomer left in the melt is both a smell and a peroxide risk as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

Established: Bulk polymerisation at 140-200 C and 20-40 bar in a stirred or plug-flow reactor with a benzoyl peroxide or a hindered phenol initiator, the classic route for general purpose and c as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

SAN capacity in the early 1980s is an order-of-magnitude estimate. Established: Styrene free radical polymerisation via resonance stabilised benzyl radical. Not established: the stated capacity and ionic route specifics as given.

chem.styrene.note: Established: styrene is vinyl benzene precursor to polystyrene and copolymers typically made from benzene via ethylbenzene. Not established: the stated tonnages dates temperatures pressures yields and 1980s operating details as given.

chem.styrene.benzene.name: Benzene
chem.styrene.benzene.description: The feedstock. In 1983 world benzene production was of the order of 15-17 million tonnes a year, and it came from three sources: catalytic reforming (about half), hydrodealkylation of toluene (roughly a quarter to a third, and the growth share of the 1980s), and coal tar from coke ovens (10-20%, and a bigger share outside North America and Western Europe). Toluene hydrodealkylation gave benzene plus methane at 500-600 C and 30-60 bar over cobalt-molybdenum or alumina, and it grew fastest through the 1980s because toluene was abundant and benzene was tight; it makes the same methane a reformer makes as hydrogen, so the two operations fit together.
chem.styrene.benzene.note: Established: The feedstock as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.abs.name: ABS resin plant, and the C64 case
chem.abs.description: Acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene is not a copolymer but a polymer blend: a SAN matrix with a grafted polybutadiene rubber phase dispersed in it as 0.1-10 micron particles. Making it is four separate unit operations - make the rubber, graft styrene and acrylonitrile onto it, make the matrix, blend and pelletise - and then a fifth that most people forget, drying. The C64's case, its keyboard surround and the beige plastic of its keys are this material.

children.name: Graft copolymerisation: growing SAN on the rubber
children.description: The heart of the process. 20-40 parts of a low-cis polybutadiene rubber dissolved in xylene or toluene is charged to a reactor, and styrene plus acrylonitrile is added at 60-80 C in the presence of a persulphate initiator, a chelating agent and a mercaptan chain transfer agent. The radicals abstract a hydrogen from the polybutadiene's 1,2-vinyl unit, creating a radical site on the rubber; styrene and acrylonitrile then copolymerise from that site, and SAN chains grow out of the rubber particle. Each particle therefore becomes a rubber core with a SAN shell. High-graft material, more than about 70% of the monomer grafted, gives a small uniform particle and the best impact strength, while low graft gives larger particles and worse impact; the particle is either salt-like (elastomeric core, rigid SAN shell) or sandwich-like, and which one forms is set by how fast the graft shell precipitates. The rubber is dissolved in xylene or toluene and the monomer emulsified in an aqueous phase carrying the initiator, chelant and transfer agent, and at the end the polymer is devolatilised at 220-250 C and 1-10 mbar to strip the xylene - the single biggest energy item in the plant, at one to two tonnes of solvent per tonne of polymer.
