children.note: Particle morphology terminology (salt-like, sandwich) and graft-level thresholds vary by producer; these are the standard descriptions. Graft level, particle morphology and reaction medium describe how this step behaves rather than a second operation. Not established: the 20-40 wt% rubber fraction, the 60-80 C graft temperature, the 40-80% graft conversion, the above-70% high-graft threshold and the salt-like and sandwich particle thresholds, which are producer- and licensor-specific. The 220-250 C and 1-10 mbar devolatilisation and the one to two tonnes of xylene per tonne of polymer vary most between plants.

children.name: Blending the graft into the matrix
children.description: The graft is mixed into the SAN at 25-50 parts graft per 100 parts SAN for a general purpose grade and up to 50-70 parts for a high-impact grade. That ratio - not the chemistry - is what a plastics buyer specifies: rubber content sets the impact strength, the heat distortion temperature and the price per kilogram.
children.note: Kept as its own node because the blend ratio is what a plastics buyer specifies, and its two ingredients are recorded as "from" edges: the blend is made of the graft and the SAN matrix, it does not contain them. ABS proportions run 15-35% acrylonitrile, 5-30% butadiene and 40-60% styrene, and the elastic butadiene phase is what makes it impact resistant. Not established: the 25-50 and 50-70 parts graft per 100 parts SAN ratios, the 25-40% figure for high-impact grades, and the 76:24 styrene:acrylonitrile matrix.

children.name: Compounding and pelletising
children.description: The dry blend is melted in a twin-screw extruder at 230-260 C, the volatile xylene and the residual styrene are pulled out under vacuum, and the melt is cut into pellets. This is the operation that turns a powder into a product a moulding machine can eat, and it is where the ABS gets its second heat history - which is why the regrind content matters.

children.name: Twin-screw extruder
children.description: Two intermeshing screws 50-90 mm in diameter at 10-30 rpm, length to diameter ratio 30-40:1, with an L/D feed zone, a melting zone, a vacuum vent and a second vent for the devolatilisation. In 1983 the counter-rotating or co-rotating twin screw was the standard compounding machine for ABS because it handles the powder blend, the pigment and the regrind in one pass; a 70 mm machine ran 500-2,000 kg/h. The xylene comes out in the compounding extruder rather than in the reactor, because the reactor melt is too viscous to devolatilise in a small unit: a falling-film or wiped-film vent at 240-260 C and 5-50 mbar with a steam ejector, or a liquid ring pump for the high-boiling tail.

facts.label: Vapour load
facts.value: 1-2 t xylene per t of polymer

children.note: Machine sizes and throughputs are typical of the era's compounding lines.

children.name: Vacuum venting
children.description: A vent at 10-100 mbar with a steam ejector or a liquid ring pump, sized to remove the residual monomer and solvent. The residual styrene specification matters: a high-styrene ABS smells, and the monomer content of a 1980s pellet was typically under 500 ppm.
children.note: Not established: the vacuum range and residual-styrene specification quoted, and the claim linking high residual styrene to odour in ABS.

children.name: Die plate, water bath and rotary cutter
children.description: The melt is extruded through a die plate as a number of strands into a circulating water bath at 20-40 C, solidifies, is pulled by a first calender and chopped by a rotary knife mounted on the extruder die. The alternative is underwater pelletising, where the die is submerged and the pellets are cut in the water - fewer steps, no strands, and it was becoming the 1980s preference for a new line. Pellet size is 2-4 mm in both cases.
children.note: Not established: the bath-temperature and pellet-size figures quoted, the equipment sequence described, and the claim that underwater pelletising was becoming the 1980s preference for new lines.

children.name: Static mixer in the melt line
children.simple_name: Static mixer in the melt line
children.description: A motionless packed element in the transfer pipe or the die adapter that blends the pigment and the regrind into the melt without shear. It matters because the impact property depends on the particle size distribution surviving, and every unnecessary shear element costs you 0.5-1 micron of particle size.
children.note: Not established: the mechanism claim that unnecessary shear costs a stated amount of rubber particle size, and the role described for the mixer in blending pigment and regrind without degrading impact properties.

Established: The dry blend is melted in a twin-screw extruder at 230-260 C, the volatile xylene and the residual styrene are pulled out under vacuum, and the melt is cut into pellets as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Drying
children.description: ABS is hygroscopic: its equilibrium moisture content is about 0.3-0.4% by weight, and a wet pellet in a mould produces a part with silver streaks on the surface, voids, and a lower impact strength than the design assumed. The moulding shop therefore dried the pellets at 80-90 C for 2-4 hours in a dehumidifying dryer before every moulding run. This is the step that separates a plastics engineer from a chemist and it is done with the pellets in a hopper with a 3A molecular sieve bed.
children.note: The 200 ppm specification is a common engineering target; typical material arrives at 0.05-0.15%. The desiccant is recorded as a "from" ingredient: a drying step is made of its molecular sieve bed, it does not contain it. Not established: the 80-90 C for 2-4 h drying cycle, the under 0.02% moisture target, and the 3A molecular sieve bed as 1980s ABS practice. The 0.3-0.4 wt% equilibrium moisture figure and the silver-streak, void and lost-impact-strength failure mode are plausible but undocumented here.

children.name: Other polymers in and around a C64
children.description: A 1983 consumer electronic device used perhaps eight different engineering plastics and two rubbers. This branch traces each of them to its monomer, because they all come out of the same crackers, the same benzene and the same phenol. Each is a node with its own subtree; chem.pvc, chem.epoxy, chem.rubber, chem.polyester and chem.silicone are the ones other parts of this tree reference.

children.name: PVC: vinyl chloride and suspension polymerisation
children.description: About 3.5 million tonnes of PVC in 1983, of which maybe 5-8% was flexible and the rest rigid. Two-thirds of the monomer came from the oxychlorination of ethylene and the rest from acetylene and HCl. The C64 used it in the power cord's jacket and insulation, in the moulded cable accessories, and in the odd keycap or knob; the stability system matters because unstabilised PVC decomposes at 140 C. Suspension polymerisation in water with a suspending agent is 65-70% of world PVC: VCM dispersed as 0.1-1 mm beads at 50-70 C and 6-12 bar for 5-10 hours to 70-85% conversion.

children.name: Acetylene plus HCl (the mercury route)
children.description: Acetylene and anhydrous hydrogen chloride over a mercuric chloride catalyst on charcoal at 20-60 C and 1-2 bar absolute, at 15-25% conversion per pass with 90-95% selectivity. This is the route that ties PVC to natural gas, because acetylene is made from methane. It survives where there is no cracker - in Western Europe, in India, in China and in the Soviet Union - and where there is one, the oxychlorination route is cheaper.
children.note: The acetylene end of this route is chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.to-vinyl-chloride. Established: Acetylene plus HCl mercury route to vinyl chloride tying PVC to gas. Not established: the stated conversion selectivity and temperature specifics as given.

children.name: PVC in a C64
children.description: The power cord: a two-core or three-core flexible PVC jacket, typically 1.5-3 mm of wall, with PVC insulation on the conductors and a PVC or PVC/rubber strain relief at the moulded connector. A C64 power cord is a couple of hundred grams of PVC. The keyboard keys and the side vents of the earlier cases were also often PVC or a PVC blend. A C64 whose power supply was the internal one had less of it, because the mains cable went to the brick.
children.note: Cable constructions varied by market and by supplier; the jacket material was almost always flexible PVC.

Established: polyvinyl chloride is a major vinyl polymer for rigid pipe profiles and flexible cable jacket and insulation. Not established: the stated tonnages dates temperatures pressures yields and 1980s operating details as given.

children.name: Epoxy: bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin
children.description: DGEBA epoxy is made by hydrolyzing bisphenol A with epichlorohydrin, then dehydrochlorinating to close the epoxide ring. About 800,000-1,000,000 tonnes of epoxy resin were made in 1983, of which the largest single use was the glass-reinforced laminate for printed circuit boards. A C64 has epoxy in its board, in the transformer and coil potting of its power supply, in the die-attach of its chips, and in the adhesive that holds the SID's heatsink tab.

children.name: Bisphenol A from cumene
children.description: Two phenol molecules plus acetone, condensed over a strong acid to give 4,4'-isopropylidenediphenol, with the water stripped. In 1983 most BPA was made this way from the cumene process's phenol, and the rest from the older two-step route using bis(4-chlorophenyl) ketone. The 1980s were the period when BPA's endocrine activity was being investigated by accident, and when the epoxy industry began to substitute boron oxides and novolac epoxies to remove it from can linings and bottle resins.
children.note: Established: Two phenol molecules plus acetone, condensed over a strong acid to give 4,4-isopropylidenediphenol, with the water stripped as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Epoxy in a C64
children.description: Four places. The board's laminate resin. The power supply's transformer bobbin and coil potting, and the mains filter capacitor's encapsulation. The die attach inside the VIC-II, the SID and the CPU packages, where the chip was bonded to a small ceramic or epoxy header with an epoxy that had to survive 180-260 C without delaminating. And the heatsink adhesive in the SID's tab, which in some designs was a two-part filled epoxy.
children.note: The mass figure is an order-of-magnitude estimate from typical laminate and encapsulation weights.

Established: DGEBA epoxy is made by hydrolyzing bisphenol A with epichlorohydrin, then dehydrochlorinating to close the epoxide ring as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Polycarbonate
children.description: Bisphenol A polycarbonate, made by the interfacial phosgene route from BPA and phosgene in dichloromethane, then melt polycondensed at 250-290 C. It is the transparent, tough, dimensionally stable engineering plastic of the 1980s, and in electronics it went into connector housings, terminal blocks, relay covers and the housings of the switchgear it replaced metal in. The C64 itself was not made of polycarbonate - the case was ABS - but the material surrounds the machine in the peripherals and in Commodore's later machines, and it shares the bisphenol A and the cumene chain with the epoxy and the polyester. Bisphenol A dissolved in aqueous caustic is reacted with phosgene in dichloromethane at 20-40 C with a tertiary amine catalyst; the chloroformate-terminated oligomer is washed and then polymerised by melt condensation at 250-290 C under 0.1-1 mbar.

children.name: Why it was chosen
children.description: Amorphous at 100-150% linear retention, glass transition near 145 C, tensile strength 60-70 MPa, and a notched Izod of 8-15 kJ/m2. It is the transparent tough polymer of the 1980s: sunglasses lenses, camera and instrument housings, the disc of a compact disc from 1982, and the dome of the keyboard on some machines. It was also the first engineering polymer to be explicitly targeted at the electronics market as a metal replacement.
children.note: The why it was chosen question is the reason polycarbonate is on a C64, not a property of a substance. The glass transition temperature is about 147 C, so this node's 145 C is slightly low, and compact discs are a major polycarbonate market. Not established: the 60-70 MPa tensile strength, the 8-15 kJ/m2 notched Izod, and the 100-150% linear retention figure.

Established: bisphenol A polycarbonate is a strong tough transparent engineering thermoplastic containing carbonate groups. Not established: the stated tonnages dates temperatures pressures yields and 1980s operating details as given.

children.name: Nylon 6 and nylon 6,6
children.description: The two polyamides that a 1980s machine used for its precision parts. Nylon 6,6 from adipic acid and hexamethylenediamine, or nylon 6 from caprolactam which itself comes from phenol. Both are condensation polymers of a diamine and an acid or of a lactam, and both need the phenol-aromatic chain, so both are downstream of the same cracker benzene as the ABS.

children.name: Nylon 6 from caprolactam
children.description: Caprolactam is opened with water at 250-270 C in a hydrolysis-polymerisation reactor under 1-15 bar, giving a nylon 6 with a very narrow molecular weight distribution because the chemistry is a step growth from a single monomer. Nylon 6 is the form used where a low melt viscosity matters, and it was the standard for the textile filament and the carpet fibre trade.

children.name: Caprolactam from phenol
children.description: Phenol hydrogenated to cyclohexanol, then dehydrogenated to cyclohexanone; cyclohexanone oximation to cyclohexanone oxime; the oxime rearranged with oleum (the Beckmann rearrangement, which expands the ring from six to seven members) to caprolactam, and the ammonium sulphate byproduct stripped and recycled. This is a five-step route from phenol and it is one of the longest petrochemical chains in the C64's ancestry. Phenol is hydrogenated over nickel or palladium at 120-180 C and 10-30 bar to cyclohexanol and dehydrogenated over copper at 250-300 C to cyclohexanone; the phenol comes from cumene and the cumene's propylene from the cracker, so nylon 6 is a third-generation descendant of the naphtha cracker. The Beckmann rearrangement needs concentrated sulphuric acid or oleum and produces 1.1-1.3 tonnes of ammonium sulphate per tonne of caprolactam, which has to be sold as fertiliser - the same sulphuric acid and the same fertiliser market the Claus sulphur plant feeds, which is why the industry was moving to oleum-free rearrangements over solid acid or a zeolite.
children.note: Phenol's own route: chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.phenol. Established: Caprolactam as lactam precursor overwhelmingly for nylon 6. Not established: the stated Beckmann rearrangement and process specifics as given.

Established: Caprolactam is opened with water at 250-270 C in a hydrolysis-polymerisation reactor under 1-15 bar, giving a nylon 6 with a very narrow molecular weight distribution because the c as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

Established: The two polyamides that a 1980s machine used for its precision parts as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Polyesters: PET, PBT and unsaturated polyester
children.description: Three families that share the same two feedstocks - ethylene glycol or propylene glycol, and a terephthalic or maleic/fumaric acid. PET in 1983 was overwhelmingly a fibre and bottle business, PBT was the engineering thermoplastic, and unsaturated polyester was the resin of the glass-reinforced mouldings. In a 1983 electronic assembly, the polyester was the transformer bobbin insulation, the relay base, the film capacitors, and any glass-filled moulding. PBT is polymerised by transesterification and polycondensation like PET but with butanediol, giving a melting point of about 225 C against PET's 260 C and a faster crystallisation, which is why it is the engineering grade: it sets in a 5-10 mm wall in 5-10 seconds where PET needs a minute.

children.name: PET from ethylene glycol and dimethyl terephthalate
children.description: Dimethyl terephthalate plus ethylene glycol transesterified at 180-280 C over an antimony or titanium catalyst, then polycondensed at 270-290 C under 1-50 mbar. The bottleneck is the transesterification methanol coproduct, which is recovered and returned to the terephthalate plant, so the plant is a big methanol recovery column. The route through dimethyl terephthalate rather than terephthalic acid was chosen in the 1970s and 1980s because the acid route's oxidation step had the corrosion and the purity problems; by the late 1980s the acid route had caught up. Para-xylene is oxidised to terephthalic acid over cobalt-manganese acetate at 175-225 C and 15-30 bar, and it is that oxidation rather than the polymerisation which is where the capital in a PET plant sits.
children.note: Established: Dimethyl terephthalate plus ethylene glycol transesterified at 180-280 C over an antimony or titanium catalyst, then polycondensed at 270-290 C under 1-50 mbar as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

Established: Three families that share the same two feedstocks - ethylene glycol or propylene glycol, and a terephthalic or maleic/fumaric acid as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Silicone (polydimethylsiloxane)
children.description: The only engineering polymer whose backbone is not carbon. Built from chlorosilanes made by the Rochow direct process - silicon plus methyl chloride over copper at 280-350 C - then hydrolyzed and condensed. In 1983 silicones were everywhere in electronics: as RTV sealing gaskets, as conformal coatings and encapsulants, as dielectric greases for the variable capacitors, and as the flexible key domes.

children.name: Rochow direct process
children.description: Metallurgical silicon plus methyl chloride over copper at 280-350 C gives dimethyldichlorosilane. The silicon comes from the quartz and coke reduction that the whole semiconductor industry depends on, so the silicone business and the chip business share an upstream - and share the same four-nines purity problem in their own way. The methyl chloride comes from the natural gas chlorination business, so the silicone plant and the semiconductor plant are both fed by chlorine and by methane.
children.note: Established: the Rochow direct process is the standard industrial route to organosilicon chlorosilanes reported by Rochow and Muller in the 1940s. Not established: the stated tonnages dates temperatures pressures yields and 1980s operating details as given.

children.name: Silicone rubber and fluids
children.description: The chlorosilane is hydrolyzed to a silanol and condensed with a silanol-terminated chain stopper, giving a silicone oil (low viscosity) or, with reinforcing silica and peroxide cure, a silicone rubber (elastomer). The 1980s mix in electronics was dominated by room-temperature-vulcanising silicone - a moisture-cured acetoxy or hydroxyl-terminated compound - because it cures in a fixture without heat, and by the fluorosilicone mould releases.

children.name: Conformal coating
children.description: A 20-100 micron film of room-temperature-vulcanising silicone brushed or dipped over a populated board, cured in humid air, to keep water, dust, sulfur dioxide and salt off the conductors. In 1980s practice it was used on power supplies and on automotive electronics rather than on consumer boards, and the industry debate was whether a conformal coating is better than a conformal coating removed badly - the rework risk is the problem. The C64's mainboard is generally described as uncoated.
children.note: Whether a given board was conformal-coated is a plant practice, not a material fact; most consumer boards of this era were not. Conformal coating is a practice described in commentary, not a substance or an operation.

Established: The chlorosilane is hydrolyzed to a silanol and condensed with a silanol-terminated chain stopper, giving a silicone oil (low viscosity) or, with reinforcing silica and peroxide cu as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.
Established: The only engineering polymer whose backbone is not carbon as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: POM (acetal homopolymer and copolymer)
children.description: Polyoxymethylene, made by polymerising formaldehyde - from the oxidation of methanol - either with an acetic anhydride chain transfer (giving the homopolymer, Delrin) or with a small amount of a diacetate comonomer (giving the Celcon-type copolymer). It is the 1980s precision engineering plastic: gears, cams, hinges, tolerance rings and the moving parts in a mechanism. The homopolymer route runs formaldehyde with acetic anhydride, the growing chain's hydroxyl end reacting with the anhydride to give an acetoxy end that stops polymerisation; the copolymer route uses formaldehyde with a 2-4% fraction of a methylol-substituted diacetate so the chain stops at an inert C-O-C end.

children.name: Formaldehyde from methanol
children.description: Methanol plus a controlled amount of oxygen over silver at 600-700 C, giving 25-35% formaldehyde in air (the Formox process), then concentrated to 60-70%. The methanol comes from synthesis gas, so this is a coal-or-gas-to-methanol-to-formaldehyde chain rather than a direct petroleum one - although in a 1980s plant the methanol would typically have been made from natural gas. Methanol plus about 0.4 mol of oxygen per mole over silver gauze at 600-700 C gives 25-35% formaldehyde at above 90% selectivity, in a packed bed of thousands of tubes.
children.note: Established: Methanol plus a controlled amount of oxygen over silver at 600-700 C, giving 25-35% formaldehyde in air (the Formox process), then concentrated to 60-70% as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Where POM sat in a 1983 machine
children.description: Small precision parts: the gear and cam of a fan, the hinges and catches, the insulator of a switch mechanism, the arm of a relay. In a 1983 home computer it was present in tens of grams at most, but it was there because nothing else moulded to a 0.05 mm tolerance with a low friction coefficient.
children.note: POM use in a C64 is likely but small and not documented in the sources used here. Where POM sat in a 1983 machine is a statement about the machine, not a substance.

Acetal chemistry is standard; the exact comonomer loadings vary by grade. Established: POM acetal homo and copolymer from formaldehyde with chain transfer or comonomer. Not established: the stated Delrin versus Celcon specifics and loading details as given.

children.name: Phenolic and amino thermosets
children.description: The two oldest synthetic plastics, still in a 1983 machine in the places where a thermoplastic will not do: phenolic for the switch and socket housings and the old-style bakelite knobs, and urea-formaldehyde and melamine-formaldehyde for the white insulating parts, the plug bodies and the coil-formers. Both are condensation networks: once cured they do not melt, and they are made from phenol or from urea, which comes from the same cumene and ammonia chain as everything else in this file.

children.name: Urea-formaldehyde and melamine-formaldehyde
children.description: Urea condensed with formaldehyde gives a thermoset used for the white insulation of plugs, sockets and coil formers, and melamine gives the tougher, heat-resistant version used for the panel fittings. Both are white, both are cheap, and both are moisture-sensitive, which is the defect that kept them out of anything structural. The urea comes from ammonia and carbon dioxide - the Haber-Bosch product - so this is a nitrogen branch rather than a hydrocarbon one. 2NH3 plus CO2 at 180-220 C and 15-25 bar gives ammonium carbamate, which dehydrates to urea, and the ammonia comes from the Haber-Bosch loop fed by steam-reformed natural gas: a white appliance plug of 1983 is, four steps back, a gas field.
children.note: Upstream: chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammonia.ammonia. Established: Urea and melamine formaldehyde thermosets for white insulation and fittings. Not established: the stated moisture and heat resistance specifics as given.

Established: The two oldest synthetic plastics, still in a 1983 machine in the places where a thermoplastic will not do: phenolic for the switch and socket housings and the old-style bakelite k as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

Established: A 1983 consumer electronic device used perhaps eight different engineering plastics and two rubbers as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.abs.note: The two feedstock edges make this branch terminate at the barrel: ABS is made of naphtha, and naphtha is a fraction of light sour crude. It also reaches butadiene, styrene and acrylonitrile through the three children below. Established: ABS resin plant, and the C64 case as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s specifics as given.

shared.chem.abs.other-polymers: Parent node for the other 1983 machine polymers: chem.pvc, chem.epoxy, chem.polycarbonate, chem.polyamide (nylon 6 / 6,6), chem.polyester (PET / PBT / UP), chem.silicone, chem.rubber, chem.pom and chem.thermosets.
shared.chem.pvc: PVC: acetylene-HCl and oxychlorination VCM, suspension polymerisation, lead and Ca/Zn stabilisation, phthalate plasticisers, and its use in the C64 power cord.
shared.chem.epoxy: DGEBA epoxy from bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin, amine / DDS / DDM / anhydride curing, branched and brominated epoxy, and the board / potting / adhesive / die-attach uses.
shared.chem.polyamide: Nylon 6,6 (adipic acid + HMDA, adiponitrile route) and nylon 6 (phenol to cyclohexanone to caprolactam to ring-opening polymerisation).
shared.chem.polyester: PET (DMT + EG, para-xylene to terephthalic acid), PBT, and unsaturated polyester from cumene-derived feedstocks.
shared.chem.polycarbonate: Bisphenol A polycarbonate by the interfacial phosgene route, and the phosgene / chlorine chain behind it.

chem.rubber.name: Elastomers: natural rubber, neoprene, EPDM
chem.rubber.description: Three rubbers for three different jobs in and around a 1983 machine: natural rubber for the feet and plinths and the moulded grips, neoprene for gaskets and the flexible cable jacket, and EPDM for the cable's weather-resistant insulation. The C64's case feet are elastomer pads stuck to the underside of the case, and they are the only rubber on the outside of the machine.
chem.rubber.note: Established: Three rubbers for three different jobs in and around a 1983 machine: natural rubber for the feet and plinths and the moulded grips, neoprene for gaskets and the flexible cable jack as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

shared.chem.silicone: Polydimethylsiloxane from the Rochow direct process, conformal coatings, and conductive elastomer key domes.
shared.chem.pom: Acetal (POM) from formaldehyde via the Formox partial oxidation.
shared.chem.thermosets: Phenolic (phenol-formaldehyde, hexamine) and urea / melamine formaldehyde thermosets.

chem.solvents.name: Solvents and degreasers in a 1980s plant
chem.solvents.description: Between half and three quarters of the organic solvent used in a 1980s electronics plant went into degreasing, mostly in a hot vapour degreaser. The solvent was almost always a chlorinated hydrocarbon - 1,1,1-trichloroethane or trichloroethylene in Europe and Asia, perchloroethylene in the United States - and the entire decade's regulatory story is the story of removing them. By 1990 in the United States, vapour degreasing with perchloroethylene and trichloroethylene was over, and what replaced it was isopropyl alcohol, N-methylpyrrolidone, or a hydrocarbon.

children.name: The vapour degreaser
children.description: A tank of boiling solvent with a cold condenser coil above it. Parts are lowered into the vapour, the vapour condenses on the part and washes the grease off, the condensate runs back into the boil tank, and the distilled clean solvent is pumped to the sump. It was astonishingly effective and astonishingly cheap, and it filled a plant with vapour - which is why it was also the plant's largest solvent loss and its largest occupational and air-emission exposure. A large plant had three or four machines with 20-40 litre tanks. The tank runs continuously with a boiling sump and a distilled-solvent reservoir, and in practice 5-20% of the charge had to be replaced each month through dragout, evaporation and the azeotroping of oil and water back into the tank.

children.name: Ultrasonic cleaner
children.description: A tank of hot solvent or water with a 20-80 kHz transducer. In 1983 the electronics plant used ultrasonic cleaning before the vapour degreaser for fine work - the watch crystals, the gears, the small press-fit parts - because a vapour degreaser will not clean a crevice and an ultrasonic tank will. It is also the machine that put solvent into the ultrasonic cleaner market, where 1,1,1-trichloroethane and perchloroethylene were the usual fills.
children.note: Not established: the frequency range quoted, the fill-solvent identities listed, and the claim that 1983 electronics plants used ultrasonic cleaning ahead of vapour degreasing for fine and crevice work.

children.name: The condenser and the tank
children.description: The machine has two working parts: a boiling sump at the bottom that supplies the vapour, and a water-cooled coil above it that condenses the vapour and drips it back clean. The whole design depends on the vapour being kept out of the room, so the machine had a lid and a draught, and the lid was opened to put the parts in - which is exactly when the vapour left. A 20-40 litre tank boiled away 1-3 litres of solvent a day in a well-run plant, and that vapour was the emission the regulator was measuring. Three losses ran at once - evaporation out of the open tank, drag-out on the parts and carry-over into the room ventilation - and the 1980s answers were a lid that stayed shut, a water-cooling coil with more area, a basket that dripped over the tank rather than the floor and, at the largest sites, a vapour condenser returning condensate to the distilled reservoir.

facts.label: Worst-case make-up
facts.value: up to 20% of tank charge per month

children.note: Established: The machine has two working parts: a boiling sump at the bottom that supplies the vapour, and a water-cooled coil above it that condenses the vapour and drips it back clean as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

Established: A tank of boiling solvent with a cold condenser coil above it as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: KPO process (from propylene)
children.description: Propylene plus acetone gives propylene oxide; propylene oxide isomerises to acetone over a base catalyst; acetone plus hydrogen is hydrogenated to isopropanol. The isomerisation-hydrogenation loop is the unit that makes the process economical, and the 1970s introduction of the low-temperature isomerisation catalysts was what made the KPO route beat the older acetone-hydrogenation route on the balance sheet. About 0.6 t of acetone per tonne of isopropanol is circulated and has to be bought in or made on site, so an isopropanol plant without an acetone source was not viable; that is why the isopropanol business grew up attached to cumene plants, and why the electronics cleaner's supply chain in 1983 ran back through cumene, phenol and the cracker.
children.note: The KPO acetone circulation ratio is commonly quoted around 0.6 t/t; exact values depend on the loop design. Established: KPO isopropanol route via propylene oxide isomerisation and hydrogenation. Not established: the stated circulation ratio and loop economics as given.

children.name: Regulation: why the solvent list changed
children.description: Three forces rewrote a 1980s solvent shelf. The US Clean Air Act's 1970 and 1977 amendments and the resulting state implementation plans constrained volatile organic compound emissions, and because a chlorinated degreaser is an emission source, they hit the degreaser directly. The 1983-1989 federal halogenated solvent action set dates for the chlorinated degreasers. And the Montreal Protocol, signed in 1987, removed the CFCs and the halon-cleaning gases.
children.note: A regulation or a treaty is a statement about the supply chain, not an operation in it. The whole regulation branch is commentary about why the solvent list changed; its children keep the detail. Established: Solvent regulation by clean air VOC and emissions constraints. Not established: the stated amendment and implementation specifics as given.

chem.solvents.note: Established: Between half and three quarters of the organic solvent used in a 1980s electronics plant went into degreasing, mostly in a hot vapour degreaser as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.isopropanol.name: Isopropyl alcohol (propan-2-ol)
chem.isopropanol.description: C3H8O, boiling 82.6 C, and by the mid-1980s the solvent that had taken over most of the cleaning work the chlorinated solvents used to do. It is flammable, it is cheap, it evaporates cleanly, it dissolves flux residue and oil, and it does not dissolve the ABS or the polycarbonate the way a chlorinated solvent can - which is exactly why it became the electronics cleaner. Almost all of it was made from propylene, so the electronics plant's replacement solvent is the same cracker as the case plastic. The older route hydrogenates acetone over copper or nickel-zinc at 100-150 C and 5-20 bar with 95-98% selectivity and was still fully in use in 1983; both routes end at the same molecule and differ only in whether the plant owns a propylene oxide unit.
chem.isopropanol.note: Not established: the 82.6 C boiling point, the 2-12% flammable range, the acetone-hydrogenation conditions of 100-150 C and 5-20 bar at 95-98% selectivity, and the 99.5-99.9% electronics purity. The two industrial routes - hydration of propene and hydrogenation of acetone - are standard.

chem.ethanol.name: Ethanol
chem.ethanol.description: C2H6O, boiling 78.4 C. In 1980s electronics it was a solvent and a cleaning fluid for a few specialist applications, and it was the fuel additive competing with MTBE for the octane that lead had given up. Chemically it can be made either by hydrating ethylene over phosphoric acid at 300 C and 60-70 bar, or by fermenting sugar. Both routes existed in 1983; the fermentation route made most of the world's ethanol in that decade because it was cheaper. The synthetic route hydrates ethylene with steam over phosphoric acid on silica at 280-330 C and 60-70 bar for 4-6% ethanol per pass with the off-gas recycled; the limit is thermodynamic, since the reaction is an equilibrium, and the industry spent decades on catalysts and on pervaporation and extractive distillation to get around it. Sugar from cane, beet or starch is fermented by yeast at 30-35 C for two to three days and rectified to 95% or dehydrated to absolute.
chem.ethanol.note: Established: C2H6O, boiling 78.4 C as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.sulfur.name: Elemental sulphur (brimstone)
chem.sulfur.description: Bright yellow solid sulphur, one of the four commodities - alongside crude, natural gas and coal - that a 1980s chemical plant could buy. It is used in vulcanisation, in the manufacture of sulphuric acid (which is then used to make titanium dioxide, fertiliser and phosphates), in 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid herbicides, and in the elemental sulphur vulcanisation of rubber. World sulphur production in 1983 was of the order of 8-10 million tonnes a year, essentially all of it recovered from H2S by Claus.
chem.sulfur.note: Not established: the world production and recovered-share figures quoted for 1983, and the end-use list as representative of early-1980s sulphur demand.

chem.rosin.name: Pine rosin (colophony)
chem.rosin.description: The sticky amber solid left when turpentine is distilled out of pine resin. Most rosin is made from pine stumps - the resinous wood left behind when a tree is cut for pulp - by destructive distillation: the stump is chipped, heated in a still to about 150-200 C, turpentine and pine oil come over, and the residue is the rosin, which is then graded by colour and by softening point. About 700,000-800,000 tonnes of rosin were made in the early 1980s, mostly in China, the United States and Brazil. The black liquor from a kraft pulp mill carries resin acids and fatty acids - tall oil - which is distilled into fatty acids, tall-oil fatty acids and a pitch and can be processed further into rosin equivalents.
chem.rosin.note: Rosin production figures for the early 1980s are order-of-magnitude; the chemistry and the softening point ranges are standard. Rosin (colophony) is a resin and is treated as a plastics material. Tall oil, which comes from a kraft mill, stays packaging.

shared.chem.photoresist: Positive diazonaphthoquinone-novolac photoresist chemistry, TMAH alkaline development, dehydration and hard bakes, and resist stripping.

chem.fab-chemicals.name: The wet chemicals of a 1980s silicon fab
chem.fab-chemicals.description: A 1983 wafer fab consumed tens of thousands of gallons a day of ultrapure water and a few thousand gallons of five electronic-grade acids, and its entire chemistry was aimed at one thing: keeping a few hundred metallic atoms per square centimetre off the wafer. This branch traces those chemicals - sulphuric acid, hydrogen peroxide, the buffered HF etch, the plasma etch gases, the dopant gases and the photoresist - back to the sulphur, the chlorine, the fluorine, the ammonia and the natural gas they were made from. The wet bench of the period used 10-20 litre recirculating baths of buffered HF and piranha, and the chemicals came in returnable fluoropolymer containers or, for the largest users, by bulk tanker.

children.name: Photoresist chemistry
children.description: The organic photoresists of 1983 were almost all positive-working diazonaphthoquinone resins on a novolac: the light-sensitive group is a diazonaphthoquinone sulphonate ester on a phenolic novolac made from phenol and formaldehyde. Exposing the resist converts the ester to a carboxylic acid, which makes the exposed resin soluble in the alkaline developer, so the image is positive. It is a strictly positive image because of the mechanism, not because of anything clever - the exposure destroys the very group that was holding the resin together. Development ran 0.2-0.3 N TMAH at 20-25 C by spray or immersion for 30-60 seconds, controlled to a fraction of a degree and a fraction of a per cent because the image is only about half a micrometre deep and the process window is correspondingly narrow; spray development, introduced in the early 1980s, removed the meniscus and particle problems of immersion and became the standard within a few years.

children.name: Dehydration bake and hard bake
children.description: A dehydration bake at 150-200 C to drive the water out of the spin-coated film before exposure, and a post-exposure hard bake at 120-180 C to crosslink or densify the remaining image. The hard bake is what makes the resist resistant to the plasma etch and to the buffered HF, and it is also what makes it harder to strip - which is why the industry moved to plasma stripping and to ozonised water by the late 1980s, and why the old solvent strippers (phenol and sulphuric acid) disappeared from the process. Stripping progressed through a phenolic-plus-sulphuric-acid liquid strip to an ozone/water clean and an oxygen plasma ash, driven by the ion contamination of the liquid strippers and by the fact that a hard-baked resist had become impossible to remove in a controlled way; plasma ashing runs at about 1 mbar and 250-400 C.
children.note: Resist stripping belongs to this step; the stripping numbers are in its description. Established: Dehydration and hard bakes for water removal and image hardening. Not established: the stated temperature ranges and plasma resistance specifics as given.

children.name: Polysilane and plasma-polymerised resists
children.description: The silicon-containing resists, in which a Si-Si backbone absorbs the deep ultraviolet and generates a silyl radical that crosslinks the exposed area. In 1983 they were in development for the 1 micron and sub-micron layers, and they are the reason the industry needed a deep-ultraviolet lithography tool at all. Their problem was exactly the same as everything else in this branch: a new chemistry with a contamination story attached.
children.note: Plasma-polymerised (polysilane) resists were a research topic through the 1980s; commercial DUV resists arrived later. The silicon-containing resists were a research topic through the 1980s, which is a statement about the state of the art rather than a step in the process. Confidence stays low.

Established: The organic photoresists of 1983 were almost all positive-working diazonaphthoquinone resins on a novolac: the light-sensitive group is a diazonaphthoquinone sulphonate ester on a as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Dopant sources
children.description: The chemicals that put boron, phosphorus and arsenic into the silicon. The chemistry here is a closed loop back to the ammonia, the chlorine and the fluorspar of the rest of this tree, and the whole business is about the fact that a dopant source is gaseous, toxic and must be delivered to a few cubic centimetres of reactor at a controlled partial pressure. Diffusion in 1983 used a gas or a solid source - phosphorus from phosphine or a doped oxide, boron from diborane or boron nitride, arsenic from arsine - in a furnace at 800-1,100 C.
children.note: The C64 chips were 2 micron NMOS designs of the late 1970s fabricated in the early 1980s; both diffusion and implantation were in use for that generation. Established: Dopant sources for boron phosphorus and arsenic closing to ammonia chlorine fluorspar and gas. Not established: the stated closed loop chemistries and generation specifics as given.

children.name: The purity ladder
children.description: The 1980s specification ladder, from technical grade to the electronic grade that a wafer demanded: a technical acid at about 5N with metals at tens and hundreds of parts per million; an electronic acid at about 8N; and the 9N-10N grade with a total metal content under 10 parts per billion. The reason the ladder existed was the relationship between a metal atom's concentration and the device: a wafer with 10 parts per billion of iron in a cubic centimetre of silicon has more iron atoms in the active volume than it has dopant atoms.
children.note: The purity ladder is a way of describing the chain, and its numbers are the substance of the node. Not established: the 5N, 8N and 9N-10N ladder and the sub-10 ppb total metal specification as 1980s figures. The comparison the node makes - that at 10 parts per billion the metal atoms in the active volume outnumber the dopant atoms - follows from the atomic density of silicon and is the part that holds.

chem.fab-chemicals.note: This node deliberately flags where practice diverged from today's; the specific substitution programmes and their dates vary by process step. Established: 1980s fab wet chemistry for metallic contamination control with ultrapure water and electronic grade acids. Not established: the stated consumption volumes bath sizes and container specifics as given.

chem.pcb-chemicals.name: The chemistry of making the board
chem.pcb-chemicals.description: A 1983 bare board goes through about eleven wet operations, and each one is a chemical plant: laminate impregnation and pressing, copper foil treatment, dry-film lamination, alkaline or ferric etching, drilling, electroless copper, electroplating, solder mask, silkscreen, and a final clean. The C64's board is a single-layer FR-4 board with through-hole parts, which is the simplest case - one copper layer, no plating on the holes - and that removes the electroless copper and the gold entirely. Solder mask and silkscreen are two inks rather than one operation: the mask is an epoxy or acrylate screen-printed or curtain-coated through a 100-150 micron stencil and cured at 150 C, the green being a phthalocyanine green in a novolac epoxy vehicle, and the legend is a separate white epoxy ink cured the same way through a 150-200 micron stainless mesh.

children.name: Dry-film photoresist
children.description: A 25-40 micron dry film laminated hot onto the copper - a polyester or polyethylene terephthalate base carrying an acrylate photopolymer and an acrylated monomer that crosslinks on exposure. The exposure crosslinks the acrylate, so the exposed areas become insoluble and the unexposed areas are developed away, and the resulting image is negative - the opposite polarity to the wafer resists of the same decade, and the reason the two industries use opposite conventions for the same word. This is the clearest dated marker in the board chemistry.

children.name: Laminating the dry film
children.description: The dry film comes off a protective polyester or polyethylene release liner, is laid on the cleaned and dried copper, and is squeezed onto it by a hot laminator at 110-150 C and 3-5 bar with a silicone rubber roller. The rollers are silicone because the film must not stick to them and the liner must, and the whole operation is a controlled vacuum or a controlled pressure depending on the machine: without the pressure, the air trapped between the film and the copper becomes a bubble and the bubble becomes an etch defect.
children.note: Established: The dry film comes off a protective polyester or polyethylene release liner, is laid on the cleaned and dried copper, and is squeezed onto it by a hot laminator at 110-150 C and 3- as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

The commercial introduction of aqueous-developable dry films dates from the early 1980s; by the middle of the decade they were the standard in North America. Not established: the 25-40 micron film thickness, the polyester (PET) or polyethylene base, the acrylate photopolymer and acrylated monomer chemistry, and the negative image convention as a description of 1980s dry film. The claim that aqueous-developable films arrived in the early 1980s and were standard in North America by the middle of the decade is the softest statement in this node.

children.name: Copper etching
children.description: Ferric chloride at 35-42 degrees Baume, or cupric chloride, dissolves the exposed copper in 30-60 minutes. Ferric chloride was the 1980s default: cheap, fast, and it etches copper at a rate that keeps the undercut manageable. Its problems were regeneration (the spent etchant is worthless unless it is oxidised back, which needs chlorine or a peroxide and an electrolytic cell) and the ferric ion's attack on the epoxy of the laminate if the etch went long. By the early 1980s the alkaline sodium persulphate etch was spreading because it regenerated in place with peroxide and sodium hydroxide and because it would etch a finer line.
children.note: Established: Ferric chloride at 35-42 degrees Baume, or cupric chloride, dissolves the exposed copper in 30-60 minutes as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Plating baths
children.description: A 1983 double-sided board is copper plated in an acid copper sulphate bath (with levelers and brighteners), then tin plated or gold plated. The chemistry is a small industry of its own: a copper electroplate with organic additives at 2-6 A/dm2 and 25-30 C; a tin or tin-lead bath; and, for the connectors, a nickel and gold stack. Immersion gold is not electroplated gold - it is a displacement reaction, a few hundred nanometres of gold out of a complexing bath, over a nickel layer that the board chemistry has to deposit first.

children.name: Immersion gold over electroless nickel
children.description: Electroless nickel-phosphorus (hypophosphite reducer) gives a hard, corrosion-resistant, solderable surface, and immersion gold in a cyanide-complexed bath gives the contact surface its low contact resistance. The gold bath contains a complexing agent (EDTA, a phosphate or a cyanide) whose job is to hold the gold in solution so the surface reaction is slow and self-limiting at a few hundred nanometres. For a C64's single-layer board none of this is used - the pads are bare copper with a surface treatment.

children.name: Electroless nickel-phosphorus and its reducer
children.description: The nickel under a gold surface is deposited by a chemical reduction: hypophosphite gives up a hydrogen atom to the nickel ion on the surface and the nickel comes down as metal, with phosphorus co-deposited at 3-9 wt% to make the layer hard and amorphous. The bath is nickel chloride or sulphate at 5-10 g/L, hypophosphite at 10-30 g/L, and 85-95 C for 30-90 minutes, and its uniformity is the reason it is the standard under immersion gold - it coats a via wall as evenly as it coats a pad.
children.note: Established: The nickel under a gold surface is deposited by a chemical reduction: hypophosphite gives up a hydrogen atom to the nickel ion on the surface and the nickel comes down as metal, wi as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.
Immersion gold chemistry and thickness are process-specific; the general mechanism (a displacement reaction with a complexing agent) is what is reliable here.

Established: A 1983 double-sided board is copper plated in an acid copper sulphate bath (with levelers and brighteners), then tin plated or gold plated as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Chlorine-free chemistry, and why it took twenty years
children.description: Nothing in the 1983 process list was unusual except that it was chlorinated: ferric chloride, trichloroethane, a chlorinated epoxy and a brominated one. By 1995-2000 the industry had moved to alkaline etching, alkaline dry-film development, and epoxy laminates with a non-halogenated flame retardant system - and the drivers were the Montreal-adjacent ozone debate, the effluent limits on copper and hexavalent chromium, and the RoHS-style restrictions that arrived later. This node is the marker for where 1983 practice differs from today, not a description of a 1983 process. The industry answer by 1995-2000 was alkaline etching, alkaline dry-film development and epoxy laminates with a non-halogenated flame retardant, driven by the ozone debate, effluent limits on copper and hexavalent chromium, and the restrictions that came later.
children.note: This is deliberately a forward-looking marker node; the substitution dates vary by region and by regulation. It marks where 1983 practice differs from today and is not itself a 1983 process.

chem.pcb-chemicals.note: The solder mask and the silkscreen legend are two inks and one cure rather than two separate operations. Established: Board wet operations including laminate plating etching and solder mask. Not established: the stated eleven operation count and sequence specifics as given.

chem.solder-chemicals.name: Solder, flux and rosin
chem.solder-chemicals.description: A wave-soldered through-hole board of 1983 is assembled with a 60/40 tin-lead solder and a rosin flux core. The two facts that make this branch worth tracing are that the flux is pine rosin - a forestry product, the clearest non-fossil material in a C64 - and that the solder is 40% lead by weight, which is the reason solder is now the single most restricted substance in electronics. By the late 1980s the halide-free no-clean flux had arrived and was beginning to replace the RMA flux that the C64 was assembled with. A solder joint is not tin-lead metal. The technology change that arrived in the middle and late 1980s was a flux with no halide at all, built on organic acids and esters rather than amine hydrochlorides and leaving an ionic residue mild enough that the board did not have to be washed.

children.name: Board cleaning after soldering
children.description: The flux residue had to come off, and the 1980s answer was either an organic solvent (1,1,1-trichloroethane, or isopropanol after 1983, or a mixture) or an aqueous detergent wash. The solvent was the same molecule as the degreaser, and its replacement by isopropanol is one of the cleanest single substitutions in the file: the board plant's solvent went from a chlorinated hydrocarbon to a propylene oxidation product in about two years, for regulatory and cost reasons rather than performance ones.
children.note: Not established: the solvent identities and timing claim for the shift to isopropanol after 1983, and the characterisation of that substitution as regulatory- and cost-driven rather than performance-driven.

children.name: The thermal profile is the process
children.description: The reason the soldering chemistry is mostly temperature management: a through-hole joint sees 250-260 C for one to three seconds in the wave, which is enough to make the intermetallic and not enough to damage the flux or the laminate; a surface-mount joint sees a 220-245 C peak for 30-120 seconds in a reflow oven or a hot plate. Over-temperature grows the intermetallic and dulls the joint; under-temperature makes a cold solder joint that fails in service. Every one of these numbers is a chemical property, because the eutectic is a chemical fact.
children.note: Not established: the wave and reflow temperature and time ranges quoted, and the intermetallic-growth and cold-joint accounts for over- and under-temperature soldering.

facts.label: Halide content
facts.value: not detected (<0.001% by the standard test)

chem.solder-chemicals.note: No-clean fluxes arrived commercially in the mid-1980s; the halide-free specification is measured against a standard ion chromatography test, and the figure quoted for it is halide not detected - under 0.001% by that test. Established: Solder flux and rosin branch with wave soldering practice. Not established: the stated arrival dates and test thresholds as given.

shared.chem.chlorine: [EXTERNAL - expected from the chlorine/metal file, not defined here] Chlorine from brine electrolysis. The brine-electrolysis node is metal.chlor-alkali.
shared.chem.glass-fiber: [EXTERNAL - minerals/fibres file] E-glass for FR-4; referenced in chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.
shared.chem.silica-fiber: [EXTERNAL - minerals/fibres file] Fused silica and quartz fibre; the sand-derived silica chain of this file starts at chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catalyst-manufacture.silica-support.soda-silica.
shared.chem.barium-carbonate: [EXTERNAL - minerals file] Barium carbonate / barite filler; barite as a drilling weighting agent is under chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.barite.
shared.facility.nitrogen.atmospheric-air: Atmospheric nitrogen - the air-fractionation leaf. Requested as chem.nitrogen; use this id. Also see chem.nitrogen-pid: the nitrogen branch under chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-r.name: Heat removal from the ammoxidation
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-r.description: The ammoxidation gives out roughly 1,000 kJ per kilogram of acrylonitrile, and the reactor has to be taken out at a rate the metallurgy can live with. That is the single hardest engineering problem in the process, and it is why the original SOVERE design was a salt-bath reactor and why the later fluidised beds were better: the fluidised catalyst carries its own heat around, so the temperature is uniform and there is no hot spot to crack the catalyst.

children.name: Molten salt bath reactor
children.description: A tubular reactor immersed in a bath of a molten nitrate-nitrite salt (the working point is around 300-330 C), with the bed of catalyst on an inert support inside the tube. It is a beautiful heat-transfer arrangement and a nasty maintenance one: the salt is oxidising, the reactor is at 400-450 C inside, and a tube failure means salt into the process. By 1983 it was being replaced by the fluidised bed for exactly this reason.
children.note: Salt bath temperatures are quoted in the 250-330 C range depending on the salt mix; the precise working point varies between licensors.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-r.note: Established: The ammoxidation gives out roughly 1,000 kJ per kilogram of acrylonitrile, and the reactor has to be taken out at a rate the metallurgy can live with as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.name: Naphtha hydrotreating before the cracker
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.description: The cracker feedstock was almost never straight-run naphtha. It was hydrotreated to under 0.5 wt% total sulphur (often 0.05-0.3 wt%) and under 0.5 ppmw nitrogen, because sulphur poisons the reforming and cracking catalysts and nitrogen poisons the polymerisation catalysts downstream. Naphtha hydrotreating is the first place refinery chemistry meets polymer chemistry.

children.name: Sour water stripper
children.description: The hydrogenating reactors make water and ammonia, and the separator water carries dissolved H2S and NH3. A stripper removes them, otherwise the recycled hydrogen carries ammonia into the cracker, where ammonia poisons the polymerisation catalysts and shows up as a colour defect in the polymer.
children.note: Established: The hydrogenating reactors make water and ammonia, and the separator water carries dissolved H2S and NH3 as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.note: Established: The cracker feedstock was almost never straight-run naphtha as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.crude.reservoir.name: The reservoir: where the oil sits
chem.crude.reservoir.description: Oil exists in pore space between grains of sandstone or in fractures and vugs of carbonate, held down by an overburden of rock and by an overlying gas cap or water. This is the physical thing that the whole upstream industry is trying to reach. Oil squeezed out of the source rock moves updip along a permeable sandstone or through a fault until it is trapped, driven by a buoyancy of roughly 0.2-0.4 degrees API per 1,000 ft, with the column height set by the capillary entry pressure of the seal.

children.name: Sedimentary basin
children.description: A subsiding basin in which organic mud is buried, buried deeper, cooked and squeezed; the whole petroleum system is source, maturation, migration, reservoir, seal and trap, and it takes 1-100 million years of that history. By 1983 the world's producing basins were a few hundred in number, with the Middle East and the Gulf of Mexico dominating reserves.
children.note: Established: A subsiding basin in which organic mud is buried, buried deeper, cooked and squeezed, the whole petroleum system is source, maturation, migration, reservoir, seal and trap, and it as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.crude.reservoir.note: Established: Oil exists in pore space between grains of sandstone or in fractures and vugs of carbonate, held down by an overburden of rock and by an overlying gas cap or water as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.name: Mud acid (HCl + HF)
chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.description: Hydrochloric acid to dissolve carbonate, with 1-3 wt% HF to attack the clay in sandstone and 2-5 wt% HF in carbonate muds. The reason for mud acid was a reserve shift: by the early 1980s mudstone was around 80% of world oil reserves, and mudstone cannot be treated with pure HCl because of its clay reactivity. Acid is pumped downhole in steel or titanium coils, with corrosion inhibitors (amines, thiourea) and a surfactant.
chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.note: HF and HCl chemistry is the same as chem.fab-chemicals in this file; HF from fluorspar, HCl from chlorine. HCl and HF are ingredients, not components: both are now "from" edges. The hydrogen route that makes the hydrochloric acid is chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen, which absorbed the deleted "hydrogen to hydrochloric acid" step.

chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.name: Acid-resistant tubing
chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.description: Coiled tubing and the acid lines were, by the mid-1980s, routinely nickel alloy - a nickel-molybdenum alloy such as Alloy C-276 or a titanium grade - rather than carbon steel, because the inhibitor was never perfect and the steel was never quite good enough. Nickel alloys and titanium come out of a metallurgical chain rather than a petrochemical one, but it is the acid chemistry that puts them into this operation.
chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.note: Alloy selection for acid service is metallurgy rather than petrochemistry; this node marks the boundary of the subsystem. Acid-resistant tubing is used by the acidising step, not contained in the inhibitor.

chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.nickel-ca.name: Nickel reforming catalyst
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.nickel-ca.description: Nickel on alumina, or the older nickel-chromium used in the pre-1957 Topsoe SMR-180. By the 1980s the modern multi-bed reformer ran 25-40 tubes of 10-16 inch diameter at 30-50 bar, with an inlet temperature near 550 C and an outlet at 850-870 C, burning gas in a process furnace alongside the tubes.
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.nickel-ca.note: Not established: the tube count and dimensions, pressures and inlet and outlet temperatures quoted for early-1980s multi-bed reformers, and how widely the older nickel-chromium formulation persisted.

chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammoni.name: Ammonia synthesis catalyst
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammoni.description: The Haber-Bosch catalyst is promoted iron: magnetite reduced to alpha-iron, promoted with potassium oxide and with alumina or calcium oxide. Ruthenium is better by an order of magnitude but was, in 1983, still a research curiosity as far as ammonia plants were concerned. The catalyst is made by melting magnetite with the promoters, granulating, and reducing it in situ with hydrogen, and a 1980s ammonia plant had a few hundred tonnes of it.
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammoni.note: Established: The Haber-Bosch catalyst is promoted iron: magnetite reduced to alpha-iron, promoted with potassium oxide and with alumina or calcium oxide as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.to-vinyl.name: Mercuric chloride catalyst
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.to-vinyl.description: Anhydrous HCl is adsorbed onto a mercuric chloride-charcoal catalyst and ethyne adds across it. The catalyst is a genuine environmental liability: mercury lost from a large acetylene plant was tens of kilograms a year, and by the 1980s both West Germany and the Netherlands were restricting mercury emission from chlor-alkali and vinyl chloride plants.
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.to-vinyl.note: Mercury restriction dates vary by country; German and Dutch controls on mercury from chlor-alkali and acetylene plants began in the 1970s and tightened through the 1980s-90s.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Drilling fluid for a gas well
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.simple_name: Drilling fluid for a gas well
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: Gas wells were drilled with the same bentonite mud as oil wells, with two differences: a low filter loss was mandatory because filtrate invasion had to be reversed before logging, and a gas-cut mud had to be controlled because entrained gas reduced hydrostatic pressure and made the well hard to control. The standard 1980s control was a mechanical gas trap plus defoamer.
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.note: The mud is the same oilfield bentonite mud as on an oil well. Established: Gas well drilling with bentonite mud requiring low filter loss and gas cut control. Not established: the stated filtration logging reversal and gas control specifics as given.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Triethylene glycol
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: A heavy glycol made by reacting ethylene oxide with diethylene glycol; the standard dehydration absorbent because of its low vapour pressure at the contactor temperature. The 1980s trend was towards 95 wt% TEG purity, because glycol vapour carried upstream into a gas turbine or a carburettor was a real emission problem.
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.note: Glycol synthesis is the ethylene oxide branch: chem.ethylene.ethylene-glycol. Established: Triethylene glycol as standard dehydration absorbent. Not established: the stated 95 wt percent purity trend and carryover specifics as given.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Alkanolamine
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: Monoethanolamine (MEA, primary), diethanolamine (DEA, secondary), methyldiethanolamine (MDEA, tertiary). MDEA was the growth amine of the 1980s because it does not form carbamate with CO2, so its degradation and reboiler duty are lower; the penalty is a slower absorption rate and a lower equilibrium loading.
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.note: Not established: the concentration and reboiler ranges quoted, and the claim that MDEA was the growth amine of the 1980s with lower reboiler duty at the cost of slower absorption.

chem.pvc.vcm.name: Vinyl chloride monomer
chem.pvc.vcm.description: C2H3Cl, boiling at -13.4 C, so it is a liquid only under pressure. It is a proven human carcinogen (angiosarcoma of the liver), it is flammable from 4-33% in air, and it is the reason the PVC industry of the 1980s had an unusual public health profile. In 1983 world VCM capacity was of the order of 9-10 million tonnes a year. Oxychlorination of ethylene with chlorine and hydrogen chloride over copper(II) chloride at 150-250 C and 4-10 bar gives vinyl chloride at 85-95% selectivity, and the chlorine-to-HCl ratio decides whether the plant makes ethylene dichloride for the chlorinated-solvent business or vinyl chloride.
chem.pvc.vcm.note: Vinyl chloride monomer is among the largest petrochemicals, is a flammable gas and is a proven carcinogen; angiosarcoma of the liver was reported from 1974. Not established: the -13.4 C boiling point, the 4-33 vol% flammable range, the 9-10 Mt/yr 1983 world capacity, and the 150-250 C, 4-10 bar CuCl2 oxychlorination at 85-95% selectivity.

chem.pvc.vcm.storage.name: VCM storage and inhibition
chem.pvc.vcm.storage.description: Bulk VCM in a refrigerated atmospheric tank at 10-15 C with a nitrogen blanket, or in a pressure vessel. It is inhibited against polymerisation with a phenolic or an organic peroxide, and it is kept below 50 C because vinyl chloride is a powerful inhibitor of its own polymerisation - a fact the industry discovered painfully, and which turned out to be a safety feature once understood.
chem.pvc.vcm.storage.note: Not established: the storage-temperature range, blanket, inhibitor and temperature-limit claims quoted, and the account of vinyl chloride self-inhibition as a painful discovery turned safety feature.

chem.pvc.polymerisation.suspending-agent.name: PVA suspending agent
chem.pvc.polymerisation.suspending-agent.description: Partially hydrolysed polyvinyl alcohol at 0.5-2% of the water phase, with a second colloid stabilizer if needed. It is the same PVA chemistry as the suspension polystyrene suspending agent - one more appearance of a polymer from the vinyl acetate chain doing structural work in a different polymer's reactor.
chem.pvc.polymerisation.suspending-agent.note: PVA suspending agents came from the same vinyl acetate hydrolysis used for the emulsion polymerisation of PVAc; the two uses share the chemistry.

chem.pvc.polymerisation.initiator.name: Initiator and chain transfer
chem.pvc.polymerisation.initiator.description: Acyl peroxide or a persulphate at 0.05-0.5%, with a chain transfer agent (often chloroform, tetrachloromethane or an ester) to control molecular weight. The transfer agents are chlorinated for a reason: they also terminate the radicals that would otherwise go on to make chlorinated by-products, and the PVC industry has always been able to sell them.
chem.pvc.polymerisation.initiator.note: Not established: the initiator dosage range quoted, the chain-transfer agents listed, and the dual-role claim that chlorinated transfer agents also suppress chlorinated by-products.

chem.pvc.stabilisation.name: Heat stabilisation, and the lead problem
chem.pvc.stabilisation.description: PVC is unstable above about 140 C: the dehydrochlorination produces HCl, which catalyses more dehydrochlorination, which is why unstabilised PVC cannot be processed at all. The 1980s stabiliser systems were lead salts - dibasic lead phosphite, tribasic lead sulphate, lead stearate - which are excellent scavengers and which put lead into millions of tonnes of consumer product. Calcium-zinc systems based on stearates and organic co-stabilisers were the 1980s technology that began to displace them, and the reason is health regulation rather than performance.
chem.pvc.stabilisation.note: Established: PVC is unstable above about 140 C: the dehydrochlorination produces HCl, which catalyses more dehydrochlorination, which is why unstabilised PVC cannot be processed at all as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.pvc.plasticiser.name: Plasticisers
chem.pvc.plasticiser.description: A flexible PVC is PVC with 30-60 parts per 100 of a liquid plasticiser, and the plasticiser is where most of the toxicology lived. Di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP, DOP) was the standard from the 1950s into the 1990s, made by esterifying phthalic anhydride with 2-ethylhexanol - itself from butyraldehyde or oxo synthesis of propylene and a C6 or C8 fraction. In 1983 there was no accepted evidence of harm at the levels in use, and the reappraisal came later.
chem.pvc.plasticiser.note: Established: A flexible PVC is PVC with 30-60 parts per 100 of a liquid plasticiser, and the plasticiser is where most of the toxicology lived as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.pvc.vcm.acetylene-route.mercury.name: Mercury in the PVC plant
chem.pvc.vcm.acetylene-route.mercury.description: The mercury chloride catalyst is a genuine environmental liability. A 1980s European PVC plant was a mercury emitter at tens of kilograms a year, and by the mid-1980s both the German and the Dutch authorities were requiring either catalyst recovery or a switch to the oxychlorination route. The engineering answer, delivered in the 1980s, was a mercury recovery system on the reactor effluent that stripped the mercury into the hydrochloric acid stream and concentrated it to about 20%.
chem.pvc.vcm.acetylene-route.mercury.note: The specific national dates and legal instruments for mercury limits in the PVC industry are jurisdiction-specific; the general direction and the mercury-recovery technology are well established.

chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.name: Brine (salt)
chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.description: A saturated sodium chloride solution, made from a salt mine or a solar evaporation pond, purified to remove calcium and magnesium because they foul the membrane and foul the diaphragm. Salt is the one raw material in this branch that is dug out of the ground rather than taken from a refinery, and it is the true end of the chlorine chain.
chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.note: Chlor-alkali electrolysis is conducted in a mercury, diaphragm or membrane cell, so the fouling this node describes is real. Not established: the saturated brine feed, the calcium and magnesium removal specification, and the Stassfurt, Salina and Hockley attributions.

chem.styrene.divinylbenzene.name: Divinylbenzene
chem.styrene.divinylbenzene.description: A 40/60 to 80/20 mixture of the two divinylbenzene isomers made by the same ethylbenzene route with a second vinyl group. About 1-2% of the styrene monomer, and essentially all of it goes into ion exchange resins and into the crosslinking monomer of unsaturated polyester. The cation exchange resin in the water treatment plant of a plastics factory is a styrene-divinylbenzene copolymer, so this molecule sits quietly in the supply chain of almost everything else in this file.
chem.styrene.divinylbenzene.note: Not established: the isomer-ratio range and treat-rate figures quoted, the stated production route, and the end-use and water-plant resin claims.

chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.be.name: Benzoyl peroxide initiator
chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.be.description: Dibenzoyl peroxide, dosed at 0.05-0.5 wt%, thermally decomposed at 60-90 C to give a benzoyloxy radical and then a phenyl radical. It leaves a benzoic acid residue in the polymer and a trace of styrene in the reactor bottoms, which is why polystyrene made with it has a characteristic faint smell and a yellowing tendency that the 1980s stabiliser industry existed to fix.
chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.be.note: Benzoyl peroxide is a chain-growth radical initiator. Its half-life is one hour at 92 C and one minute at 131 C, so a 60-90 C dosing temperature is low for this initiator and the operating figure needs checking. Not established: the 0.05-0.5 wt% loading and the benzoic acid residue and yellowing claim.

chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.su.name: Suspending agent for suspension polystyrene
chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.su.description: Gelatin, methylcellulose or polyvinyl alcohol, at 0.1-1% of the water phase. It has to hold the bead together without letting the bead coalesce, and the whole engineering of suspension polystyrene is the engineering of that balance: too little and the beads fuse, too much and the bead has a hard skin that traps monomer and leaves styrene odour in the bead.
chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.su.note: Not established: the dosage range quoted for the water phase, and the account of bead coalescence versus hard-skin monomer entrapment as the central operating balance.

chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.iron-cataly.name: Promoted iron oxide catalyst
chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.iron-cataly.description: Magnetite or hematite promoted with potassium oxide, copper oxide and sometimes molybdenum or chromium, formed as extruded rings or as a granular bed. Steam is used as a diluent to keep the partial pressure low and to suppress coking, and a trace of a polymerisation inhibitor (sulfolane or a chlorinated hydrocarbon) is fed to hold the polymer down.
chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.iron-cataly.note: Catalytic dehydrogenation of ethylbenzene gives hydrogen and styrene, and over 99% of ethylbenzene production goes to styrene. Not established: magnetite or hematite promoted with potassium oxide, copper oxide and molybdenum, the extruded ring or granular bed form, the 600-700 C, 40-50% per-pass conversion and 90-93% selectivity, and the sulfolane polymerisation inhibitor.

chem.styrene.ethylbenzene.zeolite-cataly.name: Shape-selective alkylation catalyst
chem.styrene.ethylbenzene.zeolite-cataly.description: A zeolite whose pore geometry lets a benzene molecule in, lets ethylbenzene out and does not let diethylbenzene in - the same shape selectivity that let ZSM-5 crack gasoline to high-octane and propylene, and that later let MFI zeolites make para-xylene. One catalyst family, three jobs, all in this file.
chem.styrene.ethylbenzene.zeolite-cataly.note: Not established: the selectivity figure quoted, the pore-geometry account of admitting benzene while excluding diethylbenzene, and the stated kinship with ZSM-5 and MFI para-xylene catalysis.

chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery..name: Sulfolane
chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery..description: Tetrahydrothiophene-1,1-dioxide, a polar aprotic solvent that dissolves aromatics preferentially to paraffins and is thermally stable and non-corrosive. It is also the inhibitor chemistry's solvent cousin: sulfolane is used as a polymerisation inhibitor in the styrene dehydrogenation reactors, and it belongs to a small family of molecules - NMP, sulfolane, dimethylformamide - that turns up in three different jobs in this file.
chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery..note: Not established: the thermal-stability and non-corrosiveness claims, the inhibitor-use claim in styrene dehydrogenation reactors, and the stated family relationship with NMP and dimethylformamide across jobs in this chain.

chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..name: Rosin acid soap emulsifier
chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..description: Sodium or potassium salts of pine rosins (about 60% abietic acid) and of tall oil fatty acids, mixed 50/50. Two jobs: the rosin part stabilises the polymer against oxidation, and the fatty acid part controls the particle size and the rate. Rosin emulsifiers also give the rubber a slightly tacky surface, which is why tread compounds still add tackifying resin.
chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..note: The rosin itself is chem.rosin, which also supplies the solder flux.
