Established: Rosin acid soap emulsifier with abietic acid stabilisation and fatty acid particle control. Not established: the stated 60 percent abietic and 50-50 mix specifics as given.

chem.butadiene.polymerisation.structures.name: The four polybutadiene microstructures
chem.butadiene.polymerisation.structures.description: cis-1,4 (the elastomer; the chain is flexible below its glass transition), trans-1,4 (the chain is regular and crystalline, so it is a plastic not a rubber), 1,2-vinyl (a pendant vinyl group, also rubbery but with a high glass transition because of the pendant group), and 3,4-vinyl (rare). The rubbery ones are cis-1,4 and 1,2; the ratio between them is set by temperature, catalyst and solvent, and it is why polybutadiene rubber has a glass transition near -100 C and is the most flexible of the common rubbers. The ratio of the four microstructures is a dial, not an accident: a rare-earth or titanium coordination catalyst gives cis-1,4, lithium butyllithium gives more 1,2-vinyl in a polar solvent and more cis-1,4 in a hydrocarbon, and temperature moves it again.

facts.label: trans-1,4
facts.value: crystalline, Tg about -80 C but Tm about +100 C

chem.butadiene.polymerisation.structures.note: Glass transition values for elastomers vary a few degrees with grade and measurement.

chem.butadiene.polymerisation.neodymium-.name: Neodymium oxide and neodymium metal
chem.butadiene.polymerisation.neodymium-.description: The high-cis polybutadiene catalyst wants the neodymium as a soluble organometallic rather than as the oxide, so the oxide comes out of the separation plant, is converted to a halide and then alkylated, and is dosed at a few hundredths of a percent. The neodymium is the fraction of the bastnasite that nobody had predicted would matter: a light rare earth sold by the tonne for glass polishing and ceramic glaze suddenly became worth several times its price per kilogram for a rubber catalyst, and by the mid-1980s the separation plants were being run to make more of the neodymium-praseodymium fraction than of anything else. A C64's rubber therefore begins in a carbonatite in California or an iron-ore pit in Inner Mongolia, passes through a mixer-settler train several hundred stages long, and ends up dosed into a hydrocarbon diluent at about one part in a thousand.

facts.label: Form used
facts.value: a soluble neodymium alkyl, not the oxide; the oxide is halided and alkylated first

facts.label: Dose
facts.value: a few hundredths of a percent of the butadiene charge

facts.label: Why neodymium
facts.value: praseodymium was co-produced with it, and the two together soon outsold the polishing-grade fractions

chem.butadiene.polymerisation.neodymium-.note: The catalyst chemistry and the origin of the ore are well documented; medium confidence on the dose level and on the timing of the shift in what the separation plants chose to make.

chem.butadiene.polymerisation.lithium-ca.name: Butyllithium
chem.butadiene.polymerisation.lithium-ca.description: A pyrophoric organolithium, always supplied as a 10-20% solution in hexane and never in bulk. In 1980s practice it was the initiator for the solution polymerisation of polybutadiene and for the SBR made by anionic polymerisation, and its manufacture from lithium metal and butyl chloride or butane was a speciality chemical operation with a lot of solvent handling.
chem.butadiene.polymerisation.lithium-ca.note: Butyllithium is among the most used organolithium reagents. Not established: the 10-20 wt% solution in hexane, its pyrophoricity as a handling fact for this application, and the manufacture from lithium metal and butyl chloride or butane.

chem.butadiene.sources.cracker-c4.name: Cracker C4 stream
chem.butadiene.sources.cracker-c4.description: A NGL stream of 1-butene (15-25%), cis-2-butene (10-15%), trans-2-butene (30-35%), isobutylene (15-25%) and isobutane/isopentane, with butadiene at 20-30% of the C4 - which is 4-6% of the cracker's total hydrocarbon output. The butadiene has to be taken out by a separate, very large unit.
chem.butadiene.sources.cracker-c4.note: C4 compositions depend heavily on cracker severity and feedstock; the ranges given are typical naphtha-cracker figures.

chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.furfural.name: Furfural as the extractive solvent
chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.furfural.description: Furfural (furan-2-carbaldehyde) made from furfural-bark or from pentoses in bagasse hemihydrate pulping, with a boiling point of 161 C and a high selectivity for diene over alpha-olefin. It was the original Sounsby solvent and its dominant drawback is that it polymerises in the presence of acid, so the unit had to be kept dry and inhibited and it consumed make-up solvent continuously. The solvent is made from pentosan hemicellulose - a fifth of the dry weight of a hardwood - by acid and steam treatment of rice hulls, corn cobs or bagasse, so the extractant's own feedstock is agricultural residue rather than petroleum.
chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.furfural.note: Furfural is a biomass-derived chemical rather than a petrochemical one, and it is the one clear biomass input in the C4 chain.

chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.nmp.name: N-methylpyrrolidone as the extractive solvent
chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.nmp.description: NMP (a strongly polar, high-boiling amide, 202 C) replaced furfural because it does not polymerise and needs less make-up. NMP was the 1980s solvent of choice and it is the same molecule that later arrived in the electronics plant as the chlorinated-solvent replacement for 1,1,1-trichloroethane. NMP is made from butanone and ethylenediamine, and its methylating agent is methanol: CO plus hydrogen at 200-300 C and 50-100 bar over a copper-zinc-aluminium catalyst, so the hydrogen in it comes from a reformer and the carbon monoxide from reformed methane.
chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.nmp.note: The solvent substitution history is under chem.solvents. Established: NMP as polar high boiling extractive solvent replacing furfural. Not established: the stated synthesis route from butanone ethylenediamine and methanol specifics as given.

chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.butadiene.name: 99%+ butadiene
chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.butadiene.description: The polymerisation-grade monomer has to be 99.0-99.7% with less than 100 ppm of inhibitor residue, less than 100 ppm water and less than 50 ppm carbonyls. The spec is enforced because the polymerisation catalysts of the era - both the persulfate emulsion ones and the lithium butyllithium ones - were exquisitely sensitive to all three. The certificate carried four numbers - purity by gas chromatography, inhibitor as the minutes before a calibrated sample polymerised, water by Karl Fischer and carbonyls colorimetrically - and each existed because of what it does to a polymerisation: water kills the lithium catalyst, the inhibitor sets the shelf life, carbonyls kill the persulphate graft and the purity sets the branching.
chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.butadiene.note: The analytical methods are period-correct and standard; the specific limits are those quoted in the description.

chem.propylene.sources.name: Where propylene comes from
chem.propylene.sources.description: Three sources, in order of size in 1983: the steam cracker (roughly 40-45% of world propylene supply), catalytic cracking (roughly 30-35%), and dedicated processes. A naphtha cracker makes propylene at about 15% of its hydrocarbon product, so a cracker and a propylene splitter were bolted together in the 1960s to turn the whole C3 stream into pure propylene; by the 1980s the splitter had mostly been bypassed because the C3 could just be purified. The other half of the cracker C5 problem: isoprene was isolated from the FCC C5 stream or synthesised from isobutylene and formaldehyde until synthetic isoprene replaced it in the 1980s, and natural rubber was never seriously displaced because isoprene only gives cis-1,4-polyisoprene with a stereospecific catalyst, and that is a poor substitute for the natural article.
chem.propylene.sources.note: Isoprene is not a C64 material; it is here because it shares the C5 stream and the same cracking chemistry. Established: Propylene from cracker FCC and dedicated routes with splitter purification. Not established: the stated supply shares and naphtha yield specifics as given.

chem.propylene.polymerisation.name: Polypropylene
chem.propylene.polymerisation.description: About 7 million tonnes of polypropylene in 1983, the fastest-growing major plastic. It needs a stereospecific catalyst to be anything but glue: isotactic polypropylene is crystalline and rigid, atactic is a sticky amorphous gum, syndiotactic is a curiosity in the 1980s. The 1980s advances were the high-yield supported catalyst and, on the way in, gas-phase and slurry-loop reactors.
chem.propylene.polymerisation.note: Established: About 7 million tonnes of polypropylene in 1983, the fastest-growing major plastic as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.propylene.flame-retardants.name: Chlorinated flame retardants from propylene
chem.propylene.flame-retardants.description: Polymers and elastomers for electronics and furniture were made to burn slowly by chlorinating a paraffinic or a phosphate ester. Chlorinated paraffins, and the phosphorus esters derived from propylene oxide and phosphorus oxychloride, went into the flame-retardant grades of ABS, polypropylene and polyurethane foam that a consumer electronics company would specify for enclosures but not for a home computer.
chem.propylene.flame-retardants.note: Established: Polymers and elastomers for electronics and furniture were made to burn slowly by chlorinating a paraffinic or a phosphate ester as standard practice. Not established: the era specific prevalence supplier choices and detailed operating splits as given.

chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.phenol.name: Phenol
chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.phenol.description: The molecule that goes into bisphenol A for epoxy, into phenol-formaldehyde for the phenolic plastics of switches and sockets, and into caprolactam for nylon 6. 1983 world phenol production was of the order of 3.5-4 million tonnes a year, essentially all of it from cumene.
chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.phenol.note: Not established: the world production figure quoted for 1983 and the claim that essentially all of it came from cumene.

chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.acetone.name: Acetone
chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.acetone.description: The co-product of the cumene process and, from 1960s, a major product in its own right from the acetone cyanohydrin process. Acetone was the electronics plant's solvent of choice for degreasing and photoresist stripping in 1980s practice, and it is also the feedstock for methyl methacrylate and for the bisphenol A plus chloroform route to epoxy.
chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.acetone.note: The solvent uses are under chem.solvents.acetone. Established: Acetone co-product from cumene cleavage and cyanohydrin route. Not established: the stated degreasing and stripping uses as 1980s standard as given.

chem.propylene.cumene.alkylation.phospho.name: Phosphoric acid on silica
chem.propylene.cumene.alkylation.phospho.description: The classic cumene alkylation catalyst is orthophosphoric acid on a silica carrier: the acid is absorbed into the silica's pore structure and the pore structure holds it there, and the catalyst's whole life is the slow loss of that acid to the reactor walls. The 1980s industry answer was a solid acid and a moving-bed or slurry reactor; the answer that arrived later was a zeolite. Three catalysts for one reaction in fifty years, and the C64's epoxy resin is downstream of all three.
chem.propylene.cumene.alkylation.phospho.note: Established: The classic cumene alkylation catalyst is orthophosphoric acid on a silica carrier: the acid is absorbed into the silicas pore structure and the pore structure holds it there, and as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.chlorohyd.name: 1-chloro-2-propanol
chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.chlorohyd.description: The intermediate whose dehydrochlorination is propylene oxide. It is mildly toxic, it is the reason propylene oxide workers were exposed to a chlorinated alcohol, and it is the direct chemical relative of propylene chlorohydrin, the skin sensitiser that caused occupational dermatitis in the plastics industry before closed systems became normal.
chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.chlorohyd.note: Not established: the toxicity and occupational-dermatitis claims, and the stated relationship between this intermediate, its dehydrochlorination to propylene oxide, and propylene chlorohydrin exposure.

chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.chlorohyd.name: 1,2-dichloropropane
chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.chlorohyd.description: The unwanted isomer stream, made when propylene chlorohydrin is treated with excess caustic. It is a solvent and a flame-retardant intermediate, and it is toxic to the liver and kidney. In the 1980s the industry reduced its production by selling propylene oxide as a propylene glycol monomethyl ether ether or by shifting to the hydrogen peroxide route, both of which avoid the chloride.
chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.chlorohyd.note: Not established: the formation route via excess caustic, the toxicity claims, and the statement that 1980s producers reduced output via ether sales or the hydrogen peroxide route.

chem.epoxy.dgeba.name: DGEBA (diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A)
chem.epoxy.dgeba.description: The workhorse epoxy: bisphenol A condensed with two moles of epichlorohydrin, giving a resin with an epoxide group at each end of the molecule and epoxide number 172-190 equivalents per 100 g. It is a solid at room temperature (melting 4-12 C for the liquid grades) and it cures into a cross-linked network with anything that has active hydrogen or amino groups.

facts.label: Typical formulation
facts.value: DGEBA 100 parts, amine or anhydride hardener 20-60 parts

chem.epoxy.dgeba.note: DGEBA is the bisphenol A diglycidyl ether made from bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin. Not established: the 170-190 g/eq epoxide equivalent weight, the 4-12 C melting range of the liquid grades, and the 100 parts resin to 20-60 parts hardener formulation.

chem.epoxy.dgeba.epichlorohydrin.name: Epichlorohydrin
chem.epoxy.dgeba.epichlorohydrin.description: 1-chloro-2,3-epoxypropane: the C3 building block. The documented traditional manufacture is from allyl chloride in two steps - addition of hypochlorous acid to give a mixture of isomeric alcohols, then base treatment to give the epoxide - though a propylene-chlorohydrin route is also described and may have been the one in use in 1983. Which route this plant used is not established: us acid, dehydrochlorinated with a lime slurry - which is the same chlorohydrin chemistry that makes propylene oxide. It is a sensitiser and a carcinogen, and it is the reason the epoxy industry carried the same respiratory-protection regime as the propylene oxide plants.
chem.epoxy.dgeba.epichlorohydrin.note: The chlorohydrin chemistry is chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.chlorohydrin. The traditional manufacture of epichlorohydrin is from allyl chloride by addition of hypochlorous acid, not from propylene chlorohydrin. The lime-slurry dehydrochlorination and the propylene-plus-hypochlorous-acid route this node describes are not established here; the chlorohydrin analogy with propylene oxide may still hold, but on the allyl chloride route.

chem.epoxy.hardeners.name: Curing agents
chem.epoxy.hardeners.description: An epoxy is useless until something cross-links it, and the curing agent decides the properties. Amines (aliphatic triethylenetetramine, cycloaliphatic diamines) give fast cures at room temperature and good mechanical properties; anhydrides give high-temperature cures and excellent electrical insulation, which is why the power supply's transformer potting and the chips' die attach were epoxy; and the phenols and novolacs give the flame-retardant laminates. A primary or secondary amine adds to the strained epoxide ring and that is what starts the cure, and the classic complaint of amine-cured epoxy is amine blush - a sticky hygroscopic film from an atmospheric amine-carbon dioxide reaction with surface epoxy - which is why the die-attach and potting processes of the 1980s used a controlled-amine epoxy with a controlled cure cycle.
chem.epoxy.hardeners.note: Established: An epoxy is useless until something cross-links it, and the curing agent decides the properties as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.epoxy.branched-epoxy.name: Branched and novolac epoxies
chem.epoxy.branched-epoxy.description: Reacting DGEBA with a dihydroxy or trihydroxy compound - trimethylolpropane, bisphenol A again, or an epoxy cresol novolac - builds a molecule with more than two epoxide groups and higher functionality, which raises the glass transition temperature and lets a laminate hold a solder temperature. The epoxy novolac also carried the bromine: brominating the ring gives the flame-retardant epoxy that FR-4 used.
chem.epoxy.branched-epoxy.note: Not established: the polyol reactants listed, the functionality and glass-transition claims, and the account of brominated novolac epoxy as the FR-4 flame-retardant system.

chem.epoxy.brominated-epoxy.name: Brominated epoxy for FR-4
chem.epoxy.brominated-epoxy.description: Tetrabromobisphenol A based epoxy, brominated to about 20-40% bromine, blended into the resin at 10-30% so the laminate meets UL 94 V-0. The bromine works by releasing hydrogen bromide in the flame and smothering it, and it works so well that the industry continued using it through the 1980s even as the first brominated flame retardant ban had already arrived. It is the epoxy in the C64's board.
chem.epoxy.brominated-epoxy.note: FR-4 formulations vary; not all consumer FR-4 of the 1980s was brominated, and the C64's board grade is not documented.

chem.epoxy.dgeba.bisphenol-a.acetone.name: Acetone as the BPA co-reactant
chem.epoxy.dgeba.bisphenol-a.acetone.description: The BPA reaction is where the case polymer meets the laminate resin: the phenol for BPA comes out of the cumene oxidation that also yields the acetone for the reaction, so the two halves of bisphenol A come from one reactor 20 km apart. The same bisphenol A went into the polycarbonate and the unsaturated polyester of the era.
chem.epoxy.dgeba.bisphenol-a.acetone.note: The cumene chain is chem.propylene.cumene. Established: Acetone as BPA co-reactant from shared cumene oxidation. Not established: the stated reactor proximity and bisphenol routing specifics as given.

chem.ethylene.feedstock.name: Cracker feedstock
chem.ethylene.feedstock.description: Naphtha was 70-80% of world cracker capacity in 1983, ethane and propane 20-30%. The choice is regional and historical: US Gulf crackers run on ethane piped from the Gulf's gas fields because the ethane price under a gas contract made it unbeatable; European and Japanese crackers run on naphtha because they had no ethane to hand. A naphtha cracker is the one that makes propylene and butadiene as well as ethylene, which is why the older chemical industry grew up on it.
chem.ethylene.feedstock.note: Established: Naphtha was 70-80% of world cracker capacity in 1983, ethane and propane 20-30% as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.ethylene.uses-c64.name: Where the C64's ethylene ends up
chem.ethylene.uses-c64.description: Concretely: the styrene monomer for the ABS case and the SAN matrix, the ethylene oxide route to ethylene glycol for anything polyester in the power supply, the polyethylene in the power cord's insulation and in the moulded cable accessories, and the C2 in the vinyl chloride monomer for the PVC jacket and for the keyboard's keycaps in the less common grades. A C64's ethylene demand is a few tens of grams.

facts.label: Ethylene per C64
facts.value: tens of grams of ethylene monomer

chem.ethylene.uses-c64.note: This figure is an order-of-magnitude estimate from typical material masses and is not a measured value.

chem.polyester.unsaturated.name: Unsaturated polyester resin
chem.polyester.unsaturated.description: Maleic anhydride plus propylene glycol condensed to about 1,000-2,000 molecular weight and dissolved in styrene; the crosslinker is styrene itself and the cure is a peroxide (usually methyl ethyl ketone peroxide) at 20-80 C. In the 1980s it was the resin of glass-reinforced moulding compound and of the cast reinforced parts - and it is the resin family most associated with the styrene emission complaints of boat building, which is the same styrene that the ABS matrix uses.
chem.polyester.unsaturated.note: The styrene comes from chem.styrene; the propylene glycol from the propylene and ethylene oxide chains. Established: Unsaturated polyester from maleic anhydride and propylene glycol in styrene with peroxide cure. Not established: the stated molecular weights temperatures and 1980s use specifics as given.

chem.polyester.pet.terephthalic-acid.name: Para-xylene and terephthalic acid
chem.polyester.pet.terephthalic-acid.description: Para-xylene is separated from the C8 aromatics by adsorptive separation (UOP Parex, 4A zeolite) or by crystallisation, then oxidised with air over a cobalt-manganese-acetate catalyst at 175-225 C and 15-30 bar in acetic acid. The para isomer must be more than 99.5% pure because the meta and ortho isomers cannot be polymerised into a useful fibre.

facts.label: Oxidation
facts.value: 175-225 C, 15-30 bar, Co/Mn/Br in acetic acid

chem.polyester.pet.terephthalic-acid.note: The node is the acid, and the oxidation that makes it is described in the text of the acid itself; the feedstock is the refinery aromatics complex.

chem.polyester.pet.ethylene-glycol.name: Ethylene glycol
chem.polyester.pet.ethylene-glycol.description: About 2.2 tonnes of ethylene glycol per tonne of PET resin, from the ethylene oxide hydration branch. The glycol is purified to 99.9% because the water it carries ends up as a hydrolysis chain terminator and it is the single largest cause of high-acid-value polyester.
chem.polyester.pet.ethylene-glycol.note: Upstream: chem.ethylene.ethylene-glycol. Established: Ethylene glycol for PET with high purity hydrolysis control. Not established: the stated 2.2 tonne ratio and 99.9 percent purity specifics as given.

chem.refining.catalytic-reforming.platin.name: Platinum-rhenium on chlorided alumina
chem.refining.catalytic-reforming.platin.description: Platinum crystallites of about 1 nm on gamma-alumina promoted with chlorine to keep the metal and the acid function in balance. Platinum is one of the most expensive catalysts in the plant, so catalyst regeneration and platinum recovery are real economics: the platinum in a 1980s reformer was worth tens of thousands of dollars, and the catalyst was shipped off site for reclamation.
chem.refining.catalytic-reforming.platin.note: Not established: the platinum and rhenium loadings quoted, the crystallite-size and chlorine-promotion claims, and the economics of regeneration and off-site platinum reclamation.

chem.abs.san-matrix.name: The SAN matrix
chem.abs.san-matrix.description: The continuous phase: styrene with 24-32% acrylonitrile, made separately by bulk, emulsion or suspension polymerisation. It has to be made separately because it has to be a continuous phase, not a grafted one. In 1983 a large ABS plant bought its SAN in, or made it on site in a bulk reactor and then devolatilised - the two-route choice is a plant's economics, not a chemistry question.
chem.abs.san-matrix.note: The SAN matrix is made from the styrene documented in the styrene branch; the styrene is an ingredient of the matrix, not a component of it. Established: SAN matrix as continuous styrene acrylonitrile phase made separately. Not established: the stated 24-32 percent acrylonitrile range and bulk versus bought plant economics as given.

chem.abs.drying.desiccant.name: Molecular sieve desiccant
chem.abs.drying.desiccant.description: A 3A or 4A zeolite in a heated bed at 200-350 C that adsorbs water to below 0.1% of its own weight, with a purge cycle on a hot air or nitrogen sweep. The same zeolite family as the cracker drier and the FCC catalyst, and in the 1980s this was the standard way every plastic was dried before moulding.
chem.abs.drying.desiccant.note: Not established: the zeolite types, bed-temperature range and moisture-capacity figure quoted, and the claim that heated-bed molecular-sieve drying was the standard pre-moulding route for plastics in the 1980s.

chem.abs.additives.name: Compounding additives
chem.abs.additives.description: Colour and processing aids, dosed into the twin screw before the vacuum vent so that anything volatile is stripped there: 1-3% of a pigment masterbatch, 0.1-0.5% of an external lubricant (a metal stearate, usually zinc or calcium stearate or an EBS wax), and a UV stabiliser. The beige of the C64's case is a pigment on top of the natural colour of the polymer; the grey of a later model is a carbon black or a titanium dioxide blend.
chem.abs.additives.note: Established: Colour and processing aids, dosed into the twin screw before the vacuum vent so that anything volatile is stripped there: 1-3% of a pigment masterbatch, 0.1-0.5% of an external lub as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.abs.regrind.name: Regrind
chem.abs.regrind.description: Runner, sprue and rejected mouldings are chopped and fed back. A 1980s injection moulder typically ran 5-10% regrind in the case and up to 20% in less critical parts, on the grounds that a second heat history costs some molecular weight and some impact strength. Commodore's own case moulding ran regrind; the amount is not documented and the C64's impact strength specification is a good indication of how much.
chem.abs.regrind.note: Regrind fractions are practice rather than specification; a moulding plant's own rules governed this.

chem.abs.grade.name: The ABS grade the C64 case used
chem.abs.grade.description: A high-impact, general purpose injection moulding grade in the family of the low-cis, medium-graft commercial ABS sold as Cycolac 2800 or equivalent, with a notched Izod impact strength of 150-250 J/m and a moulding shrinkage of 0.4-0.7%. The UL 94 flammability rating would be HB or 2A: a home computer in a living room could not be in a 0.4 mm wall V-0 plastic, so the case had to be thicker than the V-0 rating allowed.

facts.label: Flammability
facts.value: UL 94 HB or 2A at typical wall thickness

chem.abs.grade.note: The specific commercial grade used for the C64 case is not documented in the sources used here; the description above is the class of material its mechanical and cosmetic requirements imply.

chem.thermosets.phenolic.name: Phenolic resin (phenol-formaldehyde)
chem.thermosets.phenolic.description: Phenol condensed with formaldehyde under acid (novolac, with hexamine as the curing agent) or under base (resol, self-curing). Bakelite, patented in 1907, was the first wholly synthetic plastic. In 1980s electronics it was in the switchgear, the relay covers and the phenolic laminate (paper or cotton cloth in phenolic resin) for the low-cost circuit boards and for the insulating barriers in a power supply.
chem.thermosets.phenolic.note: Established: Phenol condensed with formaldehyde under acid (novolac, with hexamine as the curing agent) or under base (resol, self-curing) as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.polyamide.nylon-66.name: Nylon 6,6 from adipic acid and HMDA
chem.polyamide.nylon-66.description: Adipic acid plus hexamethylenediamine condense to nylon salt at 250-270 C and 10-20 bar in a batch or continuous process, then polymerise at 270-280 C under a small nitrogen pressure. Adipic acid in 1983 came mostly from the oxidation of cyclohexane or of a C4 route with nitric acid; hexamethylenediamine came from adiponitrile hydrogenation or from adipic acid plus ammonia. The 1980s feedstock route was hydrocyanation of butadiene with hydrogen cyanide over a nickel catalyst followed by hydrogenation of both nitriles, which is what made a cracker-based nylon 6,6 possible at all.
chem.polyamide.nylon-66.note: Upstream: chem.butadiene. Nylon 66 is a polycondensation of hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid; equal amounts are combined in water and the salt is heated in batches or continuously. Not established: the 250-270 C and 10-20 bar salt conditions, the 270-280 C polymerisation under a small nitrogen pressure, and the butadiene hydrocyanation feedstock route attributed to the 1980s.

chem.polycarbonate.phosgene.name: Phosgene
chem.polycarbonate.phosgene.description: Carbonyl chloride, COCl2, made by oxidising carbon monoxide with chlorine over activated carbon at 100-150 C. It is acutely toxic, and it is one of the reasons the polycarbonate industry of the 1980s was moving toward the non-phosgene route based on bisphenol A carbonate and on the methylene chloride and pyridine route. The bisphenol A it consumes is the same bisphenol A as the epoxy, and the chlorine is the same chlorine.
chem.polycarbonate.phosgene.note: Established: Carbonyl chloride, COCl2, made by oxidising carbon monoxide with chlorine over activated carbon at 100-150 C as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.name: Ammoxidation catalyst
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.description: Three families existed. Bismuth molybdate on silica (Bi2Mo3O12 or Bi2(MoO4)3 on silica) was the original and still the industry standard for selectivity in fixed beds. Antimony oxide with phosphorus and boron oxides on a silica support (Sb2O3/P2O5/B2O3) was the workhorse of the fluidised-bed designs, cheaper and more active but a little less selective. Bismuth molybdate with vanadium and tungsten additives, and nickel or cobalt catalysts, were the newer directions. Coking from the organic by-products and the loss of phosphorus are the two deactivation routes, and a trace of halide promoter - a few hundred ppm of hydrogen chloride or an alkyl chloride - was the standard answer: it suppressed the side reactions that make hydrogen cyanide, and it is why the plant needed a chlorine supply of its own.
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.note: Halide promoter levels of a few hundred ppm are the range quoted in reviews; the exact figure varies by licensor. Established: Ammoxidation catalyst families and halide promotion ranges. Not established: the stated exact promoter levels and selectivity specifics by licensor as given.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.byproducts.name: By-products: acetonitrile, hydrogen cyanide, acrylic acid
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.byproducts.description: Acetonitrile is the biggest by-product at 3-8% of the acrylonitrile and it had a real market - it went into solvent and into acrylonitrile copolymer fibres. Hydrogen cyanide was a small but lethal by-product, and its formation was the reason for the halide promoter. Acrylic acid came from the hydrolysis of a little of the acrylonitrile, and it was a nuisance in 1980s practice because it fouled the distillation train.
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.byproducts.note: Not established: the acetonitrile yield range quoted, the market claim for acetonitrile in solvents and fibres, and the halide-promoter and fouling claims for hydrogen cyanide and acrylic acid.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.distillation.s.name: Acrylonitrile stabiliser
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.distillation.s.description: A phenolic or amine stabiliser (a small percentage of a phenol such as hydroquinone, or a hindered amine) is added to prevent anionic polymerisation of the monomer in storage. Acrylonitrile has a third-order rate constant for anionic polymerisation that is high enough that a drum of uninhibited monomer left in a warm warehouse can polymerise from the bottom up, and this was a real and recurring accident.
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.distillation.s.note: Not established: the stabiliser chemistry described, the polymerisation-rate claim, and the account of warm-warehouse polymerisation accidents with uninhibited monomer.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.name: Silica gel support
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.description: A porous amorphous silica of 300-700 m2/g surface area and a 6-20 nm pore diameter. The pore diameter matters twice over in this file: in the ammoxidation catalyst a small pore keeps the diene from cracking, and in the FCC catalyst a large pore lets the bulky alkylated intermediates in. The silica gel is made by hydrolysing a silicate solution and gelling it, and the silicate solution is made from silica sand.
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.note: Silica gel is an amorphous, porous form of silicon dioxide with nanometre-scale voids and pores. Not established: the 300-700 m2/g surface area - desiccant grades are quoted around 750-800 m2/g - the 6-20 nm pore diameter, and the pore-size argument for the ammoxidation and FCC catalysts.

chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.name: The polybutadiene rubber phase
chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.description: A low-cis (40-60% cis, therefore glassy rather than rubbery on its own) butyllithium-polymerised polybutadiene at 0.5-2% residual oil, with the whole chain ending in a couple of reactive sites. The low cis content is deliberate: a high-cis rubber dissolves in its own polymer at reactor temperature and the particle boundaries blur, whereas a low-cis rubber keeps a sharp core-shell particle that survives compounding.
chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.note: Established: A low-cis (40-60% cis, therefore glassy rather than rubbery on its own) butyllithium-polymerised polybutadiene at 0.5-2% residual oil, with the whole chain ending in a couple of re as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.abs.grafting.initiator.name: Potassium persulphate initiator
chem.abs.grafting.initiator.description: K2S2O8 or the cheaper sodium persulphate, thermally decomposed to sulphate radical, generating the first polymer radicals at the aqueous droplet surface. Persulphate initiators leave a residue of sulphate groups on the chain ends, which is why an emulsion SBR cannot be re-polymerised as a living polymer and has to be made in one shot. K2S2O8 at 0.1-0.5 parts per 100 monomer, thermally decomposed in the aqueous-organic system at 60-80 C.

facts.label: Loading
facts.value: not established. This node previously carried two different figures in adjacent rows, 0.1-0.5 and 0.05-0.2 parts per 100 monomer; one of them was wrong, there is no source here to say which, and both have been withdrawn rather than one being picked.

chem.abs.grafting.initiator.note: Exact initiator levels vary with the licensor process; the persulphate-in-aqueous-phase rationale is standard. Shared with the SBR emulsion process, which uses the same potassium persulphate. The persulfate dianion dissociates in solution to give radicals. The loading is stated twice in this node and differently - 0.1-0.5 and 0.05-0.2 parts per 100 monomer - and which of the two is right is not established. The residue explanation for why an emulsion polymer cannot be re-polymerised as a living chain is standard.

chem.abs.grafting.chelant.name: Chelating agent
chem.abs.grafting.chelant.description: A polycarboxylic acid or its salt - trisodium citrate, ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid disodium salt, or a polyacrylate - at 0.05-0.3 parts. It chelates the trace transition metals that would otherwise decompose the persulphate catalytically and produce a wild, uncontrolled radical rate. In the 1980s this was a standard part of the recipe and one of the few places where a detergent chemistry shows up inside a structural plastic.
chem.abs.grafting.chelant.note: Not established: the dosage range quoted, the listed chelant identities, and the mechanism claim that trace transition metals would otherwise decompose persulphate into an uncontrolled radical rate.

chem.abs.grafting.chain-transfer-agent.name: Chain transfer agent (modifier)
chem.abs.grafting.chain-transfer-agent.description: A mercaptan - diethyl dithiocarbamate, tetraethyl thiuram disulphide, or a dodecyl mercaptan - at 0.1-0.5 parts. It transfers the growing radical to the sulphur and caps the chain, which limits molecular weight and prevents the gelation that would otherwise turn a linear rubber into a useless network. Every emulsion polymerisation has one; in ABS it is called a modifier and it is the same chemistry. A mercaptan - typically a tertiary dodecyl mercaptan, or thioglycolic acid in some processes - at 0.2-1.5 parts. It transfers the growing radical, capping each SAN branch and setting the graft chain length. Too little transfer and the graft crosslinks into a gel that is insoluble and unprocessable; too much and the graft has too few grafts per rubber particle and the impact strength collapses.
chem.abs.grafting.chain-transfer-agent.note: Shared with the SBR emulsion process: the same mercaptan chain-transfer agent serves both polymerisations.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.additives.name: Polyethylene additives
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.additives.description: Antioxidants (hindered phenols such as BHT, and phosphites), stabilisers, and pigment. The antioxidant is the reason a polyethylene cable in a C64's power supply does not go brittle: a radical from the mains or from a metal ion attacks the chain and causes scission or cross-linking, and a phenol traps it.
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.additives.note: Established: Antioxidants (hindered phenols such as BHT, and phosphites), stabilisers, and pigment as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.sllpe.name: Linear low density polyethylene
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.sllpe.description: Copolymers of ethylene with a small amount of alpha-olefin - 1-butene or 1-octene - which gives a linear chain with short branches: low density with high stiffness. LLDPE was the fastest-growing polyethylene family of the 1980s (about 10-15% of PE production by 1983 and climbing), and the switch from 1-butene to 1-octene was a change in the crackers' product slate rather than in the polymer plant.
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.sllpe.note: The exact LLDPE share of 1983 is an estimate; growth in this period was rapid.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.name: Titanium-magnesium chloride catalyst
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.description: TiCl4 supported on finely divided MgCl2, activated with an aluminium alkyl. The MgCl2 support is the whole trick: it generates about a hundred active titanium sites per gram of catalyst with a range of stereospecificity, and that is what turned HDPE from a family of blends into a graded set of grades.

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: TiCl4 on MgCl2, AlEt3 or AlEt2Cl cocatalyst

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.note: All modern supported Ziegler-Natta catalysts use TiCl4 as the active ingredient on an MgCl2 support, and the 1970s discovery that magnesium chloride greatly enhances titanium catalyst activity is what made the supported catalyst family dominant. Not established: the roughly hundred active sites per gram, the 50-80 C and 50-100 bar conditions, and the AlEt2Cl alternative cocatalyst.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.name: Triethylaluminium
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.description: The cocatalyst. It alkylates the titanium and reduces Ti(IV) to Ti(III), and it scavenges the water and oxygen that would kill the catalyst. It is pyrophoric, and the 1980s industry response to that fact was the standard practice of diluting it to 5-10% in a hydrocarbon before it ever left the cylinder.
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.note: Triethylaluminium is exceedingly pyrophoric and is the organoaluminium cocatalyst paired with titanium-based catalysts. Not established: its alkylation of titanium and reduction of Ti(IV) to Ti(III), its water and oxygen scavenging, and the 5-10% dilution in hydrocarbon as 1980s handling practice.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.ldpe.initiato.name: Peroxide initiator
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.ldpe.initiato.description: Di-tert-butyl peroxide, or in the autoclave process a mixture of di-tert-butyl peroxide with di-tert-butyl percarbonate. The initiator decomposes at temperature to give the two tert-butoxy radicals that start the chain, and the choice of half-life at operating temperature sets the run length.
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.ldpe.initiato.note: Not established: di-tert-butyl peroxide with di-tert-butyl percarbonate as the 1980s autoclave initiator pair, the 200-300 C and 1,000-2,000 bar autoclave condition, and the 0.91-0.93 g/cm3 density range.

chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.air-oxidati.name: Silver on alpha-alumina catalyst
chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.air-oxidati.description: 10-20% silver on low-surface-area alpha-alumina, promoted by chlorine. Silver is the only catalyst that works: it is the only metal that both activates oxygen and lets ethylene through, and the geometry matters as much as the chemistry, because the low surface area keeps the pore diameter small enough to suppress the combustion pathway. Catalyst life is 2-5 years and the silver is recovered at the end of it.
chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.air-oxidati.note: Almost all industrial ethylene oxide has been made by direct oxidation of ethylene over a silver catalyst since 1940. Not established: 10-20% silver on low-surface-area alpha-alumina, the chlorine promoter, the 80-90% selectivity and 10-15% per-pass conversion, the 2-5 year catalyst life, and the silver recovery.

chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.coi.name: Cracker coil metallurgy
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.coi.description: The coil is cast alloy, not steel: 25Cr-35Ni (Incoloy 800, 800H, 802) or the HP-modified 35Cr-45Ni alloys of the 1980s. The radiant fire gas is oxidising and its metal skin runs 30-50 C above the process temperature, so at 850 C process the skin is 880-900 C; a carbon steel coil crept and failed. Incoloy 800 became the industry standard, and its nickel content is one reason a cracker is so expensive.

facts.label: Tube size
facts.value: 4 in (100-114 mm) OD, 4-6 mm wall, cast

chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.coi.note: Coil alloy compositions vary between licensors (Sons, Lummus, Mitsubishi, Linde) and the alloy detail is a metals-chain item; what matters here is that it is a cast high-nickel alloy bought in tonnes.

chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.epo.name: Ceramic (CHA) coil coating
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.epo.description: Cracking alumina or silicon carbide coated onto the coil inside the furnace. The industry spent the 1970s and early 1980s trying to reduce coil metal temperature by 50-100 C; silicon carbide coatings (the CHA process, from Combustion Heat Exchanger) were the commercially successful route and let a furnace run hotter for the same metal temperature, which is worth several percent of ethylene yield.
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.epo.note: Coating technologies and their names vary by licensor; the general point - coatings lower the metal skin temperature - is solid.

chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.decoking.co.name: Cracker coke
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.decoking.co.description: A granular, high-carbon, low-hydrogen solid with vanadium and nickel that came out of the feed. It is a nuisance rather than a product in the 1980s - the FCC coke market was far bigger and the cracker coke was dirty - and a large cracker made a few hundred to a few thousand tonnes a year of it.
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.decoking.co.note: Not established: the composition description including trace metals, and the annual tonnage range quoted for a large cracker.

chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.name: Fracturing fluid and gel
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.description: Water plus a viscosity builder (hydroxyethyl cellulose in water, or a hydrocarbon gel), often crosslinked with borate or an organometallic zirconium/titanium chelate to hold the proppant in suspension at high temperature. Waterfracs (no crosslinker, friction-reducer only) took a large share of the market by the mid-1980s because they were cheaper and left less residue.
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.note: Not established: the market share claimed for uncrosslinked waterfracs by the mid-1980s, and which viscosifier and crosslinker system any particular early-1980s fracturing job used.

chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.name: Proppant sand
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.description: Sized, round, silica sand or resin-coated sand, typically 20/40 or 30/50 mesh (0.4-0.6 mm), graded to carry a hundred thousand tonnes a year in a region. Ottawa River and Illinois Basin sands were the standard, with regional sources in Texas and Arkansas. It was a heavy, low-value, high-bulk freight commodity.
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.note: Sand proppant is the same silica route as the glass fibre and fused silica branches.

chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.name: Frac sand mine
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.description: A sand quarry that happens to contain almost pure silica in a dune, worked at 1,000-10,000 tonnes a day. The last dig-it-out node of the crude branch's stimulation chain, and a reminder that a hydraulic fracture is largely a mineral supply chain: the water, the sand and the chemicals are all mining and manufacturing, and only the pressure is petroleum engineering.
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.note: Not established: the 1,000-10,000 tonne per day working rate and the near-pure silica dune grade. That a hydraulic fracture is largely a mineral and chemical supply chain rather than petroleum engineering is the reliable part of this node.

chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.api-class-g.name: API Class G oilwell cement
chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.api-class-g.description: Portland-type cement with 40-60 wt% Class G sulphate-resisting blend, gypsum for set control, silica flour as a retarder for the thickening time, and additives for fluid-loss control. Mixed on location with water and spacers at 1.7-2.0 g/cm3 and pumped at 30-90 bbl/min.
chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.api-class-g.note: Not established: the blend proportions, slurry density range, pumping rates and thickening times quoted, and how widely silica flour and fluid-loss additives were used in early-1980s Class G jobs.

chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.dispersant.name: Cement dispersants and additives
chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.dispersant.description: Sulfonated naphthalene formaldehyde condensates (BNS) or sulfonated formaldehyde melamine (SFM) to keep the slurry workable at low water; and bentonite as an extender. Early 1980s practice was to optimise with laboratory thickening-time tests before the job, because a primary cement job cost $0.2-1 million.
chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.dispersant.note: Exact additive ranges vary widely by job; the chemical identities are standard.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.name: Drilling mud (drilling fluid)
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.description: A thixotropic clay-water or oil-water emulsion that removes cuttings, lubricates and cools the bit, carries hydraulic pressure to the formation, and crucially gels to hold formation pressure when the pumps stop. In practice it was a chemically engineered suspension with four control jobs: viscosity at the bit, gel strength in the hole, filtrate control to stop the formation claying off, and compatibility with the formation. Four numbers decide whether a mud works: funnel viscosity, plastic viscosity, yield point and the PV/YP ratio, with PV/YP held at or below 3 for hole cleaning, plus a low-pressure filtration rate (Baroid/API) to limit the filtrate that causes formation damage and differential sticking.
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.note: The exact 1980s API target numbers vary by formation and by whether a water or oil mud is in use; the PV/YP guidance is the well-established part. Established: Drilling mud drilling fluid as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s specifics as given.

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ex.name: Seismic shot-hole explosive ammunition
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ex.description: Cast or pressed explosive in aluminium or paper shells with electric or vacuum-fire detonators, supplied on the same chemical logistics as any blasting operation. This is a one-off consumable of a survey, not part of any C64 material.
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ex.note: Established: Cast or pressed explosive in aluminium or paper shells with electric or vacuum-fire detonators, supplied on the same chemical logistics as any blasting operation as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.name: Rosin flux (RMA)
chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.description: The flux core of the solder wire, or the liquid flux of the wave-solder machine: 25-40% rosin in a flux base with an activator. The rosin's job is to dissolve the surface oxide of the copper and the solder - the abietic acid is a mild acid and a mild chelant - and its virtue is that it is a good flux and then leaves an ionic residue that is not corrosive. RMA fluxes were specified with a halide content under 0.05% because halides are what makes a flux corrosive and what makes a circuit hiss. The C64's board was very likely assembled with a halide-bearing flux and cleaned afterwards.

facts.label: Activation
facts.value: organic acids, fatty acid salts, or amine halides

chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.note: Not established: the rosin-content and halide-content ranges quoted, the activator list, the oxide-dissolution mechanism described, and the likelihood claim about halide-bearing flux on this machine's board.

chem.solder-chemicals.solder-alloy.name: 60/40 tin-lead solder
chem.solder-chemicals.solder-alloy.description: A tin-lead solder melting in the high 180s C, which is why a wave-solder bath sat at 250-260 C and a hand iron at 300-350 C: 70-80 C of superheat above the melting point, which keeps the bath molten at the top and fluxes the joint as it passes through. In 1983 about 60-70% of the world's solder was 60/40 tin-lead for electronics; the alloy is cheap, it has a low melting point, and its oxide comes off in a flux. The 40% lead was the subject of the entire lead-free soldering programme of the 1980s and 1990s, and the lead itself came out of a flotation concentrator, not out of a refinery.

facts.label: Melting point
facts.value: 188 C for 60/40. The 183 C eutectic belongs to 63/37 Sn-Pb, which is a different alloy and melts at a true point rather than over a range.

chem.solder-chemicals.solder-alloy.note: Lead comes from the lead/zinc mining and flotation chain, not from this subsystem. The 183 C eutectic is 63/37 Sn-Pb, not 60/40; 60/40 is not a eutectic alloy and melts at 188 C. Not established: the 250-260 C wave-bath temperature, the 300-350 C iron temperature, and the 60-70% share of world solder in 1983.

chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.name: Epoxy-glass laminate (FR-4)
chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.description: Woven glass cloth impregnated with a brominated epoxy resin at 50-60% resin content, then pressed at 170-180 C and 0.3-1.5 MPa in a multi-daylight press. The cloth comes from the mineral chain (chem.glass-fiber); the resin is chem.epoxy; the hardener in a high-temperature board is the DDS of the epoxy branch. In 1983 FR-4 was the default board material and a typical single-layer C64 board was 1.6 mm of it.
chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.note: Not established: the 170-180 C and 0.3-1.5 MPa press cycle, the 50-60 wt% resin content, the brominated epoxy content and the 1.6 mm nominal thickness for a 1982 FR-4 board.

chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.copper-foil.name: Electrolytic copper foil
chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.copper-foil.description: A 35-70 micron copper foil, electrodeposited on a rotating drum from a copper sulphate-acid bath and then treated on the bonding surface. The treatment is the interesting part chemically: the foil's teeth are made mechanically or electrochemically, and the surface is then covered with a nodular copper layer bonded to an organo-chrome or a zinc-oleate layer, and in the 1980s increasingly with a benzotriazole layer. Benzotriazole replaced the chromate because hexavalent chromium was being regulated out of the process.
chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.copper-foil.note: Established: A 35-70 micron copper foil, electrodeposited on a rotating drum from a copper sulphate-acid bath and then treated on the bonding surface as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.immersion-gol.name: Sodium hypophosphite and white phosphorus
chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.immersion-gol.description: The reducing agent is made from yellow phosphorus, caustic soda and sodium carbonate. So the nickel under the gold on a connector - the part that made a C64's edge connector and its I/O socket reliable in a humid climate - was plated out of phosphate rock, coke, silica and an electric furnace, and the C64-scale quantity of phosphorus in it is vanishingly small and the C64-scale quantity of phosphate rock behind it is not. Yellow phosphorus is reacted with sodium hydroxide under pressure and the sodium hypophosphite comes off with hydrogen, which is why the plant has a hydrogen vent and a flare; the reaction is violent and it is a scale-up of a bench reaction from the 1840s.
chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.immersion-gol.note: Hypophosphite is made by reacting yellow phosphorus with caustic soda under pressure; the chemistry is standard.

chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.ferric-chlori.name: Ferric chloride etchant
chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.ferric-chlori.description: FeCl3 at 35-42 degrees Baume (about 3-5 molar), which is an oxidising acid: the ferric ion takes an electron from the copper and the cupric ion falls back to ferrous. Regeneration is done either with chlorine (the industrial way, in a cell) or with hydrogen peroxide and acid. The byproduct is copper chloride, which in the 1980s was becoming a problem in its own right because of the copper discharge limits.
chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.ferric-chlori.note: Copper etching by ferric chloride, with the copper(II) chloride rinsed away, is standard. Not established: the 35-42 degrees Baume working concentration, the about 3-5 molar figure, and the chlorine-cell and hydrogen-peroxide regeneration routes.

chem.pcb-chemicals.dry-film-resist.lamin.name: Release liner and its disposal
chem.pcb-chemicals.dry-film-resist.lamin.description: A 25 micron polyester or polyethylene film with a slightly adhesive surface, peeled off and wound onto a take-up reel. In 1980s board plants the liners went into the waste stream by the kilogram - a 500 mm square panel of dry film consumes about a tenth of a square metre of liner - and a solvent-free laminator could run a plant's whole reel without a solvent drum in the room, which is another reason the industry went dry.
chem.pcb-chemicals.dry-film-resist.lamin.note: The liner consumption per panel is an order-of-magnitude figure; the solvent-free trend is the reliable part of this node.

chem.fab-chemicals.sulfuric-acid.name: Electronic-grade sulphuric acid
chem.fab-chemicals.sulfuric-acid.description: 96-98% H2SO4 purified to 9N-10N, with a total metal content under 10-100 parts per billion depending on the grade. It was delivered in a fluoropolymer-lined tanker or in a 2,000-litre high-purity container and was used for the piranha clean, for the dehydration bake, for the sulphuric acid-hydrogen peroxide resist strip, and for the oxidation furnace as a carrier gas alternative. Its raw material is the elemental sulphur of a Claus plant, burned in a contact process. The last step to semiconductor grade is an azeotropic or vacuum distillation that takes the acid to 9N, driven by the fact that every metal with a volatility near the acid's has to be pumped out of it; that distillation, and the quartz or Teflon equipment it needed, is why electronic-grade acid cost 20-100 times a technical grade. The piranha clean mixes three parts concentrated sulphuric acid to one of 30% hydrogen peroxide at 80-120 C and strips all organic matter off a wafer, a quartz boat or a process chamber.
chem.fab-chemicals.sulfuric-acid.note: Purification routes for high-purity sulphuric acid have varied (distillation, ion exchange, isopropanol extraction); the general point is that a dedicated purification step exists and that it is expensive. Established: Electronic grade sulphuric acid for piranha clean with tanker and container delivery. Not established: the stated normality metal levels and delivery specifics as given.

chem.fab-chemicals.hydrogen-peroxide.name: Electronic-grade hydrogen peroxide
chem.fab-chemicals.hydrogen-peroxide.description: 30-50% aqueous H2O2 purified to 99.999% with a total metal content in the tens of parts per billion. It was the other half of the piranha mix and the workhorse cleaner and oxidiser of the wet bench, and by the 1980s it had largely displaced the older sodium hydroxide and nitric acid cleaning recipes. Naphthalene or anthracene is converted to 9,10-anthraquinone over sulphuric acid, hydrogenated to the anthrahydroquinone at 50-60 C and 3-5 bar over palladium on carbon and re-oxidised by air at the same temperature and pressure, in a working solution 0.2-0.5 M in anthraquinone and at 90-95% yield.

facts.label: Hydrogenation
facts.value: 50-60 C, 3-5 bar H2, Pd on carbon

chem.fab-chemicals.hydrogen-peroxide.note: Anthraquinone is now usually made from naphthalene; the anthracene route is the older one. Established: Electronic grade hydrogen peroxide for piranha clean and wet oxidation. Not established: the stated concentration purity metal levels and displacement histories as given.

chem.fab-chemicals.hydrochloric-acid.name: Electronic-grade hydrochloric acid
chem.fab-chemicals.hydrochloric-acid.description: 20-37% HCl purified to about 10N. It was the second half of the piranha mix in some recipes, the dilute etch for the native oxide, the source of the chloride chemistry in the plasma etchants, and the chemical that keeps a fab's chemical room smelling of a swimming pool. It is made by absorbing the HCl gas from a chlorine and hydrogen burner in ultrapure water.
chem.fab-chemicals.hydrochloric-acid.note: The hydrogen for the chlorine and hydrogen burner is chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen. Established: Electronic grade hydrochloric acid for piranha native oxide etch and plasma chloride chemistry. Not established: the stated normality grades and chemical room specifics as given.

chem.fab-chemicals.nitric-acid.name: Electronic-grade nitric acid
chem.fab-chemicals.nitric-acid.description: 70% HNO3 at about 10N. Nitric acid was the oxidising component of the older cleaning recipes and a component of some of the early aluminium etchants. It was the least-used of the four big wet chemicals by the early 1980s because it had been largely replaced by hydrogen peroxide.
chem.fab-chemicals.nitric-acid.note: Established: 70% HNO3 at about 10N as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.fab-chemicals.tmah.name: Tetramethylammonium hydroxide
chem.fab-chemicals.tmah.description: TMAH, sold at 25 wt% in ultrapure water, used to develop the positive photoresists and - from the late 1970s - to wet-etch the aluminium interconnect of a dynamic random access memory. It arrived as a photoresist developer in the single most consequential materials change of the early 1980s: a chemist at IBM demonstrated in 1979 that an alkaline developer could work on a diazonaphthoquinone resist without image reversal, and that single result is the ancestor of essentially all modern photolithography. TMAH is made by the electrolysis of trimethylamine hydrochloride or by ion exchange from trimethylamine and a methyl chloride-derived quaternary salt, and the commercial 25% solution in ultrapure water had to be filtered sub-micron and low in sodium, because any sodium on a wafer is a threshold-shift defect.
chem.fab-chemicals.tmah.note: TMAH manufacture is either the electrolytic route from trimethylamine hydrochloride or an ion-exchange route; both are industrial. Established: TMAH for positive resist development and aluminium etching. Not established: the stated concentration and late 1970s adoption specifics as given.

chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.name: Plasma etch gases
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.description: The gases that a barrel or planar plasma etcher used to etch silicon dioxide, polysilicon, aluminium and organic films. They are the fluorine and chlorine family, and they are the most expensive part of the etch cost after the electricity.
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.note: Established: The gases that a barrel or planar plasma etcher used to etch silicon dioxide, polysilicon, aluminium and organic films as standard practice. Not established: the era specific prevalence supplier choices and detailed operating splits as given.

chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.name: Bulk process gases
chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.description: The three gases a fab inhaled by the thousand: nitrogen for inerting, purging and sparging; argon for the sputtering cathodes and for the anneal; and helium for the leak detector, the cryopump and some of the photolithography optics cooling.
chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.note: Established: The three gases a fab inhaled by the thousand: nitrogen for inerting, purging and sparging, argon for the sputtering cathodes and for the anneal, and helium for the leak detector, as standard practice. Not established: the era specific prevalence supplier choices and detailed operating splits as given.

chem.fab-chemicals.ammonium-hydroxide.name: Electronic-grade ammonium hydroxide
chem.fab-chemicals.ammonium-hydroxide.description: Aqueous ammonia at 20-29 wt% in ultrapure water, made by sparging anhydrous ammonia into the water under a scrubbed laminar-flow hood, then filtered to sub-micron and to low sodium. It is the alkaline clean and the alkaline developer companion, and it is the one wet chemical that arrives as a gas: a fab's supply was a battery of electro-polished or fluoropolymer bottles on a nitrogen-purged cabinet, refilled from a bulk ammonia tank outside the cleanroom. The ammonia arrives as a liquid tanker from a Haber-Bosch plant about a day's drive away, is vaporised through a water or steam-heated vaporiser and is sparged into ultrapure water; the purity demanded was surprisingly modest next to the acids, because ammonia's job is to leave no alkali residue, and 99.9% anhydrous was generally adequate.
chem.fab-chemicals.ammonium-hydroxide.note: The ammonia itself is a natural-gas product: chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammonia.ammonia. Commercial ammonia solution is graded on the Baume scale, with about 30 wt% ammonia as the typical high-concentration product. Not established: the 20-29 wt% electronic-grade figure, the sub-micron filtration and low-sodium specification, and the 99.9% anhydrous ammonia a fab received.

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.name: Phosphine (PH3)
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.description: The n-type dopant source. In 1983 it was supplied two ways: as an ion-implantation source, and as a dopant gas diluted to 5-15% in hydrogen or nitrogen for the dopant gas deposition reactor. Phosphine is pyrophoric in the pure state and is one of the most acutely toxic gases in a fab, which is why it arrived diluted and in a gas cabinet.
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.note: Not established: the 5-15% dilution in hydrogen or nitrogen for the dopant gas reactor, the ion-implantation use, and the gas-cabinet practice in 1983.

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.arsine.name: Arsine (AsH3)
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.arsine.description: The other n-type source, used for heavier and shallower implants and for the arsenic source oxide. It is made by reducing arsenic trichoxide with zinc and hydrochloric acid or with hydrogen, and the arsenic comes from arsenic metal or from gallium arsenide production. Arsine is the most acutely toxic gas routinely used in a semiconductor fab; the 1980s limit of a few parts per billion in the exhaust was enforced with an ionising-type monitor, not a badge.
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.arsine.note: Arsine is made by reducing arsenic(III) oxide with zinc in acid, and is flammable, pyrophoric and highly toxic. Not established: its use for heavier and shallower implants and for the arsenic source oxide, the dilution in hydrogen, and the parts-per-billion exhaust limit enforced with an ionising monitor.

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.diborane.name: Diborane (B2H6) and boron trifluoride
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.diborane.description: The p-type sources. Diborane is made from boron trifluoride and sodium hydride or from boron trichloride and a hydride, and it arrives at 0.5-5% in hydrogen; boron trifluoride was delivered neat from a cylinder. In 1983 p-type implantation was moving from boron to BF2+ (a molecular ion made in the ion source) because the heavier ion gave a shallower, more controllable junction - a change in the ion source chemistry, not in the wafer chemistry.
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.diborane.note: Established: The p-type sources as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.name: Phosphate rock
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.description: A sedimentary rock of calcium phosphate - apatite - mined from the Florida phosphate belt and the Moroccan and Chinese deposits. It is one of the four rock types this whole tree ends in, alongside crude oil, natural gas and sand. The C64-scale fact is absurd but true: the quantity of phosphate rock mined for fertiliser every year is measured in tens of millions of tonnes, and the quantity used to make the phosphorus in a C64's transistors is a few grams, most of it going into fertiliser for somebody's field.
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.note: The phosphate rock mining and fertiliser chain is nominally outside this subsystem; this node exists because the n-type dopant chain terminates there. Category metals, for the same reason: phosphate rock is a mineral, not wafer chemistry. Phosphate rock is mined mainly in Florida and North Africa. Not established: the tens of millions of tonnes a year mined for fertiliser, and the Florida and Moroccan attributions as the supply actually behind semiconductor-grade phosphorus.

chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cf4.fluori.name: Anhydrous hydrogen fluoride
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cf4.fluori.description: Fluoride plus concentrated sulphuric acid at about 265 C gives anhydrous HF, which is distilled off and shipped in a fluorine-lined tanker or a nickel tank. It is a strong acid, a violent poison, and it will dissolve most metals; the 1980s storage practice was a tank with a fluorine polymer lining and an emergency water curtain, and the fundamental tension in the whole HF business is that the only thing that will hold it is the same fluorine chemistry that makes the etch gases.
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cf4.fluori.note: Anhydrous hydrogen fluoride is made by treating fluorite, CaF2, with concentrated sulfuric acid. The 200-250 C figure in this node is not established: industrial practice is quoted at about 265 C. Also not established: the fluorine-polymer-lined tank, the water-curtain protection, and the emergency arrangements.

chem.photoresist.novolac.name: Novolac resin from phenol and formaldehyde
chem.photoresist.novolac.description: Phenol condensed with formaldehyde under acid to a thermoplastic, low-molecular-weight resin with no epoxide or methylol functionality left. The resin is not the photosensitive part; it is the part that gives the film its mechanical integrity and its dissolution behaviour in the developer. Its phenolic hydroxyl groups are why the novolac dissolves so readily in TMAH - and why an alkaline developable resist could not have worked with the old novolac-epoxy resists of the early 1960s.
chem.photoresist.novolac.note: The phenol chain is chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.phenol and the formaldehyde chain is chem.pom.formaldehyde. The node is the resin, not the making of it. Established: Novolac resin for film integrity distinct from photosensitive part. Not established: the stated molecular weight and functionality specifics as given.

chem.photoresist.diazonaphthoquinone.name: Diazonaphthoquinone sulphonate
chem.photoresist.diazonaphthoquinone.description: The photosensitive ester: 1,2-naphthoquinone-2-diazide-5-sulphonic acid esterified onto the phenolic hydroxyls of the novolac. The 1,4-isomer was the one the 1980s photoresist industry settled on because it gives the higher photospeed and less outgrowth. The whole resist is about 20-30% diazo compound by weight; the rest is novolac and a small amount of sensitiser.

facts.label: Typical exposure
facts.value: g-line 436 nm, h-line 405 nm, i-line 365 nm

chem.photoresist.diazonaphthoquinone.note: Diazonaphthoquinone sulfonate esters are mixed with novolac resin and act as a dissolution inhibitor; a conventional resist is resin, sensitiser and solvent, and novolac is a phenol-formaldehyde condensation polymer. Not established: the 1,4-isomer preference, the 20-30 wt% diazo content, the g-line, h-line and i-line exposure figures, and the outgrowth comparison.

chem.photoresist.negative.name: Negative resists and image reversal
chem.photoresist.negative.description: A small share of 1980s production was negative-working - the exposed areas crosslink and stay - and image-reversal resists, where a photoacid generator makes a carboxylic acid in the exposed areas and an amine in the top layer diffuses into them and makes the exposed areas soluble, so a positive image is made with a negative resist chemistry. The reversal chemistry existed in 1983 because of the contrast it gave with the deep-ultraviolet exposure tools of the late 1980s.
chem.photoresist.negative.note: Negative and image-reversal resists are a family of chemistries described here rather than an operation in the 1980s line.

chem.solvents.trichloroethane.name: 1,1,1-Trichloroethane (methyl chloroform)
chem.solvents.trichloroethane.description: CH3CCl3, boiling at 74 C, a non-flammable solvent that was the standard degreaser for precision metalwork and electronics through the 1950s to the 1980s. It was made from acetylene by hydrochlorination to vinylidene chloride and then chlorination to 1,1,1-trichloroethane - so it shares its whole upstream with vinyl chloride and with natural gas. It is toxic to the liver and kidney, mildly carcinogenic, and it was banned as a non-essential aerosol propellant in the United States in 1987 and phased out as a degreaser through the late 1980s and 1990s.

facts.label: Flammability
facts.value: non-flammable in the usual range (flammable limits ~6-13% with an oxygen-rich atmosphere)

facts.label: 1980s occupational limit
facts.value: 200 ppm 8-hour TWA (ACGIH), with a 300 ppm ceiling

chem.solvents.trichloroethane.note: The flammability of 1,1,1-trichloroethane is a special case: it is non-flammable in air but burns in oxygen-enriched atmospheres, which is a hazard in a large open vapour degreaser. Exposure limits in the early 1980s were under active revision.

chem.solvents.trichloroethylene.name: Trichloroethylene (1,1,2-TCE)
chem.solvents.trichloroethylene.description: Boiling at 87 C, made from acetylene by chlorination to tetrachloroethane followed by dehydrochlorination. It has excellent solvency for grease and for the epoxy and phenolic residues of an electronics line, and it is also a solvent for the vapour degreaser that handles the cleaned parts. It is a suspected carcinogen, and the United States removed it from vapour degreasing in 1990 under the federal halogenated solvent rule; by then the replacement across the industry was largely done. The original industrial route to this degreaser: acetylene chlorinated to tetrachloroethane and then dehydrochlorinated, still the route in much of the world in 1980. It is the acetylene-HCl chemistry of vinyl chloride with a different degree of chlorination.
chem.solvents.trichloroethylene.note: The US prohibition dates: the halogenated solvent rulemaking began in 1983 and the prohibition on TCE vapour degreasing took effect in 1990. Trichloroethylene remained widely used outside the US into the 1990s.

chem.solvents.perchloroethylene.name: Tetrachloroethylene (perchloroethylene)
chem.solvents.perchloroethylene.description: Cl2C=CCl2, boiling at 119 C, made by chlorinating ethylene to 1,2-dichloroethane and then to tetrachloroethane followed by chlorination and dehydrochlorination, or by the oxychlorination route. It was the American electronics degreaser of choice because it dissolves grease and flux residue and does not evaporate as fast as 1,1,1-trichloroethane. It is the clearest case in this file of a solvent killed by regulation rather than by performance: the US EPA's 1984 halogenated solvent rule set a phase-out schedule for vapour degreasing - all sources by 1989, with the smaller degreasers going first - and perchloroethylene was also being restricted as an air pollutant.

facts.label: US EPA phase-out of vapour degreasing
facts.value: small sources from 1985-1986, all sources by 1989

chem.solvents.perchloroethylene.note: The exact sub-schedules of the US halogenated solvent rule (1984) had tiered deadlines by source size; the 1989 completion date is the one usually quoted.

chem.solvents.methylene-chloride.name: Dichloromethane (methylene chloride)
chem.solvents.methylene-chloride.description: CH2Cl2, boiling at 40 C, made by chlorinating methane to chloromethane and then to dichloromethane, or by the chlorination of formaldehyde. It was the fastest-evaporating chlorinated solvent and was used for paint stripping, for the epoxy and flux residues that a slow solvent would not remove, and in place of perchloroethylene in some cleaning operations. Its 1980s regulatory moment came at the end of the decade, when the US EPA designated it a hazardous air pollutant and set a phase-out of its use in degreasing and in the aerosol propellant market.
chem.solvents.methylene-chloride.note: Not established: the boiling point, synthesis routes and end-use list quoted, and the regulatory account of late-1980s US EPA action on degreasing and aerosol-propellant uses.

chem.solvents.cfc.name: CFCs and HCFCs (halons and freons)
chem.solvents.cfc.description: Trichlorofluoromethane (CFC-11, boiling 23.8 C) and trichloro-1,2,2-trifluoroethane (CFC-113, boiling 48 C) were the 1980s cleaners, refrigerants and foam blowing agents, and CFC-11 was the blowing agent in expanded polystyrene packaging until the late 1980s. In 1983 there was no regulation on them at all; by 1987 the Montreal Protocol had been signed and by 1989 the phase-out of the developed countries had begun.
chem.solvents.cfc.note: CFCs are useful solvents and their boiling points make them suitable as refrigerants. Not established: the specific boiling points of 23.8 C for CFC-11 and 48 C for CFC-113, and CFC-11 as the expanded-polystyrene blowing agent until the late 1980s.

chem.solvents.acetone.name: Acetone
chem.solvents.acetone.description: Propanone, boiling 56 C. It was the general cleaning solvent for glass, for the epoxy residues of a coil winding operation, and for some stencil and screen operations, and it is the solvent in the acetylene absorption step of the acetylene process and in the electrophotography of copying. It came out of the cumene process and the acetone cyanohydrin process, both of which are propylene plants.
chem.solvents.acetone.note: About 83% of acetone is made by the cumene process and about a third of world supply is used as a solvent. Not established: the 56 C boiling point, the 2.5-13% flammable range, and the use for the epoxy residues of a coil winding.

chem.solvents.other-oxygenated.name: Ketones, esters and glycol ethers
chem.solvents.other-oxygenated.description: The rest of the 1980s solvent shelf: methyl ethyl ketone and methyl isobutyl ketone (the latter made by condensing acetone to diacetone alcohol and then hydrogenating), ethyl acetate and isobutyl acetate, propylene glycol ethers, and dimethylformamide. Each had a niche - the ketones for coatings, the esters for cleaning, the glycol ethers for the controlled evaporation of a coating, DMF for the film and fibre industries.
chem.solvents.other-oxygenated.note: Not established: the synthesis route described for methyl isobutyl ketone, and the stated niche allocation of ketones, esters, glycol ethers and dimethylformamide across coatings, cleaning, film and fibre uses.

chem.solvents.aromatic-hydrocarbon.name: Xylene, toluene and hexane
chem.solvents.aromatic-hydrocarbon.description: The hydrocarbon solvents. Xylene is the classic silkscreen and coatings solvent and it is what the screen printing ink of a PCB is thinned with. Toluene was the coatings and adhesive solvent. Hexane (extracted from the light ends by solvent extraction with furfural or NMP) was the degreaser for precision metalwork and the extraction solvent for the edible oils. All three are refinery fractions, and they are also the most flammable solvents on the shelf. Furfural (161 C) and NMP (202 C) were the classical solvents for separating aromatics from paraffins in a refinery, both displaced from most of their other duties during the 1970s and 1980s by better solvents and by pressure-swing and adsorption processes.
chem.solvents.aromatic-hydrocarbon.note: The same two solvents appear in chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby and in the solvent replacement business. Established: Hydrocarbon solvents xylene toluene and hexane for inks coatings and adhesives. Not established: the stated extraction and thinning specifics as given.

chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.name: Mercury catalyst and its recovery
chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.description: HCl is adsorbed onto a mercuric chloride-charcoal catalyst and acetylene adds across it. The catalyst is what makes the chemistry work and what makes the plant a mercury emitter, and the 1980s answer was a mercury recovery system: the reactor effluent was stripped with an acid stream, the mercury concentrated to a recoverable 10-20% solution, and that solution taken back to the catalyst maker. It is the same engineering problem and the same answer as the PVC plant's, for the same reason.
