chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.note: Established: HCl is adsorbed onto a mercuric chloride-charcoal catalyst and acetylene adds across it as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.acrylic-ac.name: Acrylic acid
chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.acrylic-ac.description: Made by hydrolysis of acrylonitrile in an 85-93% sulphuric acid solution at 90-120 C in a batch or continuous reactor in the 1980s (the later propane-oxidation route came later and took over). The acrylonitrile had to be purified first because the hydrolysis is irreversible and the by-product ammonium sulphate ends up in the polymer. Superabsorbent diapers drove the growth of this route from the late 1970s.
chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.acrylic-ac.note: Established: Made by hydrolysis of acrylonitrile in an 85-93% sulphuric acid solution at 90-120 C in a batch or continuous reactor in the 1980s (the later propane-oxidation route came later and as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.methyl-met.name: Acetone cyanohydrin
chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.methyl-met.description: A compound that made the C64 possible twice over: it is the intermediate for methyl methacrylate, and the HCN it carries is the feedstock for methyl methacrylate and for the older butadiene-adiponitrile route to nylon 6,6. It is acutely toxic and it has killed people by being absorbed through the skin, which is the reason the ACH plants had such aggressive containment.
chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.methyl-met.note: Established: A compound that made the C64 possible twice over: it is the intermediate for methyl methacrylate, and the HCN it carries is the feedstock for methyl methacrylate and for the older as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.refining.octane.tetraethyl-lead.name: Tetraethyl lead
chem.refining.octane.tetraethyl-lead.description: Pb(C2H5)4 blended at a few grams per litre, discovered in 1921 and the cheapest octane technology for fifty years. It was the cheapest route to octane and the most expensive in externalities: it destroyed the lead and phosphorus catalysts that were the whole point of the catalytic converter. Teledyne and DuPont stopped adding it to road fuel in most markets by 1985.
chem.refining.octane.tetraethyl-lead.note: Established: Pb(C2H5)4 blended at a few grams per litre, discovered in 1921 and the cheapest octane technology for fifty years as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.refining.isomerisation.mtbe.ion-exc.name: Ion-exchange resin catalyst
chem.refining.isomerisation.mtbe.ion-exc.description: A macroporous or gel-type sulphonic-acid polystyrene resin, the same chemistry as the ion exchange resins used in water treatment. MTBE resins had to be replaced every 10,000-20,000 hours in the 1980s as they aged.
chem.refining.isomerisation.mtbe.ion-exc.note: Not established: the resin lifetime range quoted in operating hours, and how widely the stated macroporous or gel-type sulphonic-acid polystyrene formulation was used in 1980s MTBE service.

chem.refining.claus.catalyst.name: Claus catalyst (activated alumina)
chem.refining.claus.catalyst.description: High-surface-area alumina, sometimes promoted with titanium, in two or three fixed beds at 200-350 C with interstage reheating. Because the reaction is exothermic and reversible, a multi-bed converter with controlled quench keeps the equilibrium favourable; a single-bed converter cannot get above about 80% overall recovery.
chem.refining.claus.catalyst.note: Not established: the bed temperatures, staging arrangement and overall recovery claim quoted, and how widely titanium-promoted alumina was used in early-1980s converters.

chem.refining.hydrotreating.acid-gas.name: Acid gas to the Claus unit
chem.refining.hydrotreating.acid-gas.simple_name: Acid gas to the Claus unit
chem.refining.hydrotreating.acid-gas.description: Every hydrotreater and every amine unit makes an acid gas of mostly H2S with some CO2. In 1983 that stream was worth real money: recovering its sulphur turns a disposal liability into a product, and about 80-90% of world sulphur production was elemental sulphur recovered this way. A 20-35 wt% MEA or DEA absorber took the H2S and CO2 out of the hydrogen recycle gas and the rich amine was stripped in a 120-130 C reboiler; the amine was degraded by the oxygen and hydrocarbons in the gas, and the amine/oil/water effluent was one of the refinery's worst waste streams of the period.
chem.refining.hydrotreating.acid-gas.note: Same amine chemistry as the gas sweetening plant: chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-gas.discovery-and-drilling.sweetening. Established: Acid gas as H2S rich stream to Claus sulphur recovery. Not established: the stated 1983 sulphur value shares and recovery specifics as given.

chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.name: FCC zeolite catalyst
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.description: A synthetic zeolite (USY, made by dealuminating Y zeolite) dispersed in a silica-alumina or silica matrix, rare-earth exchanged by lanthanum and neodymium. The zeolite gives shape-selective acid sites; the matrix gives attrition resistance and heat capacity. This is the same family of materials as the zeolites that would crack naphtha for styrene a decade later. Vanadium and nickel in the feed deposit as mobile vanadates and nickel species that destroy zeolite acid sites and accelerate dehydrogenation, so passivation additives - an aluminium monohydride slurry, antimony compounds - were standard by the 1980s, with gasoline desulphurisation additives appearing at the end of the decade.
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.note: Established: A synthetic zeolite (USY, made by dealuminating Y zeolite) dispersed in a silica-alumina or silica matrix, rare-earth exchanged by lanthanum and neodymium as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.c.name: Cracked gasoline and the propylene route
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.c.description: FCC gasoline is high in olefins, aromatics and isoparaffins, with an octane number well above the reformer's, and it is the blending component that let the industry drop lead. Its propylene stream - 2-4% of FCC feed - fed the old chemical industry: by 1983 propylene from FCC and from crackers together supplied roughly half the world's propylene, and the older propylene splitter process existed precisely to make more of it.
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.c.note: The propylene branch: chem.propylene. Established: Cracked gasoline as high octane olefinic blending component enabling lead removal. Not established: the stated octane advantage and propylene yield specifics as given.

chem.refining.delayed-coking.green-coke.name: Green coke
chem.refining.delayed-coking.green-coke.description: The unreformed coke straight out of the drum: 85-92 wt% carbon, 8-15% volatiles, with all the feed's sulphur and metals still in it. Green coke is the intermediate between the coker drum and the calciner, and it is also what the plastics industry noticed in the 1980s: green coke is a needle-coke precursor, and it is the reason carbon fibre of aerospace grade became possible after the large-scale-carbon-fibre work of the late 1960s.
chem.refining.delayed-coking.green-coke.note: Established: The unreformed coke straight out of the drum: 85-92 wt% carbon, 8-15% volatiles, with all the feeds sulphur and metals still in it as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.name: Cobalt-molybdenum / nickel-molybdenum catalyst
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.description: Sulphided Co-Mo or Ni-Mo on alumina in a fixed bed at 300-400 C and 20-50 bar hydrogen, with an H2/hydrocarbon ratio of 200-1,000. Lumping several reactors in series gave 0.2-0.5 wt% sulphur naphtha; a naphtha cracker in 1980s practice wanted 0.5 wt% S or less. The cobalt is not a promoter in the small sense - it is roughly 2-6% Co2O3 beside 10-30% MoO3 on the same alumina support, and the two together are what makes the catalyst active, so a refinery bought the same refined cobalt that a drill-bit maker bought, and it arrived as oxide on a support rather than as anything recognisable as a metal.

facts.label: Loading
facts.value: about 2-6% Co2O3 with 10-30% MoO3 on alumina

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.note: Not established: the temperature, pressure, gas-ratio and loading ranges quoted, the pre-cracker sulphur specification, and the claim that refineries bought the same refined cobalt stream as drill-bit makers.

chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.name: Acid corrosion inhibitor
chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.description: Hydrofluoric acid at 12% and hydrochloric acid at 12%, pumped down a steel coil, will remove a hundredth of an inch of steel a day. The inhibitors - a long-chain amine, thiourea, an acetylenic alcohol - adsorb on the steel and cut the corrosion rate by several orders of magnitude without touching the rock. It is a thin grey film of chemistry doing the work, and it is the reason mud-acid jobs of the 1980s could be pumped downhole at all.
chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.note: An amine corrosion inhibitor is a substance sold in drums, not an operation. Established: Acid corrosion inhibitor as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s specifics as given.

chem.natural-gas.composition.methane.name: Methane
chem.natural-gas.composition.methane.description: CH4, 80-98% of a dry gas, 39.8 MJ/m3 gross calorific value, -161.5 C boiling point. The single molecule most of this branch is about: because methane is hard to polymerise and hard to functionalise, the industry of the 1980s broke it into acetylene at extreme temperature or into hydrogen over a nickel catalyst, and those two products underwrote most of the polymer industry.
chem.natural-gas.composition.methane.note: Established: methane as 80-98 percent of dry gas and the central molecule of the gas branch. Not established: the stated 39.8 MJ per cubic metre calorific value minus 161.5 C boiling point and 1980s acetylene versus reforming splits.

chem.natural-gas.composition.ethane-prop.name: Ethane and propane (LPG)
chem.natural-gas.composition.ethane-prop.description: The C2 and C3 that make natural gas liquids, recovered as LPG at 1.5-8 bar in the field and as a debottlenecking liquid at the gas plant, then split for heating or fed to a cracker. LPG was the preferred cracker feedstock precisely because it is already light and needs no naphtha handling. A dedicated propane cracker needs far less steam dilution (20-40 mol% against 200-400 mol% for naphtha) and so makes far less process gas per tonne of ethylene, but it makes almost no co-product: the propylene and butenes streams shrink and the C4 stream effectively disappears.
chem.natural-gas.composition.ethane-prop.note: Established: The C2 and C3 that make natural gas liquids, recovered as LPG at 1.5-8 bar in the field and as a debottlenecking liquid at the gas plant, then split for heating or fed to a cracker as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.natural-gas.composition.nitrogen.name: Nitrogen in natural gas
chem.natural-gas.composition.nitrogen.description: 1-15% N2 in many fields. It is the impurity that most affects heating value, that forces the Wobbe index (a measure of interchangeability between gas supplies) onto a pipeline tariff, and that makes a gas which is 90% N2 unsaleable as town gas.
chem.natural-gas.composition.nitrogen.note: Nitrogen content is highly field-specific; the Wobbe index framing is standard.

chem.natural-gas.composition.h2s.name: Hydrogen sulphide (sour gas)
chem.natural-gas.composition.h2s.description: A lethal, corrosive, smelly component that must be taken to a few ppmv before the gas enters a steel pipeline, because H2S embrittles steel and attacks copper alloys. Sweetening it produces a concentrated acid gas stream whose H2S is the feedstock for the Claus sulphur plant in the refining branch.
chem.natural-gas.composition.h2s.note: The amine plant and the Claus plant are under chem.natural-gas.sources and chem.refining.claus. Established: Hydrogen sulphide as lethal corrosive sour gas requiring sweetening to pipeline ppm levels. Not established: the stated embrittlement alloy specifics and acid gas feed details as given.

chem.natural-gas.sources.associated-gas.name: Associated (oil-associated) gas
chem.natural-gas.sources.associated-gas.description: Gas from the gas cap of an oil field, produced at roughly 50-150 m3 of gas per barrel of oil. Around 70% of world gas production was associated gas in 1983, and a large share was still flared: world flaring ran at the order of 100-130 billion m3 a year in the early 1980s, several million tonnes of hydrocarbons a year simply burned at the wellhead. A flare tip burns whatever the oil plant cannot handle, and in 1980s practice it was sized for peak oil rate, so routine gas-cap growth had to be reinjected into the reservoir or sold.
chem.natural-gas.sources.associated-gas.note: Established: Gas from the gas cap of an oil field, produced at roughly 50-150 m3 of gas per barrel of oil as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.natural-gas.sources.methane-hydrate.name: Gas hydrate (a hazard, not yet a resource)
chem.natural-gas.sources.methane-hydrate.description: Methane trapped as a clathrate of water, stable below about 20 C at surface pressure. Known since the 1930s and already recognised in the deep ocean and permafrost as a potentially enormous resource, but in the early 1980s it was a hazard - it plugged subsea pipelines and was one reason offshore gas lines carried inhibitors and heated risers - not a supply.
chem.natural-gas.sources.methane-hydrate.note: Not established: the scale of the deep-ocean and permafrost hydrate resource as understood in the early 1980s, and how widely hydrate plugging and inhibitor practice figured in subsea gas lines of the period.

chem.natural-gas.uses.fertiliser-ammonia.name: Fertiliser ammonia
chem.natural-gas.uses.fertiliser-ammonia.description: About 80% of ammonia goes to fertiliser, a demand that sets the size of the hydrogen industry and therefore, indirectly, the amount of ammonia available for the acrylonitrile ammoxidation. The link to the C64 is indirect but real: the same ammonia plants that fertilised the fields also supplied the nitrogen that went into the case polymer.
chem.natural-gas.uses.fertiliser-ammonia.note: Not established: the share of ammonia going to fertiliser quoted, and the implied sizing link between the fertiliser market, hydrogen capacity and ammonia availability for ammoxidation.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Gas reservoir
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: Gas fills a porous sandstone or a fractured carbonate just as oil does, but with a lower density and a higher compressibility, so gas in place is quoted in trillions of standard cubic feet rather than billions of barrels. The largest gas fields in the world in the early 1980s were the giant Permian Basin fields (US), Urengoy and Yamburg in West Siberia, and Groningen (Netherlands, discovered 1959).
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.note: Established: Gas fills a porous sandstone or a fractured carbonate just as oil does, but with a lower density and a higher compressibility, so gas in place is quoted in trillions of standard cu as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Gas in place
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: Trillions of standard cubic metres of gas in the pore space. The C64-scale fact: all the natural gas used worldwide in 1983 was of the order of 3,000 billion cubic metres a year, so one machine's plastics and energy are far below a thousandth of a cubic metre.
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.note: Not established: the world gas production figure quoted for 1983, and the per-machine gas quantity implied for one computer's plastics and energy.

chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammoni.name: Magnetite from iron ore
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammoni.description: Fe3O4, the reduction product of hematite, and the raw material for the ammonia catalyst. It is also the mineral in the Claus catalyst's neighbourhood and in the polishing lapidary industry. A tonne of ammonia carries about 0.3-0.4 tonnes of iron in its catalyst, and the catalyst is replaced every few years, so the ammonia business has a real, if modest, appetite for iron ore.
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammoni.note: The iron ore chain itself belongs to the metals subsystem; this node marks where it enters the ammonia catalyst. The industrial ammonia synthesis catalyst is obtained from finely ground iron powder, itself obtained by reduction of high-purity magnetite. Not established: the 0.3-0.4 tonnes of iron per tonne of ammonia, the catalyst replacement interval, and that this is where the iron ore chain enters.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.mo.name: Montmorillonite and the bentonite bed
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.mo.description: Sodium montmorillonite is a dioctahedral 2:1 smectite: two tetrahedral silica sheets sandwiching an octahedral aluminium sheet, with the negative layer charge balanced by exchangeable sodium. Between the layers is water, and that water is why the clay swells, gels and gives the mud its thixotropy. The drilling grade comes from the Cretaceous Bentonite bed of Wyoming and South Dakota, a marine sediment about 65-72 million years old that is a calcium montmorillonite until it is mined and soda-ashed to the sodium form.
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.mo.note: Established: Sodium montmorillonite is a dioctahedral 2:1 smectite: two tetrahedral silica sheets sandwiching an octahedral aluminium sheet, with the negative layer charge balanced by exchangea as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.mo.name: The clay pit
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.mo.description: A 10-20 m thick bentonite bed, opened up and worked as an open pit or a shallow underground mine, in a landscape that looks like a lunar plain because the clay is grey-white when fresh and weathers to a pale crust. It is the last dig-it-out node of the crude branch's drilling chain, and it is the point at which a machine that will one day hold a C64's case first touches something that came out of the ground with no hydrocarbons in it at all.
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.mo.note: Not established: the 10-20 m bed thickness and the open-pit versus shallow-underground working method. The grey-white lunar appearance and the Wyoming and South Dakota locations are consistent with the type locality but are not documented.

chem.pvc.plasticiser.dehp.name: Di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate
chem.pvc.plasticiser.dehp.description: C8H17OOC-C6H4-COOC8H17, 391 g/mol, a colourless liquid with a very slight odour. About 200,000-250,000 tonnes of DEHP a year were made in 1983, most of it for PVC. The C8 alcohol comes from propylene and from ethylene via butyraldehyde, so a PVC cable jacket is a direct consumer of the cracker.
chem.pvc.plasticiser.dehp.note: DEHP production volumes in the early 1980s are order-of-magnitude estimates.

chem.pvc.stabilisation.lead-stabiliser.name: Tribasic lead sulphate and lead phosphite
chem.pvc.stabilisation.lead-stabiliser.description: The lead salts are cheap, opaque, and superb at scavenging HCl and chelating chlorine. The cost is that lead is a cumulative neurotoxin and PVC was, until recently, a major route of human lead exposure through pipes, and in 1983 the limits on lead in consumer products were tightening. The chemistry is basic: the metal salt of sulphuric or phosphorous acid, made by precipitating the oxide or sulphate onto a lead base.
chem.pvc.stabilisation.lead-stabiliser.note: Not established: the loading range quoted for rigid PVC, the scavenging and chelation mechanism described, and the regulatory-tightening claim for lead in consumer products around 1983.

chem.pvc.stabilisation.ca-zn.name: Calcium-zinc stabilisers
chem.pvc.stabilisation.ca-zn.description: Calcium and zinc carboxylates (stearate, hydrostearate) with an organic co-stabiliser such as a beta-diketone or a polyol. Zinc carboxylates are the primary stabilisers and calcium carboxylates are the co-stabilisers that exchange zinc for calcium at the right moment. The 1980s engineering problem was matching the zinc-to-calcium ratio and the lubricant balance so the compound did not plate out on the extruder die, which is a real and stubborn processing problem rather than a trivial substitution.
chem.pvc.stabilisation.ca-zn.note: Not established: the formulation and co-stabiliser list described, the zinc-calcium exchange mechanism, and the die plate-out account as a real processing constraint on substitution.

chem.styrene.benzene.coal-tar.name: Coke oven benzene
chem.styrene.benzene.coal-tar.description: Byproduct benzene from the coking of coal in an integral coke plant: the coke oven gas is cooled and the aromatics stripped out with a wash oil, which is then steam-stripped, giving a crude benzole with toluene and xylenes. In 1983 coal tar benzene was still a major share of world benzene - more so in Europe and Asia than in the United States - and it is the one benzene of that era that is not a petrochemical at all.
chem.styrene.benzene.coal-tar.note: Not established: the wash-oil and steam-stripping process description, and the claim about coal-tar benzene share of world benzene in 1983 by region.

chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..name: Fatty acid emulsifier and tallow
chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..description: About half of a cold SBR or ABS emulsifier system is a fatty acid salt, and the fatty acid came from tallow - the rendered fat of cattle and sheep - split into oleic and stearic acid and neutralised with sodium or potassium hydroxide. So part of the emulsifier that keeps the rubber particles apart in the graft reactor was, in 1983, a byproduct of the meat industry, which is a genuinely surprising provenance for a molecule that ends up inside a computer case.
chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..note: Established: About half of a cold SBR or ABS emulsifier system is a fatty acid salt, and the fatty acid came from tallow - the rendered fat of cattle and sheep - split into oleic and stearic ac as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..name: Tallow
chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..description: Rendered animal fat, roughly 50% palmitic, stearic and oleic acid. Historically a by-product of the meat industry and increasingly, through the 1980s, a rendering industry of its own. Its oleic acid was the emulsifier and its stearic acid was the release agent, and both ended up in the polymer. The C64's case therefore contains a trace of a livestock product through the soap that helped the rubber particles form.
chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..note: The tallow provenance of fatty-acid emulsifiers is well established; synthetic fatty acids were substituting for it through the 1980s.

chem.propylene.cumene.alkylation.phospho.name: Silica carrier (the same silica as the cracker drier)
chem.propylene.cumene.alkylation.phospho.description: A silica gel of 200-400 m2/g surface area, and a strong family resemblance to the 3A molecular sieve's carrier and to the FCC catalyst's matrix and to the ammoxidation catalyst's support. One amorphous silica, made from sand by the soda-silica route, appears in this file as a support four different times, and it is the petrochemical branch's quietest link to a mineral.
chem.propylene.cumene.alkylation.phospho.note: Silica gel is amorphous and porous with nanometre-scale voids, and the same material does appear as a support elsewhere in this chain. Not established: the 200-400 m2/g surface area of the alkylation catalyst's carrier, and the claim that all four supports in this file are one material.

chem.propylene.flame-retardants.chlorina.name: Chlorinated paraffin
chem.propylene.flame-retardants.chlorina.description: Paraffins chlorinated to 40-70% chlorine, used as a secondary flame retardant and, in the 1970s, as a plasticiser for PVC. It is a cheap and effective flame retardant and a persistent environmental contaminant, which is why the 1980s trend in electronics housings was towards phosphorus systems and towards thin walls that did not need as much of it.
chem.propylene.flame-retardants.chlorina.note: Not established: the chlorination range quoted, the PVC-plasticiser use claim for the 1970s, and the statement that 1980s electronics housings moved toward phosphorus systems and thinner walls.

chem.propylene.flame-retardants.tdcpp.name: Tris(2,3-dichloropropyl) phosphate
chem.propylene.flame-retardants.tdcpp.description: The organophosphate flame retardant made from propylene oxide and phosphorus oxychloride. It is an effective flame retardant for ABS, rigid polyurethane foam and polyester resins, and its precursor, tris(2,3-dibromopropyl) phosphate, is the classic story of a flame retardant that was banned in the United States in the 1970s after it caused animal tumours. That ban is the single clearest link between a 1960s consumer polymer and a 1990s regulation.
chem.propylene.flame-retardants.tdcpp.note: The US ban on tris(2,3-dibromopropyl) phosphate under the Consumer Product Safety Act dates from 1977; the chlorinated phosphate was its less-toxic replacement.

chem.propylene.polymerisation.stereospec.name: Stereospecific titanium catalyst
chem.propylene.polymerisation.stereospec.description: Titanium trichloride or titanium tetrachloride on magnesium chloride with an aluminium alkyl, refined in the 1970s and 1980s to give activities high enough that no catalyst removal was needed. The MgCl2-supported catalyst with an internal donor (a phthalate or a diether) was the technical development that made modern polypropylene economics work, and the diether donors were commercialised around 1980-83.

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: TiCl4 or TiCl3 on MgCl2 with AlEt3/AlEt2Cl, internal donor

chem.propylene.polymerisation.stereospec.note: The activity figures for late-1980s catalysts are order-of-magnitude and were rising quickly year to year.

chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.name: Cracker C3 stream
chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.description: The propylene and propane that distil out of the cracker's quench separator. Naphtha crackers make roughly 0.15 t of propylene per tonne of feed, which on a 500,000 t/yr cracker is about 75,000 t/yr of propylene - more than a small polypropylene plant needs.
chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.note: Not established: the propylene-per-tonne-of-feed ratio and the annualised tonnage illustration for a 500000-tonne-per-year cracker.

chem.thermosets.phenolic.hexamine.name: Hexamethylenetetramine (hexamine)
chem.thermosets.phenolic.hexamine.description: Formaldehyde plus ammonia, and it does double duty: it is the curing agent for novolac phenolic and it is a slow accelerator and a decomposition source of formaldehyde in rubber compounds. It is one of the few molecules in this file that reaches into three unrelated chemistries.
chem.thermosets.phenolic.hexamine.note: Not established: the dual-role claim for hexamine as novolac curing agent and as rubber accelerator and formaldehyde source, and the statement that it reaches into three unrelated chemistries.

chem.epoxy.hardeners.dds.name: 4,4'-Diaminodiphenyl sulfone (DDS)
chem.epoxy.hardeners.dds.description: The high-temperature laminate hardener: about 80 parts per 100 of DGEBA, cured at 180-200 C. DDS is made by sulphonating diphenyl sulphone, nitrating it to the dinitro compound and reducing the nitro groups - an aniline and chlorobenzene route for the aniline part. It is the hardener in the aerospace laminates and in the higher-temperature grades of FR-4, and it costs several times what the amine does.
chem.epoxy.hardeners.dds.note: Not established: the loading and cure-temperature figures quoted, the sulphonation-nitration-reduction synthesis route described, and the cost and FR-4 grading claims.

chem.epoxy.hardeners.ddd.name: 4,4'-Diaminodiphenylmethane (DDM/MDA)
chem.epoxy.hardeners.ddd.description: Made by condensing aniline with formaldehyde, it is the first-generation hardener: cheap, and it is the amine that showed up in the early carcinogenicity work on epoxies in the 1970s, which pushed the industry toward DDM's less toxic relatives. It is still in laminates and in the rubber industry as a vulcanisation accelerator.
chem.epoxy.hardeners.ddd.note: The 4,4'-methylenedianiline classification work dates from the 1970s-early 1980s and was a driver of substitution in both epoxy and elastomer applications.

chem.epoxy.hardeners.anhydride.name: Anhydride cure
chem.epoxy.hardeners.anhydride.description: A cyclic anhydride (a methyl substituted tetrahydrophthalic or nadic anhydride) catalysed by an amine or a tertiary amine. The cure is slower and needs 150-200 C, but the network is very tight and the dielectric properties are excellent - which is why anhydride epoxy was the potting and the chip-attach system of the 1980s, where a chip sitting on a cured epoxy die attach with a controlled coefficient of thermal expansion was worth the cure temperature.
chem.epoxy.hardeners.anhydride.note: Not established: the cure-temperature range quoted, the anhydride and catalyst identities listed, and the dielectric and thermal-expansion claims for 1980s potting and die-attach service.

chem.rubber.natural.name: Natural rubber (cis-1,4-polyisoprene)
chem.rubber.natural.description: Field latex tapped from Hevea brasiliensis, coagulated, smoked and pressed into bales. In 1983 world production was of the order of 3.0-3.5 million tonnes a year, two thirds of it in Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia. It is cis-1,4-polyisoprene with a glass transition near -70 C, so it is the most resilient rubber at room temperature, and it needs vulcanisation with sulphur because the cis double bond is what makes it elastic. A quarter-spiral cut is made into the tapping panel about every other day and the latex is collected in a cup; about 30% of a mature tree's latex can be taken without killing it over a 25-30 year tapping life. Before the 1930s the whole article had to be vulcanised in the mould; by the 1930s the compound could be prevulcanised in a mixer - deliberately introducing some crosslink - so it was a flowable, uncured-on-the-surface material that could be shaped and then cured in the mould. Heated with sulphur and an accelerator, a thiuram or a sulphonamide, the cis double bonds get a short sulphur bridge between neighbouring chains: crosslinked, so the chains can no longer slide.
chem.rubber.natural.note: World natural rubber production in the early 1980s was around 3 million tonnes a year; the figure is approximate.

chem.rubber.neoprene.name: Neoprene (polychloroprene)
chem.rubber.neoprene.description: Chloroprene polymerised in emulsion at 40 C. It is oil-resistant, weather-resistant and flame-resistant, which makes it the rubber for gaskets, for the flexible jacket of a power cord, and for the cable's outer sheath when the cable is not PVC. It is made from acetylene and chlorine through vinylacetylene and dichloroacetylene - one more route that ends in acetylene, and therefore in natural gas. Acetylene dimerises to vinylacetylene, which chlorinates to 1,2-dichloro-2-butene; dehydrochlorination gives chloroprene, which polymerises in emulsion at 40 C.
chem.rubber.neoprene.note: Neoprene's process chemistry is standard; the intermediate toxicity warnings are well established. Established: Neoprene as emulsion chloroprene rubber for gaskets and cable jackets. Not established: the stated polymerisation temperature and use specifics as given.

chem.rubber.epdm.name: EPDM
chem.rubber.epdm.description: Ethylene copolymerised with a diene (norbornene or a cyclic diene), the diene content giving the vulcanisable double bonds. It has no unsaturation in the main chain, so it is ozone-resistant and will not crack in sunlight, which is why it replaced natural rubber in weather-exposed cable insulation and in the C64's power cord as the flexible jacket material of preference.
chem.rubber.epdm.note: The ethylene comes from the cracker: chem.ethylene. Established: EPDM as ethylene diene copolymer with ozone resistance. Not established: the stated diene types and replacement histories as given.

chem.polycarbonate.phosgene.chlorine.name: Chlorine and carbon monoxide
chem.polycarbonate.phosgene.chlorine.description: Chlorine from brine electrolysis plus carbon monoxide from a reformer or from coke. This is the point at which the chlor-alkali industry - which needs hydrogen to sell its chlorine, and therefore needs natural gas - touches the plastics industry through a molecule with two chlorine atoms and one oxygen.
chem.polycarbonate.phosgene.chlorine.note: Chlorine electrolysis belongs to the chlorine subsystem; the hydrogen requirement is chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen. Established: Chlorine from brine electrolysis plus carbon monoxide for phosgene. Not established: the stated reformer versus coke sourcing specifics as given.

chem.abs.additives.pigment-masterbatch.name: Pigment masterbatch
chem.abs.additives.pigment-masterbatch.description: A pre-dispersed concentrate - typically titanium dioxide (rutile, for weather resistance), carbon black, ultramarine blue, phthalocyanine green, or an iron oxide - at 20-60% loading in an ABS or LDPE carrier, dosed at 1-3% into the compounding line. A masterbatch exists because a pigment dropped into a twin screw as a powder will not disperse, and undispersed pigment is visible as specks in the moulding.
chem.abs.additives.pigment-masterbatch.note: Not established: the carrier, loading and let-down ranges quoted, the pigment list as representative of 1980s ABS colouring, and the dispersion mechanism claimed for masterbatch versus raw powder.

chem.abs.additives.stearate.name: Metal stearate release agent
chem.abs.additives.stearate.description: Calcium stearate or zinc stearate, 0.1-0.5%, dosed to stop the ABS sticking to the screw and the die, and to help the mould release. The stearates come from stearic acid (from tallow or from a C18 fraction) neutralised with lime; the metal itself is the only heavy metal routinely added to a consumer plastic.
chem.abs.additives.stearate.note: Not established: the dosage range quoted, the tallow and C18-fraction origin claim for stearic acid, and the statement about the metal being the only heavy metal routinely added to a consumer plastic.

chem.abs.drying.desiccant.molecular-siev.name: The 3A molecular sieve itself
chem.abs.drying.desiccant.molecular-siev.description: The desiccant in the dryer is a synthetic zeolite with a 3 angstrom pore opening, which admits the water molecule (kinetic diameter about 2.65 angstrom) and excludes anything bigger. That single geometric fact is why a molecular sieve can dry a plastic to 200 ppm: it is a molecular filter, not an absorber. The zeolite is made by hydrothermal synthesis from an alumina gel, a silica source and an organic template at 150-200 C and autogenous pressure in an autoclave - and then the template is burned out of the pore at 500-550 C, which is what opens the pores. A zeolite powder cannot go in a dryer bed - it dusts and it fluidises - so it is formed into 2-4 mm extruded pellets with about 4% of clay and silica binder, and the binder is the part that stops the pellet taking up water itself, because the bed's capacity is only 20-22% of its own weight. Alumina, sodium silicate and sodium hydroxide are gelled, seeded with a few crystals of the product zeolite and heated in an autoclave at 150-200 C for 24-96 hours, and nucleation and growth control is the whole art - which is why crystal size distribution is a commercial specification and a 2-micron zeolite for a cracker drier costs more than a 50-micron one.
chem.abs.drying.desiccant.molecular-siev.note: Established: The desiccant in the dryer is a synthetic zeolite with a 3 angstrom pore opening, which admits the water molecule (kinetic diameter about 2.65 angstrom) and excludes anything bigge as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.bismu.name: Bismuth molybdate on silica
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.bismu.description: The standard catalyst, chosen for its selectivity to acrylonitrile and its resistance to reduction by ammonia. The 1980s development targets were the vanadium- and tungsten-promoted versions and, later in the decade, the bismuth-molybdenum-phosphorus systems aimed at raising the acrylonitrile yield above 90%.

facts.label: Catalyst family
facts.value: bismuth phosphomolybdate (Bi9PMo12O52) on silica is given as one of the first useful catalysts; bismuth molybdate on silica with V or W promoters is the general ammoxidation catalyst. Which the 1983 plant ran is not established.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.bismu.note: Acrylonitrile comes from catalytic ammoxidation of propylene, and bismuth phosphomolybdate on silica was one of the first useful catalysts - a phosphorus-containing bismuth molybdate, not the Bi2Mo3O12 this node names. Not established: resistance to reduction by ammonia, the vanadium- and tungsten-promoted versions, and the above-90% acrylonitrile yield target.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.antim.name: Antimony-phosphorus-boron oxide catalyst
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.antim.description: The fluidised-bed catalyst: a silica support promoted with phosphorus and boron oxides so that the phosphorus does not volatilise away at 450 C. It was less selective but far more active and far more mechanically robust than the bismuth catalyst, which matters in a fluidised bed.
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.antim.note: Not established: the support and promoter description, the operating-temperature reference, and the selectivity, activity and mechanical-robustness comparison against the bismuth catalyst.

chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene.name: Butadiene monomer
chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene.description: 99.0-99.7% butadiene from a cracker C4 extraction unit. The chain is why the C64's rubber phase is a petrochemical and not a natural rubber: the natural rubber alternative is cis-1,4-polyisoprene from latex, and the graft chemistry that works on polybutadiene's pendant vinyl group does not work on isoprene's chain. The 99.7% monomer comes out of the cracker C4 stream by the extractive route at chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.
chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene.note: Upstream: chem.butadiene and chem.butadiene.polymerisation.lithium-catalyst. Established: Butadiene monomer as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s specifics as given.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.additives.bht.name: BHT (2,6-di-tert-butyl-4-methylphenol)
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.additives.bht.description: The workhorse antioxidant, dosed at 0.05-0.2 wt%. It is made by alkylating para-cresol with isobutylene over a solid acid or an aluminium chloride catalyst, and it was also in the C64's power supply as a capacitor-filling fluid (as the antioxidant of the impregnant).
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.additives.bht.note: Not established: the 0.05-0.2 wt% loading and the para-cresol alkylation with isobutylene. In particular the claim that BHT was the antioxidant of the C64 power supply's capacitor-filling fluid is unsupported - no such material appears in the 1992 service manual parts list.

chem.ethylene.feedstock.naphtha.name: Naphtha feedstock
chem.ethylene.feedstock.naphtha.description: A C5 to 200-220 F hydrocarbon cut, hydrotreated to under 0.5 wt% sulphur and under 0.5 ppmw nitrogen. Beyond its hydrocarbon content what matters is the coniocarbon and the asphaltene content: those are what coke the coil. The naphtha from an Arabian light crude is comparatively clean, which is one reason Gulf crackers could run at a lower steam dilution than a naphtha cracker fed with heavy California naphtha.
chem.ethylene.feedstock.naphtha.note: The refinery side of this handover is chem.refining.polymer-feedstocks.naphtha-to-ethylene. A refinery fraction: naphtha is cut from light sour crude, so this leaf now terminates the whole cracker chain at chem.petroleum. Established: Naphtha feedstock hydrotreated for sulphur nitrogen and coking precursors. Not established: the stated cut points and contaminant limits as given.

chem.ethylene.feedstock.ethane.name: Ethane feedstock
chem.ethylene.feedstock.ethane.description: Ethane cracks cleanly with little coke and needs almost no steam dilution, so an ethane cracker is cheaper to run and its ethylene yield (50-55%) is much higher. But it makes almost no propylene and no butadiene, so a pure ethane cracker has to buy its co-products. The 1980s US Gulf argument about ethane versus naphtha was really an argument about whether propylene and butadiene were worth more than the extra ethylene.
chem.ethylene.feedstock.ethane.note: Not established: the ethylene-yield and steam-dilution figures quoted, and the characterisation of the 1980s Gulf feedstock debate as a co-product valuation argument.

chem.ethylene.feedstock.gas-oil.name: Gas oil feedstock (the third choice)
chem.ethylene.feedstock.gas-oil.description: The heavier option, chosen when naphtha and gas oil were both dear: a 300-700 F cut cracked harder to get ethylene, coking heavily, and yielding the most propylene of the three. Gas oil cracking existed in the Middle East and in Japan through the 1970s and mostly disappeared in the 1980s because its cost per tonne of ethylene was the worst of the three.
chem.ethylene.feedstock.gas-oil.note: Not established: the boiling-range cut, the relative ethylene cost claim, and the statement that gas-oil cracking had mostly disappeared by the 1980s.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.name: Bentonite (montmorillonite clay)
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.description: Sodium montmorillonite from the Cretaceous Bentonite beds of Wyoming and South Dakota; the single most important mud component. It gives the thixotropy: at rest a high gel strength to suspend cuttings, under shear it drops to low viscosity so the bit can cut. Drilling-grade bentonite is API 13/14 with a viscosity of 30+ s/qt and a low montmorillonite ratio.

facts.label: Typical mud loading
facts.value: 20-60 kg/m3 of bentonite in a water mud

facts.label: Yield stress target
facts.value: 3-20 Pa for hole cleaning; gel 10-30 Pa on the low-yield muds

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.note: Montmorillonite is a dioctahedral 2:1 smectite; Wyoming sodium bentonite is the reference grade because of its high cation-exchange capacity and layer charge. Bentonite suspensions are usually thixotropic and shear-thinning, the Cretaceous Benton Shale near Rock River, Wyoming is the type locality, and United States production comes from between the Black Hills of South Dakota and the Bighorn Basin of Wyoming. Not established: the API 13/14 grading, the 30+ s/qt viscosity, the 20-60 kg/m3 loading and the 3-20 Pa yield stress targets.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.chromate-lim.name: Chrome/lime mud (invert emulsion)
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.chromate-lim.description: The classic high-temperature mud: a water-in-oil (invert) emulsion with oil as the continuous phase, bentonite in the aqueous phase, and calcium carbonate and a lime (Ca(OH)2) emulsion. Chrome/lime muds were standard to about 120-150 C but they fail in a cement job because the calcium in cement breaks the emulsion, so a salt-water mud or a chrome-free lime mud had to be switched in first.
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.chromate-lim.note: The name comes from the use of sodium chromate as a corrosion inhibitor on the ferrous cutting and drilling hardware, which had to be neutralised before disposal.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.oil-based-mu.name: Oil-based (diesel) mud
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.oil-based-mu.description: Diesel or mineral oil as the continuous phase with water as the dispersed phase, organophilic clay (amine-treated montmorillonite) for viscosity. Chosen for high-temperature deep wells and for formations where water filtrate would swell clay. Its environmental reputation in the Gulf in the 1980s was poor, and it had to be stabilised with organophilic bentonite and lime.
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.oil-based-mu.note: Petroleum diesel is the same distillate stream as the refining branch: chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation. Established: Oil-based diesel mud as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s specifics as given.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.weights-mix.name: Mixed-weight additive (iron ore + barite)
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.weights-mix.description: Where barite was unavailable or too expensive, ground iron ore was blended in as a second weighting agent. It attacks steel components by corrosion and needs a passivation layer of lime or sulphide film, but it saved cost in a tight barite market.
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.weights-mix.note: Not established: how widely ground iron ore substituted for barite in early-1980s drilling muds, and whether lime or sulphide-film passivation against steel corrosion was standard practice.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.chelant-bioc.name: Chelants, biocides and defoamers
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.chelant-bioc.description: The 1980s mud chemist's standard additive cabinet: phosphate and polyphosphate sequestrants for calcium, lignosulphonate and polyacrylamide viscosifiers, benzyl alcohol defoamer, and glutaraldehyde or formaldehyde-based biocides against sulphate-reducing bacteria, which produce hydrogen sulphide and sour the cuttings.
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.chelant-bioc.note: Not established: which sequestrant, viscosifier, defoamer and biocide formulations any particular early-1980s mud programme used, and at what dosages.

chem.crude.reservoir.source-rock.name: Source rock and kerogen
chem.crude.reservoir.source-rock.description: Organic-rich marine shale. Type I and type II kerogen give oil; type III, humic and mainly terrestrial, gives gas. Maturation is measured by vitrinite reflectance, with the oil window at roughly 0.6-1.3% Ro and the gas window above about 1.3%. Between about 60 and 160 C the kerogen breaks down into oil and at higher rank into wet and then dry gas: the same thermal-cracking chemistry, far slower and uncatalysed, that a steam cracker performs in seconds.
chem.crude.reservoir.source-rock.note: Established: Organic-rich marine shale as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.crude.reservoir.trap.name: Geological trap
chem.crude.reservoir.trap.description: Anticline, fault, pinch-out or stratigraphic trap. The Ghawar field in Saudi Arabia, discovered in 1948, remained the largest oil field on earth for decades, holding some 100+ billion stock-tank barrels in a stacked series of Arabian carbonate reservoirs.

facts.label: Ghawar field
facts.value: >100 billion stock-tank barrels recoverable (Arabian Suwayb member carbonates)

chem.crude.reservoir.trap.note: Established: Anticline, fault, pinch-out or stratigraphic trap as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.crude.reservoir.reservoir-rock.name: Reservoir rock: sandstone and carbonate
chem.crude.reservoir.reservoir-rock.description: Porosity 15-35% and permeability 50-2,000 mD for a good sandstone; carbonate reservoirs have most of their porosity as vugs and fractures and typically 5-25% matrix porosity. Around 60% of world oil reserves and 80% of world gas reserves were in carbonate rock, most of it fractured Arab-type in the Middle East.
chem.crude.reservoir.reservoir-rock.note: Established: Porosity 15-35% and permeability 50-2,000 mD for a good sandstone, carbonate reservoirs have most of their porosity as vugs and fractures and typically 5-25% matrix porosity as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.crude.reservoir.oil-column.name: Oil column in the pore space
chem.crude.reservoir.oil-column.simple_name: Oil column in the pore space
chem.crude.reservoir.oil-column.description: An oil column of tens to hundreds of metres stands between a gas cap and a water contact, with oil saturation in the pay zone often only 50-80% of pore volume. That gap, plus the reservoir rock and the seal, is why recovery factors are 15-35% and why hydraulic fracturing and acidising exist.
chem.crude.reservoir.oil-column.note: Established: An oil column of tens to hundreds of metres stands between a gas cap and a water contact, with oil saturation in the pay zone often only 50-80% of pore volume as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.crude.reservoir.oil-column.oil-in-p.name: Oil in place
chem.crude.reservoir.oil-column.oil-in-p.description: The volume of hydrocarbons physically present in the rock, before any recovery factor. Multiply it by the C64 scale: the entire world shipped about 200,000 Commodore 64s in 1983, so the machine is a rounding error on a single wellhead's hourly output.
chem.crude.reservoir.oil-column.oil-in-p.note: Established: The volume of hydrocarbons physically present in the rock, before any recovery factor as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.petroleum.asphaltene.name: Asphaltenes and resins
chem.petroleum.asphaltene.description: The heavy, aromatic, high-molecular-weight end of crude. Roughly 2-20% of crude, soluble in the light ends and precipitated by heptane in the standard n-heptane asphaltene test. Asphaltenes are the coke precursors in every thermal cracker, coker and reformer, and their content is what decides whether a crude makes a good or bad feedstock.

facts.label: n-C7 asphaltene content
facts.value: 2-10 wt% for a light sour crude

chem.petroleum.asphaltene.note: Established: The heavy, aromatic, high-molecular-weight end of crude as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.crude.reservoir.reservoir-rock.mari.name: Marine carbonate (Arab-type) reservoir
chem.crude.reservoir.reservoir-rock.mari.description: Dolomitised limestone and dolomite of the Arabian shelf: high initial productivity, typically 4,000-10,000 bbl/d per well with strong water drive, but rapid flow assurance decline and high water cut. Saudi production was essentially all of this rock type in 1983.
chem.crude.reservoir.reservoir-rock.mari.note: Established: Dolomitised limestone and dolomite of the Arabian shelf: high initial productivity, typically 4,000-10,000 bbl/d per well with strong water drive, but rapid flow assurance decline as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.solder-chemicals.solder-alloy.tin-s.name: Where the tin came from
chem.solder-chemicals.solder-alloy.tin-s.description: The tin in a 60/40 solder was smelted from cassiterite, the tin ore, and cassiterite is one of the rarer tin deposits in the world: Bolivia's placer and vein cassiterite, the Cornish tin belt, the Nigerian and the Indonesian deposits, and the alluvial cassiterite of Malaysia and Thailand. In 1983 the world mined something like 25,000-30,000 tonnes of tin a year - a small metal market by volume and a strategically awkward one, because the electronics industry's solder demand is a large fraction of it.
chem.solder-chemicals.solder-alloy.tin-s.note: Established: The tin in a 60/40 solder was smelted from cassiterite, the tin ore, and cassiterite is one of the rarer tin deposits in the world: Bolivias placer and vein cassiterite, the Corni as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.activat.name: Flux activator
chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.activat.description: Rosin alone is a weak flux. The activator is what makes the flux work, and it is also what makes the residue corrosive, so the whole specification of a flux is a trade: enough acid to remove the oxide, not enough ion to eat the board. The 1980s activators were carboxylic acids (stearic acid, abietic acid itself, succinic acid and its anhydride), fatty acid salts such as the zinc and amine stearates, and - in the older RMA grades - amine hydrochlorides, which is where the halide came from.
chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.activat.note: Established: Rosin alone is a weak flux as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.rosin-f.name: The flux base and its solvent
chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.rosin-f.description: A liquid flux is rosin, activator and solvent, and the solvent is what makes it a liquid. Through the 1980s the solder wire's core was a rope of activated rosin flux in an alcohol or glycol ether solvent (isopropyl alcohol, or a glycol ether), and the core was drawn into a wire of solder by a wire-drawing machine. The active rosin in the core had to be clean enough to be drawn: any acid-value drift or gum would tear the wire. A solder wire is a core-drawing operation: a rope of activated flux is drawn together with a tube of alloy through successive dies until the wire is 0.3-0.8 mm across and the flux core 0.1-0.3 mm.
chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.rosin-f.note: Not established: the solvent identities listed, the wire and core diameter ranges quoted, the flux-content figure, and the core-drawing process description including the acid-value drift claim.

chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.activat.name: Amine halide activator (the halide source)
chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.activat.description: A triethanolamine or an alkylamine neutralised with a mineral acid, giving a halide ion in the flux. It is the reason a halide flux is corrosive if the residue is left on, and it is the reason the halide-free no-clean flux of the mid-1980s removed them rather than replacing them: the halide was never functional, it was just the most convenient way to get an acid and an amine together. The MIL-F-14161 halide-free standard of the late 1970s is what the industry measured against. The whole trick of a halide flux is the neutralisation: enough amine to dissolve the resin, enough mineral acid to supply the fluxing acidity and the halide ion, and not so much of either that the residue eats the board.
chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.activat.note: The halide-free flux specification (MIL-F-14161) is the standard US military specification that the 1980s flux industry measured against; its date is the origin of the practice rather than of the specification's current form.

chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.copper-foil..name: Benzotriazole coupling agent
chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.copper-foil..description: BTA, a seven-membered ring with three adjacent nitrogens, adsorbs onto copper and stops it reacting with anything else - it is the corrosion inhibitor and the adhesion promoter in one. It is a beautiful small molecule for this tree because the same triazole ring chemistry appears in the corrosion inhibitors of every other metal in the book, and because the copper underneath is a metal chain node and the BTA is a petrochemical.
chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.copper-foil..note: BTA's use as the standard copper coupling agent dates from the 1970s and displaced chromate-based treatment; the exact formulations are proprietary.

chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.nitroge.name: Nitrogen
chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.nitroge.description: 99.999% and, for the very best, 99.9999%. Produced by cryogenic air separation for the large users and by pressure swing adsorption for the small ones. Its uses were the furnace tube atmospheres, the photoresist spin-coat bowl, the drying cabinets, the solvent flush and the packaging seal. A large C64 production line would have used a few hundred cubic metres of nitrogen a week.
chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.nitroge.note: Established: 99.999% and, for the very best, 99.9999% as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.helium.name: Helium
chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.helium.description: Almost all helium is recovered as a by-product of the cryogenic separation of natural gas liquids - 0.05-0.7% of a helium-rich gas stream, separated to 99.999%. It is the cleanest gas in the plant and it is used in the helium leak detector that is how a fab proves a chamber is sealed, and in the cryopumps of the etch machines. It is the one process gas in a fab whose feedstock is unambiguously natural gas.
chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.helium.note: Helium separation from a natural gas plant belongs to the gas processing branch: chem.natural-gas.processing. Established: Helium as cryogenic natural gas liquids byproduct for leak detection and cooling. Not established: the stated concentration ranges and purity specifics as given.

chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.argon.name: Argon
chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.argon.description: A by-product of the air separation unit at 1-3% of the air, purified to 99.999%. It fills the sputtering cathodes - the argon ions are accelerated across the gap and knock atoms out of the aluminium or titanium target - and it is the inert atmosphere of the annealing and ashing steps. The sputtering itself is the metals chain, but the gas that drives it is an air separation product.
chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.argon.note: Argon is a byproduct of cryogenic air separation. Not established: the 1-3% of air figure, the 99.999% purity, and the description of argon filling sputtering cathodes and inerting the annealing and ashing steps in a 1980s fab.

chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cf4.name: Tetrafluoromethane
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cf4.description: CF4, the workhorse oxide etch gas and the fluorine chemistry's workhorse generally. It is made from fluorine (from fluorspar) and carbon, or from a chlorofluorocarbon feedstock. In a plasma etcher it dissociates to fluorine radicals that etch silicon dioxide - it does not etch silicon, which is what made the selectivity possible - and it is the gas that made the barrel reactor the standard 1980s oxide etch.
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cf4.note: CF4 boils at -128 C. Not established: the dissociation to fluorine radicals as the reason selectivity against silicon works, manufacture from fluorine and carbon or from a chlorofluorocarbon feedstock, and CF4 as the standard 1980s oxide etch gas.

chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cl2.name: Chlorine and boron trifluoride
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cl2.description: A chlorine-based plasma - Cl2, or BCl3 with Cl2 - is used for aluminium, because fluorine does not etch aluminium cleanly. BCl3 also supplied boron, so the etch gas doubled as the p-type dopant source, which is one of the reasons the boron trifluoride and boron trichloride business ended up as one business.
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cl2.note: BCl3 is made by chlorinating boron oxide or elemental boron; the chemistry is standard but the 1980s supply details are not well documented.

chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.nf3.name: Nitrogen trifluoride
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.nf3.description: An emerging chamber-cleaning gas in the 1980s, and later a feedstock for the NF3-based etch chemistry. It is a very strong oxidiser, it is a gas at room temperature, and the reason it took so long to industrialise in the United States was a supply constraint rather than a performance one - the production chemistry needed fluorine.
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.nf3.note: NF3 chamber cleaning was in commercial use in the late 1980s; this node's presence is a marker rather than a core technology of the 1983 C64 chips.

chem.solvents.aromatic-hydrocarbon.white.name: White spirit and mineral spirits
chem.solvents.aromatic-hydrocarbon.white.description: A petroleum distillate boiling 150-200 C - roughly C8-C12 - sold as the standard paint and stencil solvent. It was the cheapest coating solvent there was and it was used in the silkscreen shop, in the stencil shop and in the assembly shop's fixture cleaning. Its defect was the same defect as xylene's: flash point around 30-40 C, which means it belongs in a room with no open flame and a bonded-earth tank.
chem.solvents.aromatic-hydrocarbon.white.note: White spirit definitions vary by standard; the 150-200 C range and the flash point are representative.

chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.name: Activated charcoal support
chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.description: A 2-4 mm charcoal pellet, impregnated with mercuric chloride and dried. Activated charcoal is made by carbonising wood or coal at 800-1,000 C and steam activating it, so it is - like the rosin in the solder flux - a forestry product. The charcoal support in the degreaser's ancestor chemistry is therefore, like almost everything else in this file, something dug up or grown and then refined.
chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.note: Activated charcoal manufacture by steam activation of a carbonised precursor is standard; the specific precursor used for this catalyst is not known here.

chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.acrylic-ac.name: Ammonium sulphate by-product
chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.acrylic-ac.description: One tonne of acrylic acid from acrylonitrile hydrolysis throws out about one tonne of ammonium sulphate, which is a low-grade fertiliser that is expensive to dry and transport. It is the classic penalty of the hydrolysis route and the reason the later oxidation route won.
chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.acrylic-ac.note: Not established: the one-to-one mass ratio quoted between ammonium sulphate by-product and acrylic acid, and the claim that drying and transport cost as low-grade fertiliser drove adoption of the later oxidation route.

chem.refining.claus.catalyst.alumina-cat.name: Claus alumina catalyst and its support
chem.refining.claus.catalyst.alumina-cat.description: The catalyst is not a mystery material: it is activated alumina, and the alumina is refined from bauxite. A Claus unit's catalyst life is measured in years and its loss rate is what sets the unit's sulphur recovery, so a good 1980s unit used a promoted, high-surface-area alumina with a shape (extrudate or cylindrical) chosen to hold surface area at 300-400 C.
chem.refining.claus.catalyst.alumina-cat.note: Established: The catalyst is not a mystery material: it is activated alumina, and the alumina is refined from bauxite as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.name: Silica-alumina matrix
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.description: Amorphous silica-alumina, precipitated from sodium silicate and aluminium sulphate and caustic-gelled, then spray dried as 40-90 micron microspheres. The matrix is what gives the catalyst its attrition resistance and its heat capacity; it also carries a good part of the cracking, because the matrix surface area is large and the zeolite is expensive.
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.note: Not established: the microsphere size range quoted, and the allocation of cracking activity and attrition resistance between matrix and zeolite.

chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.name: ZSM-5 octane additive
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.description: A small-pore zeolite (mordenite framework, 10-membered rings) blended at 3-15% into the USY catalyst to crack the C7-C10 straight chains that were killing octane after the lead phase-down. This is the direct ancestor of the propylene and isobutylene it also made: ZSM-5 selectively shapes the products towards C3 and C4 olefins.
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.note: Not established: the blend-level range quoted, the framework and ring-size description, and the claim linking lead phase-down octane demand to C3 and C4 olefin selectivity.

chem.natural-gas.processing.name: Gas processing and transport
chem.natural-gas.processing.description: The plants that turn a wet, sour wellstream into a pipeline gas, a liquefied gas or a natural-gas-liquids fraction. A large 1980s gas plant handled 5-30 billion standard cubic feet a day; the North Sea, Gulf and Middle Eastern plants of that decade were among the largest chemical plants ever built. Ethane, propane, butane and pentane are stripped out as natural gas liquids - ethane for crackers, propane and butane for LPG, C5+ for gasoline - and a cryogenic plant recovers 90-99% of the methane but less of the heavy end, so the design trade is expander against absorption.

children.name: Cryogenic separation (expander plant)
children.description: The JT-expander process that became the industry standard for large gas plants in the 1980s: the gas is chilled by expansion through a turbine to -30 to -80 C and the resulting cold box distils methane from ethane and heavier. The plant cost is dominated by the aluminium cold boxes, which remain one of the largest single uses of aluminium in the world per tonne produced.

children.name: Cryogenic turboexpander
children.description: A radial or axial turbine in the cold box, handling 10,000-40,000 kW on a big plant, recovering 5-15% of the gas enthalpy and reaching -30 to -80 C. The expander train was the mechanical heart of the 1980s gas plant and its efficiency set the plant cost.
children.note: Established: A radial or axial turbine in the cold box, handling 10,000-40,000 kW on a big plant, recovering 5-15% of the gas enthalpy and reaching -30 to -80 C as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Aluminium cold box
children.description: A brazed plate-and-fin aluminium exchanger 10-30 m long, cryogenic to -80 C, containing dozens of channels. Aluminium-brazed cold boxes replaced copper wound exchangers in the 1970s and are one reason the gas plant business grew so fast in that decade.
children.note: Established: A brazed plate-and-fin aluminium exchanger 10-30 m long, cryogenic to -80 C, containing dozens of channels as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

Established: The JT-expander process that became the industry standard for large gas plants in the 1980s: the gas is chilled by expansion through a turbine to -30 to -80 C and the resulting col as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: LNG liquefaction
children.description: Chilling gas to -162 C so it becomes a liquid at atmospheric pressure, cutting volume about 600-fold for the same energy. In 1983 world LNG trade was roughly 55-70 billion m3 a year, about 2-3% of world gas production, on a network of roughly 60-70 liquefaction trains. The dominant cycles were the propane-precooled mixed refrigerant (9 stages, about 7-8% specific power) and the nitrogen expander cycle.

children.name: Mixed refrigerant cycle
children.description: Propane pre-cooling to -30 to -40 C, then an ethylene/ethane/propane mixture expanded through a series of exchangers to -120 C, then a nitrogen expander to -162 C. The hydrocarbons in the refrigerant are the same ones the petrochemical industry buys; the nitrogen expander cycle burns almost nothing but needs a lot of power and very large exchangers, which suited a plant with cheap power and no other outlet for its fuel gas.
children.note: Kept as a node because its three numbers (the -162 C liquefaction temperature, the 1:600 volume reduction and the 7-8% specific power) are the cycle, not a detail of it. The refrigerant hydrocarbons are recorded as ingredients.

children.name: LNG storage and regasification terminal
children.description: A vacuum-insulated cylindrical tank of 20,000-160,000 m3 with a nickel-alloy inner tank over perlite insulation, plus a jetty for a 125,000-165,000 m3 carrier. Regasification burns about 0.3 tonnes of fuel gas per tonne of LNG, which is where the C64-scale fact becomes visible: the fuel burned to regasify enough LNG to make one machine's plastics is tens of grams.
children.note: The regasification fuel figure of about 0.3 t/t LNG is the standard design value; the C64 extrapolation is order-of-magnitude.

children.name: LNG carrier
children.description: A 70,000-125,000 m3 membrane or independent-tank ship with a re-liquefaction plant, because LNG boils off at 0.1-0.3% a day and the load has to be reliquefied in transit. The world LNG fleet in 1983 was of the order of 90-130 ships at $40-90 million each.
children.note: LNG carrier prices and fleet size in the early 1980s are order-of-magnitude figures.

Established: Chilling gas to -162 C so it becomes a liquid at atmospheric pressure, cutting volume about 600-fold for the same energy as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Gas pipeline
children.description: Line pipe 0.6-1.4 m in diameter, API 5L grade X52-X70, laid by a lay barge or a trenching spread and internally coated with epoxy and polyethylene powder. Transmission lines run at 60-100 bar with compressors every 100-200 km. The 1980s were the years of the great gas transmission builds: the Central Asia-Centre system, the Norwegian and North Sea systems and the Trans-Med pipelines all date from this decade.

children.name: Subsea pipeline and riser
children.description: Concrete weight-coated line with a hot-water or electrical trace heater for hydrate prevention, and a wet-insulated riser with a buoyancy module for the first 100-300 m of water. Deepwater gas tiebacks of the 1980s established the standard development: subsea wellhead manifold, a dedicated line to a central platform, gas gathered ashore.
children.note: Established: Concrete weight-coated line with a hot-water or electrical trace heater for hydrate prevention, and a wet-insulated riser with a buoyancy module for the first 100-300 m of water as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

A pipeline and an LNG carrier move a bulk stream, they do not make one, so transport is the category here and the gas plant that feeds them is a plant. Established: Gas pipeline as bulk transport with epoxy and polyethylene coating. Not established: the stated diameters grades pressures and compressor spacings as given.

chem.natural-gas.processing.note: LPG end point: chem.natural-gas.composition.ethane-propane. Established: Gas processing to pipeline LNG and liquids fractions. Not established: the stated plant capacities and regional plant specifics as given.

chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.name: Acetylene from natural gas
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.description: The Reppe process, commercialised from 1959-1965: a mixture of roughly 6-8% methane with 30-38% air and 55-60% hydrogen is fired through a water-cooled burner at 1,200-1,800 C and quenched to below 100 C within milliseconds. The acetylene yield per pass is only 2-3% of the feed, so the process has to recycle a large stream, and the furnace consumes several GWh of electricity per tonne of acetylene. It survived because it made a C2 unit out of a C1 feed - the only route that can make vinyl chloride, and hence PVC, without cracking a barrel of naphtha. Cracking acetylene at 1,200-1,400 C in a water-cooled steel retort and quenching in nitrogen gave a fine high-surface-area channel black for rubber reinforcement and printing inks, largely displaced in tyres during the 1960s by furnace black made from natural gas. Acetylene plus chlorine also gives tetrachloroethane and from it trichloroethylene and chloroform, while methyl chloride for the chlorosilane chain comes from the same high-temperature HCl chemistry, so field gas reaches the C64's chips as well as its case.

children.name: Partial oxidation burner
children.description: Methane is partially oxidised to CO and H2, which then combine to acetylene at flame temperature. The furnace runs at atmospheric to 2 bar with the flame held above the acetylene decomposition point; the burner is water-cooled because copper and steel both survive the flame while the mixture would otherwise decompose to soot. The process is violently sensitive to soot: any carbon in the gas feed poisons the burner.

facts.label: Furnace temperature
facts.value: 1,200-1,800 C depending on variant and measurement point

children.note: Not established: the furnace temperature range, pressure range and per-pass acetylene yield quoted, and the burner-material and soot-sensitivity claims.

children.name: Quench and acetylene recovery
children.description: The hot gas is quenched to below 100 C within milliseconds, then acetylene is absorbed selectively from the acetylene-hydrogen-methane-hydrogen-sulphide mixture by acetone at 10-20 C and 5-15 bar (about 2.2 volumes of acetylene per volume of solvent), stripped and the solvent recirculated. Recovered acetylene is 99.5-99.8% pure once hydrogen sulphide and water are removed. The last step before the acetylene goes to the vinyl chloride plant is a drying and finishing train - a molecular sieve or a chilled water wash to get the water under 10 ppm, then a caustic or amine wash for the last of the hydrogen sulphide - because vinyl chloride hydrolyses in water and the last drying step is not optional.

children.name: The absorption and recovery train
children.description: The acetylene is absorbed out of the cracked mixture in a solvent and taken off the top of the tower at high purity, which is the whole reason for doing the separation this way. Acetone's job is to hold acetylene - which at 20 C and 12 bar will dissolve to about 2.2 volumes of solvent per volume of acetylene - while letting the hydrogen, methane and carbon monoxide straight through. The dark, dangerous part of this plant is not the chemistry but the acetylene itself: above 2 bar in the presence of a metal, acetylene will detonate into its own decomposition products, and the whole extraction plant is designed around never letting that happen.

children.name: Absorber and stripper
children.description: A 20-40 tray absorber at 10-20 C and 5-15 bar with the acetone circulated, and a stripper that takes the pure acetylene overhead at 3-5 bar and the solvent off the bottom for recycle. The solvent must be regenerated at intervals because it accumulates the hydrogen sulphide and the water from the feed gas, and because the acetylene polymerises in it if it is left standing - the plant has a permanent low-temperature nitrogen blanketing problem.
children.note: Established: A 20-40 tray absorber at 10-20 C and 5-15 bar with the acetone circulated, and a stripper that takes the pure acetylene overhead at 3-5 bar and the solvent off the bottom for recyc as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

Established: The acetylene is absorbed out of the cracked mixture in a solvent and taken off the top of the tower at high purity, which is the whole reason for doing the separation this way as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

Not established: the quench temperature and timing, the acetone absorption conditions and solvent-capacity figure, the purity range quoted, and the sequence of the final drying and finishing steps for vinyl chloride service.

children.name: Acetylene to vinyl chloride
children.description: The reason the whole acetylene industry existed. Acetylene plus anhydrous hydrogen chloride over a 0.3-0.5% mercuric chloride catalyst on charcoal at 20-60 C and 1-2 bar absolute gives vinyl chloride at 15-25% conversion per pass and 90-95% selectivity, the low conversion forced by the HCl ratio and by the fact that vinyl chloride is a vinylogous acrylate that polymerises readily.
children.note: Established: The reason the whole acetylene industry existed as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.note: The semiconductor chain itself belongs to the silicon subsystem; the chloromethane source is gas-derived and belongs here. Established: Acetylene from natural gas via Reppe type burner and quench. Not established: the stated feed mixtures temperatures yields and commercialisation dates as given.

chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.name: Hydrogen by steam methane reforming
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.description: CH4 + H2O -> CO + 3H2 over nickel at 750-850 C and 20-30 bar, followed by the water-gas shift (iron oxide/chromia, 350-450 C) to raise the hydrogen fraction, then CO2 removal and cryogenic or PSA purification. A world-scale 1980s plant made 50-100 million m3 of hydrogen a day. Almost all of it went to ammonia; the rest to hydrotreating and to hydrochloric acid. The second largest industrial use of hydrogen is hydrochloric acid: H2 + Cl2 at 250-400 C over a synthesis catalyst, absorbed into demineralised water to 31-37%. The refinery's hydrogen - desulphurisation, hydrocracking, reforming - came from naphtha reformers and, as sour crudes grew, from dedicated gas reformers; in 1983 hydrogen was roughly 3-5% of refinery energy consumption and a genuine bottleneck.

children.name: Hydrogen to ammonia (Haber-Bosch)
children.description: N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3 over promoted iron or ruthenium at 400-500 C and 150-250 bar, in a 1,000-2,500 tonne a day synthesis loop fed from a purge cascade. Ammonia is the single largest use of hydrogen, and it matters to the C64 in two places: the nitrogen for the polybutadiene and SAN polymerisations, and the acrylonitrile ammoxidation. The aqueous form the fab buys is at chem.fab-chemicals.ammonium-hydroxide.
