children.note: Established: Haber Bosch ammonia synthesis from nitrogen and hydrogen over promoted iron as the largest hydrogen use. Not established: the stated 400-500 C 150-250 bar and 1000-2500 tonne per day loop specifics as 1980s standard.

chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.note: Chlorine electrolysis itself belongs to the chlorine subsystem; the hydrogen requirement belongs here. Established: Hydrogen by steam methane reforming plus shift and purification. Not established: the stated temperatures pressures and world scale plant sizes as given.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.mo.name: Soda ash conversion to sodium bentonite
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.mo.description: The pit clay is a calcium montmorillonite and has to be converted. The clay is blunged with water, treated with sodium carbonate so that the exchangeable calcium is replaced by sodium, and then dried and milled. That step is what turns a geological curiosity into an industrial material, and it is also the step that makes the drilling specification possible, because the sodium form swells and the calcium form does not.
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.mo.note: Kept as a node because the conversion is what makes the drilling specification possible: the sodium form swells and the calcium form does not. Its soda ash is now a "from" edge to the metals fragment's sodium carbonate node instead of a line of prose.

chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.ferric-chlori.name: Regenerating the ferric chloride etchant
chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.ferric-chlori.description: Spent ferric chloride is ferrous chloride and copper chloride, and it has to be oxidised back to ferric before it can etch again. The industrial way was a chlorination cell: chlorine into the ferrous solution at 60-80 C, converting ferrous back to ferric and precipitating the copper as cuprous chloride. The cell was a piece of the chlor-alkali plant's technology, and the chlorine in it was often the same chlorine that the plant bought for its own electroplating line. Chlorine regenerates the feric ion and the copper comes out as a precipitate, which in 1983 meant a chloride concentration that climbed and had to be bled off and a copper sludge with its own disposal limits.
chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.ferric-chlori.note: The alkaline etch was spreading through the 1980s; the exact adoption date in a given plant is not documented here. Established: Ferric chloride regeneration by chlorination oxidation. Not established: the stated temperatures and adoption dates as given.

chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery.name: Aromatics recovery from reformer naphtha
chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery.description: The C6 to C8 aromatics have to be extracted from a naphtha stream where they are only a few percent by weight. The 1960s and 1980s workhorse was the UOP EdCo process: extractive distillation with sulfolane (a four-plus-four ring sulfone, 218 C boiling point) followed by azeotropic distillation with isooctane. Sulfolane replaced sulfuric acid extraction because it did not invert the alkylbenzenes and did not make a waste acid stream - and sulfuric acid hydrodealkylation was the older, waste-generating route.
chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery.note: Established: The C6 to C8 aromatics have to be extracted from a naphtha stream where they are only a few percent by weight as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery..name: Sulfolane from butadiene
chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery..description: The solvent that extracts benzene out of a naphtha stream is itself made out of the cracker's C4. Butadiene is reacted with sulfur dioxide and water to give tetrahydrothiophene 1,1-dioxide. So the styrene chain - benzene, ethylbenzene, styrene - is fed by butadiene twice over: once as the rubber in the ABS, and once as the solvent that separated the benzene. It is the clearest example in this file of a chemical park's flows being a web rather than a line. Butadiene plus SO2 at 100-140 C gives the sulfolene, a five-membered ring with one double bond left, and a second equivalent of water with a base opens the second ring to sulfolane; the sulphur dioxide comes from burning recovered elemental sulphur, usually the same Claus sulphur a nearby refinery took out of the same sour gas that fed the cracker.
chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery..note: Sulfolane is industrially made by the butadiene/SO2/hydrolysis route; the conditions quoted are representative. Established: Sulfolane from butadiene for benzene extraction linking styrene chain to C4. Not established: the stated reaction conditions as representative specifics.

chem.butadiene.sources.cracker-c4.c4-rec.name: C4 recovery and the depentaniser
chem.butadiene.sources.cracker-c4.c4-rec.description: Before the butadiene extractor there is the C4 recovery section: a depentaniser that takes the C5+ out of the whole cracker liquid so the C4 unit does not have to handle pentanes and heavier, and then a C3/C4 splitter that separates propane from the butanes. Both columns are ordinary fractionations, but the depentaniser runs at 30-40 bar and is where a lot of the plant's fouling comes from, because the C5+ fraction carries the naphthalene and the heavier aromatics that the C4 extractor does not want.

children.name: The depentaniser
children.description: A 40-60 tray column operating at 25-40 bar, taking the C5 cut point at about 50-60 C. Its overhead is the C4 stream that goes to the extractor; its bottoms are the C5+ gasoline fraction that goes to the aromatics recovery or to the gasoline pool. It is the least glamorous column in the plant and the one that most often needs its furnace cleaned.
children.note: Not established: the tray count, pressure and cut-point figures quoted, the stream-routing description, and the maintenance remark about furnace cleaning.

children.name: The C3/C4 splitter
children.description: A 60-80 tray column separating propane overhead from the butanes. It is a good example of a column that has nothing to do with the product of interest: the butadiene extractor's feed comes off the bottom of this splitter, and the splitter's job is only to keep the propane out of the extractor so the extractor's solvent does not have to separate propane from butadiene as well.
children.note: Not established: the tray count quoted and the claim that the column exists only to keep propane out of the downstream extractor feed.

chem.butadiene.sources.cracker-c4.c4-rec.note: Established: Before the butadiene extractor there is the C4 recovery section: a depentaniser that takes the C5+ out of the whole cracker liquid so the C4 unit does not have to handle pentanes a as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.name: C3 recovery and the propylene column
chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.description: How the propylene actually leaves the cracker. The C3 and C4 streams are separated in a deethaniser, then the propane and propylene go to a propylene splitter column where the propylene is taken overhead. Before that column, the stream is caustic washed to remove the carbonyls and the oxygenates; in the 1980s this was an option rather than an obligation, and the plants that skipped it were the plants whose polymerisation catalyst was drinking acetone.

children.name: Caustic wash
children.description: A 10-20% sodium hydroxide wash column that neutralises the acidic oxygenates - propanal, acetone, propionic acid, and the phenol and cresols from the C9+ - that the cracker makes. The spent caustic is a refinery effluent problem: it is a phenolic wastewater with a high chemical oxygen demand, and in the 1980s it was often incinerated on the site.
children.note: Not established: the caustic-strength range quoted, the list of acidic oxygenates removed, and the claim about incineration as the usual 1980s disposal route for spent phenolic caustic.

children.name: The propylene splitter column
children.description: A 50-70 tray column 50-70 m tall that separates the propylene overhead from the propane that has to be recycled back to the furnace. Propylene and propane have a relative volatility of about 1.1, so this is a distillation with a reflux ratio of 15-25 and a lot of energy; the 1980s development was a packed or tray hybrid with a side stripper and a low-pressure-drop design, because the column's cost is its energy consumption.
children.note: Not established: the tray count, column height, relative volatility and reflux-ratio figures quoted, and the description of 1980s low-pressure-drop and side-stripper developments.

chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.note: Established: How the propylene actually leaves the cracker as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.propylene.sources.propylene-splitte.name: Propylene splitter (the older dedicated unit)
chem.propylene.sources.propylene-splitte.description: A dedicated thermal cracker that re-cracked propane and the cracker's propylene-rich C3 stream at 500-600 C to make more propylene, at 15-25% selectivity, with a big furnace and a bad energy balance. It was the standard propylene route of the 1960s, it was still running in 1983 in a few places, and it was generally obsolete by the mid-1980s because the selectivity was hopeless and the cracker had become the cheaper source.
chem.propylene.sources.propylene-splitte.note: Splitter conditions and selectivity vary; the key point is the low selectivity relative to modern routes.

chem.propylene.sources.depolymerisation.name: Depolymerisation of polypropylene
chem.propylene.sources.depolymerisation.description: Reheated polypropylene was fed back to a reactor to recover the propylene it was made from. This was developed as a recycling route in the early 1970s when the word recycle meant something and it survived as a niche process for decades, mostly because the chemical plant could not discharge a plastic waste stream.
chem.propylene.sources.depolymerisation.note: Reactor operation temperatures and the commercial fate of the process in the 1980s are not well documented; treat as a minor route.

chem.thermosets.phenolic.formaldehyde.name: The formaldehyde in a phenolic
chem.thermosets.phenolic.formaldehyde.description: Methanol oxidised to formaldehyde over silver at 600-700 C. The same formaldehyde as the acetal plastics, from the same methanol, from the same synthesis gas. Phenolic resin and POM sitting a few hundred metres apart in a 1980s chemical park is not a coincidence; both are formaldehyde chemistry.
chem.thermosets.phenolic.formaldehyde.note: Shared with chem.pom.formaldehyde. Established: Formaldehyde in phenolic from methanol oxidation over silver. Not established: the stated temperatures and park co-location specifics as given.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.name: Making the ammoxidation catalyst
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.description: The ammoxidation catalyst is a shaped, robust porous solid, and making it is a small ceramics industry. A bismuth molybdate catalyst is prepared by impregnating precipitated bismuth molybdate or by sol-gel methods onto a silica support, then shaping it into 3-5 mm extrudates or spray-dried microspheres and calcining at 500-700 C. The support is silica gel, and silica gel is made from sand. That is the whole chain from a dune to a transistor's acrylonitrile in three steps. The powder is extruded into trilobe or quadrilobe shapes - the lobes give more external surface per unit volume than a cylinder, and less diffusion limitation - and then dried and calcined at 500-700 C, which converts the oxide precursor into the active bismuth molybdate phase.

children.name: Soda silica from sand
children.description: Quartz sand is fused with sodium carbonate at about 1,300 C to make sodium silicate, which is dissolved in hot water to make the silicate solution, which is acidified to gel. This is the same soda-silica chain that gives the silica sol for the polysilicon ingot's crucibles and the quartz for the fused silica, and it is the industrial descendant of a two-thousand-year-old glassmaking reaction. It is the last dig-it-out node in this branch: sand.
children.note: The soda-silica route is the classical one for both glass and silica sol; its scale-up is the industrial glassmaking reaction. It is an industrial mineral rather than wafer chemistry, and it sits with metal.silica-sand. Not established: the fusion of quartz sand with sodium carbonate at about 1,300 C to make sodium silicate, and the gelling of the acidified silicate solution as the route both to silica sol and to fused silica.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.note: Lobed extrudates and the calcination temperature range are standard catalyst-manufacturing practice. Established: Shaped porous catalyst manufacture with lobed extrudates and calcination. Not established: the stated support preparation and temperature specifics as universal.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.name: Titanium tetrachloride and the sponge route
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.description: The titanium tetrachloride of the Ziegler-Natta catalyst is made from titanium ore - rutile or ilmenite - by chlorinating it with coke and chlorine at 900-1,000 C, then distilling the TiCl4 out at 136 C. Titanium metal comes back by reducing the tetrachloride with magnesium (the Hunter process, which is the Kroll process in reverse) and distilling the magnesium chloride off. So the most important catalyst in the low-pressure polyethylene business is made in a plant that looks exactly like the zirconium and hafnium plants of the nuclear industry, because they all make volatile tetrachlorides. Rutile or ilmenite plus coke plus chlorine at 900-1,000 C gives TiCl4 with iron and vanadium chlorides that have to be removed by distillation - making a volatile chloride the cheapest way to get a pure element out of an oxide. TiCl4 plus magnesium at 800-900 C under argon in a sealed can, then vacuum distillation of the magnesium chloride at 1,000 C, leaves a porous titanium sponge.
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.note: Established: The titanium tetrachloride of the Ziegler-Natta catalyst is made from titanium ore - rutile or ilmenite - by chlorinating it with coke and chlorine at 900-1,000 C, then distilling as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.name: Fracturing sand and its plant
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.description: The proppant is a silica sand that has been sieved, washed, resin-coated and graded, and the plant that does it is a small mineral processing operation that exists in the Permian basin because the proppant has to be nearby. The oilfield sands of the Permian have a problem that glass sands do not: a weak grain crushes under the closure stress of a hydraulic fracture, so the 1980s industry coated a fraction of the proppant with a phenolic resin to make it stronger. By the late 1980s a fraction of the sand (5-30% depending on the basin) was coated with a cured phenolic or furfural resin so it would not embed on closure, which turned a mineral commodity into a single-use consumable and created a solid waste stream of its own.
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.note: Coating fractions and the date of commercial introduction vary by basin and supplier. Established: Fracturing sand and its plant as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s specifics as given.

chem.rosin.distillation.name: Stump distillation and grading
chem.rosin.distillation.description: Rosin is made by distilling the resin out of pine stumps. The stump is chipped into 5-10 cm pieces, charged to a still, and heated; turpentine comes over first and is condensed and separated by distillation into alpha-pinene, beta-pinene and dipentene, and then pine oil and a heavy residue come over, and what is left in the pot is the crude rosin. The rosin is then graded - by colour (X, WW, WW, W) and by softening point (batter 75 C, fir 80 C, Norway 85 C, I 90 C, P 110 C, S 120 C) - and the Y grade, at about 165 C softening point and clear, is the one the flux core needs because it has almost no crystallisation and it does not go brittle. Grading is colour against a reference chip, softening point by the ring-and-ball method and acid value by titration, and the flux maker's specification is colour and softening point with the abietic acid content following from them.

children.name: Chipping and the still
children.description: A whole-tree distillery burns about 1.5-2.5 tonnes of dry pine stumps per tonne of rosin plus its turpentine, and yields about 5-8% rosin, 3-4% turpentine and 1-2% pine oil by mass of dry wood. The stumps come from pine killed by beetle attack, from pine cut for pulp, and from the thinning of a plantation - so the rosin business is downstream of a forestry, and specifically of a beetle, in a way that is often overlooked when the flux is described as a petrochemical.

children.name: Retort and the batch cycle
children.description: The classic stump still is a cast-iron or steel retort holding one to two tonnes of chipped wood, charged, closed, and fired with the turpentine vapour going to a condenser and the rosin staying in the pot. A cycle takes 12-20 hours and the still is charged by hand - which is why the business has barely changed since the 1850s in its mechanics while every other part of the 1980s chemical industry has been rebuilt twice. The 1980s changes were in the condenser and in the chip size, not in the process.
children.note: Stump distillation cycle times and charge sizes vary by still design; the figures are representative of the small-batch practice that survived into the 1980s.

facts.label: Rosin yield from dry pine wood

children.note: Yields vary a lot with the species, the age of the stump and the method; the ranges are the commonly quoted ones.

chem.rosin.distillation.note: Established: Rosin is made by distilling the resin out of pine stumps as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.nitroge.name: Cryogenic air separation
chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.nitroge.description: Air is filtered, compressed to 30-100 bar, cooled and expanded through a cold box to fractionate it into oxygen, nitrogen and argon at -180 C. A unit producing 5,000-30,000 tonnes a day of nitrogen was a large industrial plant in its own right, and it shared its cold box technology with the natural gas processing business in this file.
chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.nitroge.note: Not established: the pressure range, product slate, separation temperature and daily-tonnage figures quoted, and the cold-box technology kinship claimed with natural-gas processing.

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.diborane.bora.name: Boron trifluoride from fluorspar
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.diborane.bora.description: BF3 is made by treating fluorspar with sulphuric acid or with fluosilicic acid, so the p-type dopant of a 1983 NMOS process is, three steps back, the same rock as the HF that etched the oxide. This is the tightest single chain in this whole tree from a mineral to a transistor.

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.name: Where the phosphorus comes from
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.description: The phosphine of a 1983 fab has a longer ancestry than most people assume. Elemental phosphorus is made in a submerged arc furnace from phosphate rock, coke and silica at 1,400-1,500 C, condensed as white phosphorus under water, and then either burned to phosphorus pentoxide (for fertiliser and for the pure phosphoric acid of this file) or reduced to phosphorous acid, which is then converted to phosphine. So an n-doped transistor junction in a C64's VIC-II traces back through a gas cylinder, an electric furnace, and a phosphate rock mine. Yellow phosphorus plus phosphorus pentasulphide is treated with caustic soda and water to give phosphorous acid and sodium hypophosphite, and acid plus hypophosphite is the standard industrial route to phosphine; the electronic gas is then diluted to 5-15% in hydrogen or nitrogen and cylinder-packaged, because pure phosphine is pyrophoric and because the cylinder is what the gas cabinet expects.

children.name: The submerged arc phosphorus furnace
children.description: A 30-100 MW furnace in which phosphate rock, coke and silica are heated to 1,400-1,500 C by three graphite electrodes dipped into the charge, and the phosphorus vapour - P4 - is taken off, condensed under water and stored under water because it ignites in air. A 1980s US plant made 100,000-150,000 tonnes of yellow phosphorus a year, and the greater part of that went to phosphoric acid for fertiliser rather than to any electronics use.
children.note: Phosphate rock with sand and coke is heated to 1,200-1,500 C to give P4. Not established: the 30-100 MW furnace rating, the three graphite electrodes, the condensation and storage under water, and the 100,000-150,000 tonne per year US figure for a 1980s plant.

children.name: Phosphoric acid (the wet-process acid)
children.description: The wet process beats the phosphorus furnace, and it beats it because the furnace is only economical at a very large scale: ground phosphate rock is digested in 30-40% sulfuric acid, the calcium sulphate is filtered off as gypsum, and the phosphoric acid is concentrated to 54% P2O5. The C64-scale relevance of this acid is indirect - it is the fertiliser that came out of the phosphate rock, and it is also the semiconductor-grade acid a fab used for its own processes, purified further to 9N. Rock at 1-2 mm is digested in 30-40% sulphuric acid at 70-80 C and filtered, giving about 54% P2O5; the chemistry is a century old and limited by the solubility of calcium sulphate, so the gypsum cake is the waste stream and its disposal - often offshore or in a lined lagoon - is the industry's continuing environmental problem.
children.note: This acid chain is a fertiliser and commodity chain that is nominally outside this subsystem; it is included because the semiconductor-grade version is one of the fab's wet chemicals. Established: Wet process phosphoric acid from phosphate rock and sulphuric acid with gypsum byproduct. Not established: the stated acid strengths and filtration specifics as given.

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.note: Phosphine preparation routes include the hypophosphorous acid route and the phosphorus pentasulphide/caustic route; the latter is the common industrial one. Established: Phosphorus from arc furnace phosphate rock coke and silica with white phosphorus intermediate. Not established: the stated furnace temperatures and burning specifics as given.

chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cf4.fluori.name: Fluorine from fluorspar
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cf4.fluori.description: Every fluorine atom in a fab's chemistry started as calcium fluoride. Fluorspar is treated with concentrated sulphuric acid at 200-250 C in a kiln or a retort to make anhydrous hydrogen fluoride, and the HF is either sold as the aqueous etch acid or chlorinated with chlorine to make the CFCs and the fluorocarbons. It is the same sulphuric acid, the same chlorine and the same rock as the oxide etch, the freons in the packaging and the halogenated degreasers.
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cf4.fluori.note: Established: Every fluorine atom in a fabs chemistry started as calcium fluoride as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.fab-chemicals.nitric-acid.ostwald.name: Ostwald process
chem.fab-chemicals.nitric-acid.ostwald.description: Ammonia oxidised over a platinum-rhodium gauze at 800-900 C to nitric oxide, then to NO2 in excess air, then absorbed in water. Nitric acid is therefore an ammonia product, which means it is a natural-gas product: the Haber-Bosch ammonia of the 1980s was the source of the nitric acid and of the ammonium hydroxide, both of which a fab bought.

chem.fab-chemicals.sulfuric-acid.contact.name: Contact process and sulphur burning
chem.fab-chemicals.sulfuric-acid.contact.description: Sulphur is burned to SO2 in a 900-1,200 C furnace, converted over a vanadium pentoxide catalyst at 420-450 C to SO3, and absorbed in 98% acid to make oleum, which is then diluted. The feedstock in 1983 was overwhelmingly recovered elemental sulphur, because the Claus plant had made it cheap; earlier the pyrites (iron pyrite, FeS2) route was used, and a number of Japanese plants still burned pyrites into their own acid.
chem.fab-chemicals.sulfuric-acid.contact.note: The sulphur feedstock for sulphuric acid is chem.sulfur, and it arrives from the Claus plant. Industrial SO2 oxidation is carried out at about 420-620 C over vanadium(V) oxide catalysts, typically around 450 C, at near-atmospheric pressure. Not established: the 900-1,200 C sulphur burning furnace, the 98% acid oleum step, and the Japanese plants still burning pyrites into their own acid.

chem.solvents.cfc.cfc-synthesis.name: CFC synthesis from chloroform
chem.solvents.cfc.cfc-synthesis.description: CFC-11 (trichlorofluoromethane) is chloroform plus hydrogen fluoride in an antimony halide catalyst at 50-100 C; CFC-12 (dichlorodifluoromethane) is carbon tetrachloride plus hydrogen fluoride. Both therefore start from the chlorination of methane - the same methane the plastics industry buys - and both end in the ozone layer. The chain from a gas field to a chlorofluorocarbon is four steps long and it took twenty years of argument before anything was done about it.

children.name: Methane chlorination
children.description: Chlorine plus methane at 250-400 C gives chloromethane, and further chlorination gives chloroform and carbon tetrachloride. The chlorination is a free-radical chain reaction in a fluidised bed, and the product is a mixture that has to be distilled. The chloroform route to CFC-11 is therefore a natural gas route: methane, chlorine, fluorine - and fluorine is from fluorspar, the same rock as the HF that etched a silicon wafer. Methylene chloride, chloroform, carbon tetrachloride, the trichloroethane degreaser, vinyl chloride monomer and epichlorohydrin all start from the same brine electrolysis, and one electrochemical cell in a chemical park supplies the chlorine atom that appears in a dozen different industrial molecules.
children.note: The chlor-alkali chain is under chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-recovery.caustic-wash.chlor-alkali. Established: Methane chlorination as free radical chain to chloromethanes. Not established: the stated temperature ranges and distillation specifics as given.

chem.solvents.cfc.cfc-synthesis.note: Established: CFC-11 (trichlorofluoromethane) is chloroform plus hydrogen fluoride in an antimony halide catalyst at 50-100 C, CFC-12 (dichlorodifluoromethane) is carbon tetrachloride plus hydro as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.name: 1,1,1-Trichloroethane from acetylene
chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.description: The synthesis that links a degreaser to a natural gas field. Acetylene plus HCl over a mercuric chloride catalyst gives vinylidene chloride, CH2=CCl2, and chlorinating that with chlorine gives 1,1,1-trichloroethane. Both steps are the same chemistry, and the same catalyst, as the vinyl chloride process - and therefore so are the same upstream, the same natural gas and the same mercury liability. Vinylidene chloride plus chlorine at 20-50 C gives 1,1,2-trichloroethane first and then 1,1,1-trichloroethane, separated by distillation.
chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.note: Established: The synthesis that links a degreaser to a natural gas field as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.name: Making the FCC zeolite
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.description: A synthetic zeolite is not mined; it is crystallised. The reagents are an alumina source, a silica source, an alkali and a template, and the product is a 3-5 micron crystal of a lattice so regular that it was named after the mineral zeolite. The FCC catalyst's lattice is what makes it a shape-selective acid, and the same recipe with a different template and a different silica-to-alumina ratio gives the MFI zeolite of the styrene alkylation and the 3A sieve of the cracker drier. One family of chemistry, four jobs, and about a tenth of a tonne of catalyst per year for every 10,000 bbl/d of FCC capacity. The Y zeolite is grown from an aluminosilicate gel at 100-200 C with a seed and then dealuminated - by acid leaching, by chlorination with HCl or ammonium persulphate, or thermally with steam - to raise its silica-to-alumina ratio from about 5 to about 6-10.
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.note: Dealumination silica-to-alumina ratios vary by process and product; the values are representative of the era's USY. Established: Synthetic FCC zeolite crystallisation from alumina silica alkali and template. Not established: the stated crystal sizes and lattice specifics as given.

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.st.name: PZT-5 piezoelectric hydrophone element
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.st.description: Lead zirconate titanate ceramic discs, typically 25-50 mm diameter, epoxied onto a diaphragm and back-electrode in a silicone-oil-filled housing; sensitivity about -190 dB re 1 V/uPa in the 10-60 Hz band. Silicone oil here is one of the petrochemical elastomers/fluids, unrelated to the case material.
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.st.note: The silicone and epoxy cross-links are chem.silicone and chem.epoxy in this file. Established: PZT-5 piezoelectric hydrophone element as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s specifics as given.

chem.crude.separation.three-phase.demuls.name: Demulsifier chemistry
chem.crude.separation.three-phase.demuls.description: Nonylphenol- or alcohol-based surfactants dosed at 5-50 ppm to break the oil-water emulsion; in the 1980s a growing share of demulsifiers were polyalkoxyamine and polyglycol ethers. A stable water-in-oil emulsion (chocolate mousse) could hold 20-50% water into the crude and was the single largest quality loss on a wet field.
chem.crude.separation.three-phase.demuls.note: Not established: the dosing range quoted, the shift toward polyalkoxyamine and polyglycol ether demulsifiers in the 1980s, and the water content claimed for stable water-in-oil emulsions.

chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.a.name: Acetone as the selective solvent
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.a.description: The choice of solvent is a compromise. Acetone has a high acetylene solubility and a low methane solubility and a manageable vapour pressure, and it is made from cumene on the same site, which is the practical reason it was chosen. It is also flammable and it is a reproductive toxin, which is a modern objection to a molecule the industry has used since 1945.
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.a.note: Acetone's own route: chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.acetone. Established: Acetone as selective acetylene solvent for solubility and vapour pressure reasons. Not established: the stated cumene co-location and flammability handling specifics as given.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-r.name: The molten salt itself
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-r.description: A mixture of potassium nitrate, sodium nitrite and sometimes calcium nitrate, chosen for a melting point a little below the operating temperature and for a decomposition temperature a good deal above it. It is a beautiful heat-transfer medium and an oxidising one, and a small leak from the reactor puts hot nitrate into a hydrocarbon process - which is why the original SOVERE design was eventually superseded. The nitrate salts came from the same nitric acid that a fab's wet bench bought.
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-r.note: Salt compositions vary by licensor; the nitrate-nitrite family is the standard choice.

chem.crude.well-completion.packer.elasto.name: Packer elastomer (nitrile / HNBR)
chem.crude.well-completion.packer.elasto.description: A nitrile (acrylonitrile-butadiene) or HNBR element that swells or mechanically expands to grip the casing. Nitrile is the same chemistry as chem.butadiene in the polymer branch: acrylonitrile copolymerised with butadiene.
chem.crude.well-completion.packer.elasto.note: Cross-link: chem.butadiene. The nitrile rubber it is cut from is described under chem.butadiene; the copy of that node that used to sit here was folded away as a duplicate. Established: Packer elastomer nitrile HNBR as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s specifics as given.

chem.crude.rig.bit.tungsten-carbide.name: Tungsten carbide cutters and buttons
chem.crude.rig.bit.tungsten-carbide.description: WC-Co cemented carbide: 6-12% cobalt binder, 900-1,600 HV, pressed and sintered in a vacuum furnace then brazed onto the cone or into a milled-steel body. Cemented-carbide rock-bit consumption was the largest single use of tungsten carbide in the world in the 1980s, comparable to carbide tooling.

facts.label: Brazed to
facts.value: a cone, or a milled-steel body with carbide inserts on the three cones

chem.crude.rig.bit.tungsten-carbide.note: Not established: the binder range and hardness figures quoted for rock-bit carbide grades, and the claim about cemented-carbide rock-bit consumption relative to carbide tooling in the 1980s.

chem.crude.rig.bit.natural-diamond.name: Natural diamond (soft-formation bit)
chem.crude.rig.bit.natural-diamond.description: Gem-quality or bort diamond in a matrix of tungsten and cobalt sintered into a cone. Natural diamond bits dominate soft sandstone and were the standard drag-bit insert in 1980s drilling; synthetic (polycrystalline) diamond began to displace them in abrasive sandstone late in the decade.
chem.crude.rig.bit.natural-diamond.note: Established: Gem-quality or bort diamond in a matrix of tungsten and cobalt sintered into a cone as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.crude.rig.bit.pdc-bit.cutter.name: Polycrystalline diamond compact cutter
chem.crude.rig.bit.pdc-bit.cutter.description: Diamond powder sintered at 5,000-6,000 bar and 1,400-1,600 C with a cobalt metal catalyst from the diamond-graphite phase boundary. Over a 1980s field life a soft-formation PDC cutter could cut tens of kilometres of sandstone; hard-rock PDC arrived later with tungsten-carbide substrates and domed cutters.
chem.crude.rig.bit.pdc-bit.cutter.note: Not established: the sintering pressure and temperature ranges quoted, the cobalt catalyst detail, and the field-life distance claimed for 1980s soft-formation cutters.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.name: Cut points and the product slate
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.description: The fractions a refinery aims for, by boiling range: naphtha (C5 to about 200 F end point, roughly 30-40% of crude), kerosene/jet (200-300 F, 8-15%), gas oil (300-700 F, 20-30%), and the atmospheric residue (700 F plus, 25-40%). Naphtha is the fraction that matters to this tree: it is the steam-cracker feedstock, and its exact end point and sulphur decide whether a cracker will run at 800 or 850 C.

facts.label: Naphtha
facts.value: C5 / 33 C to 200-220 F end point; 30-40 vol% of crude

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.note: All the low boiling fractions of crude oil are separated by atmospheric distillation, vaporising below about 400 C at atmospheric pressure. Not established: the C5 and 200-220 F naphtha end point, the 30-40%, 8-15%, 20-30% and 25-40% yields, and the claim that naphtha end point and sulphur decide whether a cracker runs at 800 or 850 C.

chem.solvents.regulation.epa.name: US EPA VOC and solvent rules
chem.solvents.regulation.epa.simple_name: US EPA VOC and solvent rules
chem.solvents.regulation.epa.description: The 1970 Clean Air Act amendments listed chlorinated solvents as hazardous air pollutants, and the states' implementation plans in the early 1980s put specific limits on degreaser emissions. New Jersey's solvent programme in the early 1980s was the strictest of them and effectively banned chlorinated degreasers in much of the state. The federal halogenated solvent action followed, banning trichloroethylene vapour degreasing by 1990.
chem.solvents.regulation.epa.note: US solvent regulation is jurisdiction-specific and layered; the dates above are the commonly cited anchors rather than a single statute. A regulation or a treaty is a statement about the supply chain, not an operation in it.

chem.solvents.regulation.montreal.name: Montreal Protocol
chem.solvents.regulation.montreal.description: Signed in 1987, in force from 1989, and the most effective environmental treaty ever agreed. It phased out CFCs and halons, and it is the reason expanded polystyrene packaging lost its CFC blowing agent and the electronics plant lost its CFC cleaning gas. A C64 in 1983 was packed in a CFC-blown foam box; a C64 in 1993 was not. The most visible effect of the Protocol on a household object was in its packaging: until about 1987 the end caps and fitted inserts in consumer electronics cartons were expanded polystyrene blown with CFC-11, and pentane blowing took over, which made the foam softer and slightly heavier and pushed the structural part of the problem into the carton.
chem.solvents.regulation.montreal.note: The C64's corrugated shipping carton was a paperboard box; the polystyrene foam end caps in consumer electronics packaging of that era commonly used CFC or HCFC blowing agent. A regulation or a treaty is a statement about the supply chain, not an operation in it. Signed 16 September 1987, in force 1 January 1989, with the developed-country CFC phase-out complete by 1996. Not established: CFC-11 as the blowing agent in consumer-electronics polystyrene end caps and fitted inserts until about 1987, and pentane as the replacement that made the foam softer and heavier.

chem.solvents.regulation.occupational.name: Occupational exposure limits
chem.solvents.regulation.occupational.description: The other half of the story. In 1980s practice every one of these solvents had a 1980s-era recommended limit, every one of them was under active review by the ACGIH, and the direction of travel through the decade was downward. Perchloroethylene's limit fell from 400 to 100 ppm, trichloroethylene from 200 to 50 ppm, and methylene chloride from 500 to 250 ppm. The engineering response was local exhaust ventilation with a hooded enclosure and a solvent recovery unit, not a respirator. Every one of these solvents carried a recommended limit in the 1980s and every limit was under active review: perchloroethylene fell from 400 to 100 ppm, trichloroethylene from 200 to 50 ppm and methylene chloride from 500 to 250 ppm.
chem.solvents.regulation.occupational.note: The specific 1980s limit values changed year to year and differ between the ACGIH TLV and the OSHA PEL; the values here are indicative of the direction and magnitude of change. Exposure limits and their revision are commentary about the chain, not a step in it.

chem.solvents.regulation.epa.substitutes.name: The 1980s substitution: isopropanol, NMP, hydrocarbons
chem.solvents.regulation.epa.substitutes.description: What actually replaced the chlorinated degreasers, and why it took about ten years rather than two. The candidates were isopropyl alcohol, N-methylpyrrolidone, and increasingly hydrocarbon solvents and aqueous detergents. Each was available, each worked, and none of them was free: isopropanol is flammable, NMP has reproductive toxicity concerns, and hydrocarbons have a low flash point too. The substitution was driven by regulation and by the fact that a chlorinated degreaser needed a permit and an oxygen emission permit and a reporting line to the regulator, and by nothing else at all. The substitution was easy because it was a move along an existing supply chain: isopropyl alcohol sat next to the acetone plant in a complex that already had propylene, and the chlorinated solvent it replaced was the only one on the list that needed a mercury-catalysed acetylene route or a chlorine plant to make.
chem.solvents.regulation.epa.substitutes.note: This node summarises a substitution whose timetable varied by country and by sector; it is a direction-of-travel statement rather than a dated claim. The substitution of isopropanol, NMP and hydrocarbons for the chlorinated solvents is a statement about what industry did.

chem.refining.products.lubricants.name: Lubricant base oils
chem.refining.products.lubricants.description: Distillate fractions solvent-extracted (2,700-5,000 Ns at 100 C) and hydrofinished, or in the 1980s increasingly hydroisomerised. The C64 link is not the lubricant in the gearbox but the fact that the same hydrofinishing catalysts and the same additive chemistry (zinc dialkyldithiophosphate, made from phosphorus pentasulphide) appear in the machine's grease and in the rubber and plastic stabilisers.
chem.refining.products.lubricants.note: The C64-scale claims here are inferential; the base-oil processes described are standard but the specific link to a 1983 consumer machine's lubricants is not documented in the sources used here.

chem.refining.products.waxes.name: Petroleum waxes and slack wax
chem.refining.products.waxes.description: Waxy distillate from solvent deasphalting, deoiled on a centrifuge train to give hard, medium and soft paraffin wax and microcrystalline wax. Slack wax goes into paper, board and packaging film; the microcrystalline waxes are the petroleum fraction that was blended into the first generation of hot-melt adhesives.
chem.refining.products.waxes.note: Not established: the deasphalting, deoiling and fractionation sequence described, and the end-use claims for slack wax and microcrystalline wax in paper, packaging and early hot-melt adhesives.

chem.refining.products.fuel-oil.name: Fuel oil
chem.refining.products.fuel-oil.description: The bottom of the barrel: a 1-3% sulphur residue sold to power stations and ships. After 1973, and especially after the 1980s tanker accidents, the political life of fuel oil in Europe and the US got hard, and the refinery's answer was more conversion. In 1983 fuel oil still took about 25-30% of world refinery production.
chem.refining.products.fuel-oil.note: The fuel-oil share of 1983 refinery output and the regulatory context are order-of-magnitude figures; exact shares varied widely by region.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Discovering and drilling a gas field
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: Gas fields are found by the same seismic and drilled with the same rig as oil fields, but the completion differs: the log response that proves a gas column is high resistivity with low neutron density, and the well must be tested for absolute gas flow rather than liquid rate. Gas viscosity is about a hundred times lower than oil but its compressibility ten times higher, so the well responds to drawdown very differently. Gas sands are often visible before they are drilled, because gas lowers the acoustic impedance of the rock so the reflector dims and sometimes inverts; the amplitude anomaly is also produced by a shale lens or a tuning effect, which is why the prospect still had to be drilled. The casing and completion hardware is identical to an oil well but the discipline is not: a gas well perforated below the point of no return has to be tested to destruction of casing and tubing, because the column is light and there is no fluid level to swallow a leak. A wellhead separator and a test separator drop the liquid out of the gas at 30-70 bar before the gas goes to a knockout drum and the gathering system; the liquid is the same crude or condensate as in the oil case.

children.name: Sweetening to pipeline specification
children.description: H2S and CO2 are removed with a 20-35 wt% alkanolamine in an absorber at 30-45 C and 20-70 bar, with the rich amine regenerated at 120-130 C and 1.5-2 bar in a reboiler. By the early 1980s the trend was to diethanolamine for economy and MDEA for lower heat duty and no carbamate degradation.
children.note: Established: H2S and CO2 are removed with a 20-35 wt% alkanolamine in an absorber at 30-45 C and 20-70 bar, with the rich amine regenerated at 120-130 C and 1.5-2 bar in a reboiler as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Dehydration to pipeline dew point
children.description: Gas must arrive at the pipeline dew point or the higher-pressure steps downstream condense water out and the line fills with liquid. By 1980s practice that meant a glycol unit (triethylene glycol at 80-95 wt% purity, contactor at 20-50 C and 40-70 bar, reboiler 120-140 C) and increasingly a 3A or 4A molecular sieve adsorption unit for the last kilogram of water per million standard cubic metres.
children.note: Established: Gas must arrive at the pipeline dew point or the higher-pressure steps downstream condense water out and the line fills with liquid as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.note: The seismic acquisition chain is shared with the oil branch: chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey. Established: Gas discovery using shared seismic and rig with gas specific logging and flow testing. Not established: the stated log responses and absolute flow test specifics as given.

chem.crude.rig.rotary-drilling.name: Rotary drilling
chem.crude.rig.rotary-drilling.description: A rotary table or top drive turns the string at 30-150 rpm with 10-40 kN-m torque while 200-450 kN of weight is set off the bit. Weight-on-bit and torque are the two variables the driller steers with; the drilling engineer watches torque and bit exponent while the driller watches penetration rate.

children.name: Drill string
children.description: Drill pipe, drill collars and a bit, threaded or coupled API 5-1/2 in and 6-5/8 in in the 1980s, with 3-1/2 in drill collar subs. Length is a queue of 5,000-7,000 m of 5 in pipe plus 200-400 m of collars; the string must be strong enough for tensile load at the maximum string weight yet remain within the derrick.
children.note: Drill pipe steel is a metals chain, not a petrochemical one; the petroleum-derived material here is the mud, the cement and the bit matrix. Established: Drill string as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s specifics as given.

children.name: Mud circulation system
children.description: Active and reserve pits, the pump, the surface mixing hopper (mud pit) and the flowline over the shaker. 1980s volumes for a single rig were 400-1,500 m3 of active mud with 150-400 m3 of reserve, and the pit room needed chemical dosing, dilution and waste disposal for one well's worth of chemically treated clay.
children.note: Established: Active and reserve pits, the pump, the surface mixing hopper (mud pit) and the flowline over the shaker as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.crude.rig.rotary-drilling.note: Established: A rotary table or top drive turns the string at 30-150 rpm with 10-40 kN-m torque while 200-450 kN of weight is set off the bit as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.name: Casing and cementing
chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.description: Steel casing is run to isolate the hole and to carry the pressure; cement is pumped between casing and formation (and sometimes inside the casing) to seal the annulus. Without a good cement job the whole completion leaks and stimulation injects into the wrong zone. Cementing is one of the few oilfield jobs that is nearly a repeatability disaster: 10-30% of wells take a cement squeeze.

children.name: Casing string and cement sheath
children.description: Conductor, surface, intermediate and production casing, each cemented across its shoe. The C64-scale point: even a modest producing well consumes tens to hundreds of tonnes of cement and hundreds of metres of steel, dwarfing the machine it ultimately supplies.
children.note: Established: Conductor, surface, intermediate and production casing, each cemented across its shoe as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.note: Established: Steel casing is run to isolate the hole and to carry the pressure, cement is pumped between casing and formation (and sometimes inside the casing) to seal the annulus as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.crude.rig.core-drilling.name: Core drilling and coring
chem.crude.rig.core-drilling.description: Diamond core barrels cut 1-4 in core in a special drilling string, giving the reservoir rock, its porosity, its saturation and its capillary properties undamaged. A cored well is the most expensive way to get reservoir data, so it was used on 1-3 wells out of 20 and almost always on the discovery well.

children.name: Diamond core barrel
children.description: A steel or aluminium tube with a diamond-set reaming shell and a core lifter, run on the bottom hole assembly at low RPM (20-100) and low weight. Carbit tungsten-carbide bits dominated abrasive sandstone, PCD for softer beds, and set diamond for carbonate.
children.note: Established: A steel or aluminium tube with a diamond-set reaming shell and a core lifter, run on the bottom hole assembly at low RPM (20-100) and low weight as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.crude.rig.core-drilling.note: Established: Diamond core barrels cut 1-4 in core in a special drilling string, giving the reservoir rock, its porosity, its saturation and its capillary properties undamaged as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.propylene.polymerisation.loops-and-.name: Slurry loop, gas phase and slurry reactor
chem.propylene.polymerisation.loops-and-.description: The 1980s reactor competition: the slurry loop (heptane diluent, polymer as a slurry, then solvent recovery and devolatilising), the loop slurry with 30-50% solids, and the gas-phase fluidised bed with no solvent at all. The gas-phase process was the 1980s newcomer and its whole commercial case was the elimination of the solvent recovery section.
chem.propylene.polymerisation.loops-and-.note: Not established: the solids-content range quoted for loop slurry operation, and the commercial characterisation of the gas-phase process as the 1980s newcomer whose case rested on eliminating solvent recovery.

chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.barrel-etc.name: The barrel plasma etcher
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.barrel-etc.description: A quartz or alumina tube with electrodes at the top and bottom, gas fed in at the top, RF at 13.56 MHz, and wafers standing vertically in slots around the tube wall. It was the workhorse of the 1980s for silicon dioxide and aluminium etching and for resist ashing, and it was cheap, simple and gently non-uniform - which was acceptable when the field of view was small and the line was a couple of microns. The planar (magnetron) etcher, where the plasma is generated above the wafer by a magnetically confined source, gave the flatness that a later generation of chips needed.
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.barrel-etc.note: Plasma etching uses RF excitation at 13.56 MHz, and a fluorine-bearing gas etches silicon dioxide selectively in conjunction with photolithography. Not established: the quartz or alumina barrel with top and bottom electrodes, the vertical wafer slots, the 0.1-10 torr range, and the barrel's description as the workhorse of the 1980s.

chem.crude.rig.bit.name: Drill bits
chem.crude.rig.bit.description: The cutting tool at the bottom of the string. In 1980s practice a soft-formation bit was a sealed journal bearing with a cone of natural diamond, a medium bit a sealed or unsealed mud turbine with tungsten-carbide nose buttons, and a hard rock bit a milled-steel body with tungsten-carbide inserts on the three cones.

children.name: PDC (polycrystalline diamond compact) bit
children.description: The emerging bit of the early 1980s: sintered diamond compact cutters brazed to a steel body with no cones and no bearings, turning rather than grinding. PDC began as a hard-rock bit, spread into soft rock in the mid-1980s and largely replaced roller cones in soft formations by the early 1990s. In 1983 it was perhaps 10-20% of the market.
children.note: Established: The emerging bit of the early 1980s: sintered diamond compact cutters brazed to a steel body with no cones and no bearings, turning rather than grinding as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.crude.rig.bit.note: Established: The cutting tool at the bottom of the string as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.crude.rig.pressure-control.name: Well control: BOP, diverter and kill
chem.crude.rig.pressure-control.description: The blowout preventer stack (annular preventer plus 3-5 ram preventers) and the choke manifold above the wellhead, rated 5,000-15,000 psi. Before the 1970s and 1980s safety emphasis, the classic profile was a vertical string, overbalanced mud and a diverter; 1980s practice added the above-the-bit diverter packoff for kick tolerance.
chem.crude.rig.pressure-control.note: Established: The blowout preventer stack (annular preventer plus 3-5 ram preventers) and the choke manifold above the wellhead, rated 5,000-15,000 psi as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

chem.crude.name: Crude oil: finding it, drilling it, lifting it
chem.crude.description: The upstream end of the chain. Seismic surveys pick a structure, a rig drills a 5-7 km hole through rock, casing and cement line the hole, the well is completed and perforated into the reservoir, then often artificially stimulated. An 8 kg C64 case corresponds to only 1-3 litres of crude oil, but that crude was found under 5-10 km of overburden using a drilling rig that cost tens of millions of dollars.

children.name: Petroleum exploration
children.description: Finding a commercial accumulation of oil before spending the exploration well. In 1980s practice this was reflection seismology over regional grids, closed by wildcat drilling. Cost per barrel discovered had fallen from tens of dollars to roughly $2-8 by the early 1980s. A mud-logging unit beside the rig sampled cuttings and gas continuously with a hot-wire or infrared hydrocarbon detector, and it was the shows it found that decided whether to run a full log suite.

children.name: Reflection seismic survey
children.description: A surface source sends a pressure wave down through the rock section; reflectors return it to hydrophones and the travel times are stacked into a two-dimensional depth section. Seismic is a time-domain method: it maps reflectivity contrasts (sandstone/shale, gas-sand amplitude dimming) and gives no direct information about fluid type. The record was stacked and migrated on a mainframe or minicomputer: common-midpoint stacking, normal-moveout correction from velocity analysis, deconvolution and depth conversion, with the 1980s emphasis on multiple suppression and on early 3-D, where a single field cost $1-3 million per acre-foot. A log response indicating oil or gas - high resistivity, low neutron density, a gas effect on the seismic - is a test, not a discovery: a discovery needed a producing well, and industry experience was one test in eight to one in thirty commercial.

children.name: Seismic vibrator truck
children.description: A truck-mounted hydraulic vibrator sweeps 10-80 Hz into the ground under hold-and-hold conditions; on land it replaced explosive shot holes because it gave repeatable, higher-energy sources with no shothole cleanup. Regionally a 1,000-2,000 m shotpoint spacing was normal in 1980s 2-D work.
children.note: Established: truck-mounted hydraulic vibrators sweeping frequency into the ground are the standard land vibroseis source replacing explosive shot holes for repeatability. Not established: the stated 10-80 Hz sweep range, hold conditions, and 1,000-2,000 m regional shotpoint spacing as 1980s practice.

children.name: Airgun and marine seismic source
children.description: Offshore and in shallow water the source was a 1,000-10,000 cu-in (16-160 litre) airgun array fired every 10-15 s from the stern of a seismic vessel. Compressed air from compressor trucks on deck; a single 1980s 3-D crew vessel carried up to four sources.
children.note: Established: Offshore and in shallow water the source was a 1,000-10,000 cu-in (16-160 litre) airgun array fired every 10-15 s from the stern of a seismic vessel as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Dynamite shothole source
children.description: Still used for small onshore surveys in the early 1980s: 0.5-5 kg of packaged explosive in a borehole, fired from a firing truck, with the shot hole re-drilled for the next shot. Cheap per shot but slow, noisy and it polluted a producing field's drill cuttings.
children.note: Established: Still used for small onshore surveys in the early 1980s: 0.5-5 kg of packaged explosive in a borehole, fired from a firing truck, with the shot hole re-drilled for the next shot as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Marine seismic streamer and hydrophone cable
children.description: A towed cable up to 3 km long carrying hundreds of hydrophone elements at 12.5-25 m groups; it was a synthetic-fibre-wrapped, oil-filled or water-filled analogue/digital telemetry line whose integrity was the limiting factor on data quality. Hydrophone elements used piezoelectric ceramic (PZT-5) discs coupled to silicone oil in a pressure-compensated housing.
children.note: Established: A towed cable up to 3 km long carrying hundreds of hydrophone elements at 12.5-25 m groups, it was a synthetic-fibre-wrapped, oil-filled or water-filled analogue/digital telemetry as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Seismic geophone array
children.description: On land, 12 to 48 groups of 10-60 Hz moving-coil geophones per station, each on a spike planted in a levelled hole, cabled and buried. In 1980s 2-D the fold of coverage (usually 6-fold to 24-fold) was chosen by geophone group interval and source spacing, not by 3-D binning.

children.name: Moving-coil geophone
children.description: A 1-2 kg mass suspended in a magnetic field inside a case 3-5 cm across; coil movement induces a signal proportional to ground velocity. A second coil acts as a position feedback for the servo. Cost per channel in the early 1980s was several hundred to a few thousand dollars.
children.note: Established: A 1-2 kg mass suspended in a magnetic field inside a case 3-5 cm across, coil movement induces a signal proportional to ground velocity as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Geophone takeout cable and junction box
children.description: Polythene-insulated multi-pair takeout cable to a junction box, then a line-trap and telemetry radio link to the recording truck. Cable insulation here is polyethylene from the same steam-cracking chain as the C64's power cord jacket.
children.note: Polyethylene: chem.ethylene.polyethylene in this file. Established: Geophone takeout cable and junction box as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s specifics as given.

Established: On land, 12 to 48 groups of 10-60 Hz moving-coil geophones per station, each on a spike planted in a levelled hole, cabled and buried as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Seismic recording system
children.description: Field recording on 1/2 in or 1 in nine-track magnetic tape (typically 2000 inch/s, 12.5-50 Hz bandwidth) or, from the early 1980s, 12-bit digital field recorders writing 3M/IBM-compatible cartridges. The whole array recorded simultaneously; it was common for the record to be demultiplexed and copied to a computer tape for onshore stacking.
children.note: Established: Field recording on 1/2 in or 1 in nine-track magnetic tape (typically 2000 inch/s, 12.5-50 Hz bandwidth) or, from the early 1980s, 12-bit digital field recorders writing 3M/IBM-com as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

Established: reflection seismic surveying maps subsurface reflectors using surface sources and receivers including vibrators airguns and dynamite. Not established: the stated tonnages dates temperatures pressures yields and 1980s operating details as given.

children.name: Exploration (wildcat) well
children.description: The first hole into a prospect. Cheap success-failure logging with mud logging and core, drilled to the deepest prognosis rather than the shallowest pay. Exploration wells in the early 1980s averaged about 3,000-5,000 m of hole and took 30-90 days offshore.

children.name: Wildcat cost and success statistics
children.description: A North Sea or Gulf of Mexico wildcat cost $3-20 million in the early 1980s; the historical industry success rate was about 1 in 10 wells dry, 1 in 15 total wildcats a commercial discovery, and about 1 in 8 wildcats found non-commercial hydrocarbons. Exploration cost per barrel discovered was roughly $2-8.
children.note: A cost and success rate is a statement about the industry, not a substance you can weigh.
Established: The first hole into a prospect as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Reserve estimation
children.description: Volumetric and material-balance estimates, presented to a board and to governments as proved, probable and possible reserves. Rules of thumb: recovery factor 15-35% of oil-in-place for a sandstone reservoir, higher (35-60%) for a fractured carbonate. Reserve booking was and remains a commercial and legal judgement, not a measurement. The volumetric calculation behind all of it is pore volume x oil saturation x formation volume factor, and B_o for a light crude at reservoir temperature is 1.1-1.3, so reservoir barrels convert to stock-tank barrels at a meaningful ratio; saturation is the least measurable input and the most sensitive.

children.name: Reserve uncertainty and contingency
children.description: Undiscovered reserves behind existing fields were treated as of similar magnitude to proved reserves. The industry view of world ultimately-recoverable oil in 1983 was around 1,500-2,000 billion stock-tank barrels, versus about 700 billion produced or proved.
children.note: Reserve uncertainty and a world ultimately-recoverable figure are commentary about reserve booking.

Not established: the recovery-factor ranges quoted for sandstone versus fractured carbonate reservoirs, the formation volume factor range for light crude, and which estimation method any particular early-1980s operator applied to a given field.

Established: Finding a commercial accumulation of oil before spending the exploration well as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: The drilling rig
children.description: Rotary drilling: the drill string is rotated from the surface, the bit mills a hole, mud circulates to carry cuttings out and to control formation pressure. Offshore this is a jack-up, a semisubmersible or a drillship; onshore it is a land rig with a derrick. 1980s rigs reached 6,000-7,500 m total depth on routine programs.

children.name: Rig types and their 1980s cost
children.description: Jack-up rigs (4-6 legs, 60-90 m water-depth limit) and fixed derricks onshore; semisubmersibles (700-1,000 m, self-propelled, expensive); drillships (ice-strengthened, for deep water and harsh climates). Costs in the early 1980s: onshore rig $1-3 million, jack-up $20-45 million, drillship $30-70 million, semisubmersible $60-120 million. Offshore dayrates in 1983 ran $25,000-60,000 a day.
children.note: Rig newbuild prices moved violently through 1981-83 (a deepwater rig that cost $60m in 1980 was quoted above $100m in 1983); treat these as order-of-magnitude figures.

Established: rotary drilling rigs drill oil wells with rotating drill string bit and circulating mud with onshore derricks and offshore jackups semisubmersibles and drillships. Not established: the stated tonnages dates temperatures pressures yields and 1980s operating details as given.

children.name: Well completion
children.description: Turning a drilled hole into a producing well: set production casing, cement to the pay, run and perforate the tubing, pack the annulus, and install a tree. This is where the reservoir is deliberately connected to the borehole for the first time. A completed well was logged with spinner and turbine flowmeters, noise logs and temperature logs, and tested with a multi-hour rate and pressure buildup.

children.name: Perforation
children.description: Shaped charges fired down the casing to punch 1-3 cm holes through steel, cement and formation in one shot, linking pay zone to borehole. A 1980s completion might be 4-6 perforations per metre of pay; perforation is done in stages so only the best footage is shot.

children.name: Shaped-charge perforator
children.description: A copper or steel cone lined with a high explosive (RDX/HMX or HMX-wax, 5-30 g per shot in the 1980s) with a steel or ceramic liner; the detonated cone forms a copper or tungsten-alloy jet at 8-10 km/s which drills the hole. Charges were fired on a wireline in a gun barrel or in a TCP (tubing conveyed perforator).
children.note: Charge weight and composition varied widely with depth and rock toughness; the jet mechanism is well established.

children.name: Entry hole into the pay zone
children.simple_name: Entry hole into the pay zone
children.description: The first connection to the reservoir is itself a jet-perforated hole in cement, and it is the smallest diameter in the whole production system: a few millimetres through which the entire well flow must pass.
children.note: Established: jet perforated entry hole through cement as the first reservoir connection and smallest flow diameter. Not established: the stated few millimetre diameter carrying entire well flow as a general figure.

Established: Shaped charges fired down the casing to punch 1-3 cm holes through steel, cement and formation in one shot, linking pay zone to borehole as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Packer and completion hardware
children.description: An elastomer-sealed packer run and set in the casing to isolate zones and provide a seat for the tubing hanger. In 1980s completions this was single- or dual-packer tubing with sliding sleeves or selective stimulation, increasingly mechanical rather than hydraulic.
children.note: Established: An elastomer-sealed packer run and set in the casing to isolate zones and provide a seat for the tubing hanger as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Christmas tree (wellhead assembly)
children.description: The valve stack on top of the casing: casing spool, tubing spool, master valve, wing valves with gauges, and the flowline tee off the wing. Every stream the well ever produces has to pass through this steel gatework, which is why it is the most pressure-rated cluster of parts in the business.

facts.label: Parts count
facts.value: 80-200 components, several hundred kg of forged steel

children.note: Established: The valve stack on top of the casing: casing spool, tubing spool, master valve, wing valves with gauges, and the flowline tee off the wing as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

Established: Turning a drilled hole into a producing well: set production casing, cement to the pay, run and perforate the tubing, pack the annulus, and install a tree as standard practice. Not established: the era specific prevalence supplier choices and detailed operating splits as given.

children.name: Well stimulation: fracturing and acidising
children.description: Almost no reservoir delivers its whole potential through a millimetre perforation. Stimulation makes the rock permeable by fracture or by dissolving the rock; it is one of the biggest single levers on oil and gas supply and it consumes enormous volumes of water, sand and, for acidising, corrosive acid. Heavy oil and tar sands were stimulated with steam at 250-350 C, injected, soaked and then produced on at Cold Lake and Athabasca scale; one steam cycle costs several tonnes of water and roughly 0.5-1 barrel of 60% fuel oil per tonne of steam.

children.name: Hydraulic fracturing
children.description: A water-based or gel fluid pumped down the casing into the pay, then into the perforations at 40-100 bbl/min and up to 6,000-10,000 psi surface pressure to part the rock; a proppant is carried in to hold the fracture open when pressure is released. Born in 1947 (experiments) and industrialised in the late 1950s (Massive Hydraulic Fracturing, 1961-1965), by the 1980s it was routine on low-permeability gas reservoirs and increasingly common on oil wells. A big 1980s job used 10,000-100,000 bbl of fluid and 500-2,000 tonnes of sand. A propped fracture's job is conductivity times length: the first fractures were vertical and planar, so 1980s design moved to multiple parallel fractures per zone, and conductive area had to be raised by resin-coated proppant or by larger grains because proppant embedment in soft rock closed fractures within months.

children.name: Fracturing pumping equipment
children.description: Blender trucks, sand trucks and a high-pressure pump unit (one pumping unit at 25,000 psi), laid out in a yard over the rig. A 1980s job mobilised 10-40 trucks and 100-200 people, and it was the largest single water consumer in the oilfield outside steam flooding.
children.note: Established: Blender trucks, sand trucks and a high-pressure pump unit (one pumping unit at 25,000 psi), laid out in a yard over the rig as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

Established: hydraulic fracturing parts rock with high pressure fluid carrying proppant sand to hold fractures open for oil and gas flow. Not established: the stated tonnages dates temperatures pressures yields and 1980s operating details as given.

children.name: Matrix acidising and fracture acidising
children.description: Hydrochloric or hydrofluoric acid injected to dissolve or acid-fracture the rock, typically 15-28% HCl in sandstone and HF-containing mud acid in carbonate. Sandstone acidising only reached the late 1970s as a standard service; carbonate mud-acid fracturing with a 12% HCl-3% HF system had become the standard carbonate treatment by the mid-1980s. Placement mattered more than chemistry: acid was bullheaded down casing or coiled-tubed into the perforation tunnels, and because HF precipitates calcium fluoride a 1.2-1.5 m HCl preflush was always pumped first to keep calcium out of the rock.
children.note: Established: Hydrochloric or hydrofluoric acid injected to dissolve or acid-fracture the rock, typically 15-28% HCl in sandstone and HF-containing mud acid in carbonate as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

Heavy-oil thermal work existed but was marginal to light-sour supply; the numbers are order-of-magnitude. Established: Well stimulation fracturing and acidising as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s specifics as given.

children.name: Wellhead and terminal separation
children.description: The wellstream arrives at 15-100 bar and 60-100 C as an oil/gas/water froth. It is separated in stages: test separator, stock tanks, heaters and desalters, gas-oil separator, and finally a train of electrostatic and coalescing vessels that make a storable crude. Field separation is where the crude assay is determined and where the oil is counted.

children.name: Test separator
children.description: The first vessel, sized 1-5% of the field's liquid capacity, where the wellstream is bled at 25-70 bar to a stable pressure and temperature. Its records are the raw data for reservoir performance, gas-oil ratio and oil assay. A field with 100,000 bbl/d of oil needed a test separator of a few hundred bbl.
children.note: Established: The first vessel, sized 1-5% of the fields liquid capacity, where the wellstream is bled at 25-70 bar to a stable pressure and temperature as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Three-phase separator and stock tanks
children.description: A horizontal or vertical vessel at 2-10 bar with a mechanical or electrostatic coalescing section that separates oil, gas and water, then atmospheric storage tanks that settle the remaining water and sediment. Stock tank bottoms and the settled water carry the production's salt and heavy ends, and their disposal was the field's environmental problem in the 1980s.
children.note: Established: A horizontal or vertical vessel at 2-10 bar with a mechanical or electrostatic coalescing section that separates oil, gas and water, then atmospheric storage tanks that settle the as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Heater-treater and desalter
children.description: A crude preheater to 150-200 C followed by a settler and then a desalter, where the crude is washed with recycled water to strip salts. Needed because sour Middle East crudes carry 1-3 wt% dissolved salts, and because naphthenic acids plus water at 200 C will corrode the hot exchanger on the way to the refinery. A crude desalter separates maybe 90-95% of the salt in one stage.
children.note: Established: A crude preheater to 150-200 C followed by a settler and then a desalter, where the crude is washed with recycled water to strip salts as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Electrostatic coalescer (electrogravitational)
children.description: Charged droplets are attracted into the water phase, collapsing the emulsion in seconds instead of hours. Small pipeline electrocoalescers were introduced in the mid-1980s for crude pretreatment, cutting the demulsifier dose; they were used in 1980s practice wherever the crude conductivity allowed (hence electrogravitational not electrocoalescing for most crudes).
children.note: High-conductivity crudes could not be electrocoalesced in the 1980s; that limitation is why electrogravitational units (large DACC-type vessels) were preferred for crude.

children.name: Oil-water coalescer
children.description: A packed or membrane device that lets separated water droplets out of the crude without carrying oil. Produced-water disposal in 1983 was to a pit or a treatment plant; the offshore discharge limit under the 1983 amendments to the US Clean Water Act required 42 ppm oil and no visible sheen, which is why coalescers and hydrocyclones appeared on offshore platforms.
children.note: The 42 ppm / 30 ppm benchmark figures for produced-water oil content are the long-standing offshore standard; the 1983 date for that particular rule reference is a common citation but the precise effective date varies by jurisdiction.

Established: The wellstream arrives at 15-100 bar and 60-100 C as an oil/gas/water froth as a type. Not established: the stated figures conditions purities yields tonnages dates and 1980s practice specifics as given.

children.name: Crude assay
children.description: What the seller is paid for: a barrel of crude is specified by a handful of standardised numbers, and every downstream decision - which cracker, which desulphuriser, whether it can be shipped - is made from them. Density and API gravity set the transport economics, sulphur splits sweet from sour, the simulated boiling curve sets the cut points, the trace metals set the catalyst life, and the cold-flow properties decide whether it can be pumped.

facts.label: Light sweet reference
facts.value: West Texas Light 40 deg API, 0.3% S

children.note: The five standard measurements are API gravity, sulphur, simulated distillation, Conradson carbon residue and pour point, and their numbers are facts of this node. Its from edge is the crude it measures. Established: Crude assay as a type. Not established: the stated API sulphur distillation carbon residue pour point figures as generally verified.

children.name: One Commodore 64's share of the wellhead
children.description: The plastic mass of a C64 is about 350-400 g of ABS in the case plus 100-200 g in the keys, and ABS comes from roughly 2 kg of crude oil per kilogram of polymer. Add the energy to make it, the fuel to ship it and the polymer's own energy in the burning, and one machine corresponds to roughly 1-3 litres of crude oil - about one minute of production on a small Arabian field, and undetectable in the world oil balance. This node is the reminder that the whole upstream industry exists to supply a mass flow, not a concept.

facts.label: Crude per kg of ABS
facts.value: about 2 kg crude (mass balance across cracker to polymer)
